title: Basic Water Resources Engineering — practice questions
$comment: Answer positions were distributed while authoring, per the discipline recorded after the chapter 1 bank was found to key 55% of its questions to option (b).

questions.stem: Newton's law of viscosity states that the shear stress in a fluid is proportional to the:
questions.solution:
**The RATE of shear strain — the velocity gradient du/dy.**

> **τ = μ (du/dy)**

**This is the defining difference between a fluid and a solid**, and it is worth stating precisely:

| | **SOLID** | **FLUID** |
|---|---|---|
| Stress is proportional to | **STRAIN** (Hooke: τ = G γ) | **RATE OF STRAIN** (Newton: τ = μ dγ/dt) |
| Under a constant shear stress | Deforms a **finite amount** and **stops** | **Deforms CONTINUOUSLY** — it flows |
| At rest | Can sustain shear | **Cannot sustain any shear stress** |

> **A fluid is a substance that DEFORMS CONTINUOUSLY under ANY shear stress, however small.** That is the definition, and everything else follows from it.

**The consequence for a fluid at rest** is immediate and is the foundation of hydrostatics:

> If a fluid at rest could sustain shear it would flow — so **a fluid at rest has NO shear stress**, and the only stress is the **normal** stress, which is the **pressure**. That is why hydrostatic pressure acts **equally in all directions** (Pascal's law).

**Dynamic viscosity μ:**

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **SI unit** | **Pa·s** = N·s/m² = kg/(m·s) |
| **CGS unit** | **poise** (P); **1 Pa·s = 10 poise** |
| Water at 20 °C | **1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s** = 1 centipoise |
| Air at 20 °C | 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ Pa·s |

**Kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ**, with SI unit **m²/s** and CGS unit **stokes** (1 m²/s = 10⁴ stokes). Water at 20 °C: **1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s**.

**Note that air is about 55 times LESS viscous than water in DYNAMIC terms but about 15 times MORE viscous in KINEMATIC terms** — because air's density is so much lower. Which viscosity matters depends on the problem: **dynamic** viscosity governs the shear stress, **kinematic** viscosity governs the diffusion of momentum and appears in the Reynolds number.

**Fluid classification by the τ – du/dy relationship:**

| Type | Behaviour | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **NEWTONIAN** | **τ ∝ du/dy**, straight line **through the origin** | **Water, air, oil**, most common fluids |
| **Dilatant** (shear-thickening) | Viscosity **increases** with shear rate | Starch suspension, wet sand |
| **Pseudoplastic** (shear-thinning) | Viscosity **decreases** with shear rate | Paint, blood, polymer solutions |
| **BINGHAM PLASTIC** | Needs a **YIELD STRESS** before flowing at all | **Toothpaste, drilling mud, fresh CONCRETE, sewage sludge** |
| Ideal fluid | **μ = 0**, no shear stress ever | A **hypothetical** fluid; a useful idealisation |

**The Bingham plastic is the one a civil engineer meets most often**: **fresh concrete** will not flow until the applied stress exceeds a yield value, which is exactly why it can be placed on a slope and hold its shape, and why the **slump test** measures something meaningful.

examTip.trap: "Shear strain" is the deliberate near-miss — that is **Hooke's law for a SOLID**. A fluid responds to the **rate** of strain.
examTip.trick: That one word is the whole definition of a fluid: a solid deforms a finite amount and stops; a fluid **keeps deforming** under any shear, however small.
examTip.mnemonic: **Solid: stress ∝ strain. Fluid: stress ∝ RATE of strain.** It follows immediately that a fluid **at rest carries no shear** — which is the foundation of all hydrostatics.

questions.stem: A plate 0.5 m² in area moves at 2 m/s over a fixed surface, separated by an oil film 1 mm thick of viscosity 0.1 Pa·s. The force required is:
questions.solution:
**100 N.**

**Assuming a linear velocity profile across the thin film:**

> **du/dy = U/t = 2 / 0.001 = 2000 s⁻¹**
> **τ = μ (du/dy) = 0.1 × 2000 = 200 Pa**
> **F = τ A = 200 × 0.5 = 100 N**

**Two assumptions were made, and both are worth naming:**

| Assumption | Justification |
|---|---|
| **Linear velocity profile** | Valid for a **THIN film** — the profile has no room to curve |
| **NO-SLIP** at both surfaces | The fluid **sticks** to the boundary: velocity **U at the plate, 0 at the fixed surface** |

**The no-slip condition** is fundamental and worth stating:

> A **real (viscous) fluid in contact with a solid boundary has ZERO velocity RELATIVE to that boundary.** The fluid does not slide along the surface; it adheres to it.

**Everything about viscous flow follows from no-slip**: it is what creates the **velocity gradient**, hence the **shear stress**, hence the **drag** on every surface and the **head loss** in every pipe. Without it there would be no boundary layer, no friction factor, and no need for pumps.

**Watch the units**, which is where this calculation is most often lost:

| Quantity | Correct unit | Common error |
|---|---|---|
| Film thickness | **0.001 m** | Leaving it in **mm**, giving 0.1 N |
| μ | **Pa·s** | Confusing with **poise** (÷10) |
| du/dy | **s⁻¹** | — |

**A variant worth knowing — the torque on a rotating shaft in a bearing:**

> **τ = μ (πDN/60) / t** where πDN/60 is the surface speed
> **Torque T = τ × (πDL) × (D/2)**, and **Power = 2πNT/60**

since the shear stress acts over the curved surface area πDL at a radius D/2. The same physics, in cylindrical geometry — and the basis of journal bearing design.

**A second variant — a plate midway between two fixed surfaces**: the shear acts on **both** faces, so the force is **doubled**. And a plate at an unequal distance from two surfaces has different gradients on each face, which must be added:

> **F = μUA(1/t₁ + 1/t₂)**

**The physical reading of the result**: 100 N to drag half a square metre at walking speed over a millimetre of thin oil. Halve the film thickness and the force **doubles** — which is why bearing clearances are specified so tightly, and why a loss of oil film thickness raises friction sharply before seizure.

examTip.trap: Leaving the film thickness in **millimetres** gives 0.1 N — a factor of 1000 out, and it is the commonest slip in this calculation.
examTip.trick: **τ = μU/t = 0.1 × 2/0.001 = 200 Pa; F = τA = 100 N.** Convert every length to metres before you start, not at the end.
examTip.mnemonic: **Force ∝ 1/thickness.** Halve the film and the force doubles — which is why bearing clearances are held so tightly, and why losing oil film raises friction sharply before seizure.

questions.stem: With increasing temperature, the viscosity of a liquid and of a gas respectively:
questions.solution:
**A liquid's viscosity DECREASES; a gas's viscosity INCREASES.**

**They behave oppositely because the viscosity arises from different mechanisms:**

| | **LIQUID** | **GAS** |
|---|---|---|
| Viscosity arises from | **COHESION** — intermolecular attraction between closely packed molecules | **MOLECULAR MOMENTUM EXCHANGE** — molecules crossing between layers and carrying momentum with them |
| Rising temperature | **Weakens cohesion** → viscosity **FALLS** | **Increases molecular speed** → more momentum exchange → viscosity **RISES** |

**The everyday confirmation for liquids**: heating oil, honey or bitumen makes it **runnier**. That is why bitumen is heated before spraying, why engine oil thins when the engine warms, and why lubricant grades specify a viscosity at temperature rather than a single number.

**For gases the effect is counter-intuitive but real**: hot air is **more** viscous than cold air. The molecules are further apart than in a liquid, so cohesion contributes almost nothing; the entire viscosity comes from molecules **wandering between layers** and transferring momentum, and they do that faster when hotter.

**Approximate magnitudes for water:**

| Temperature | μ (× 10⁻³ Pa·s) |
|---|---|
| 0 °C | **1.79** |
| **20 °C** | **1.00** |
| 40 °C | 0.65 |
| 100 °C | 0.28 |

> Water at 0 °C is **six times** as viscous as at 100 °C — a substantial variation, and one that matters when a hydraulic calculation is made at one temperature and the system operates at another.

**Pressure**, by contrast, has **little effect** on the viscosity of either at ordinary pressures — which is why viscosity is normally tabulated against temperature alone.

**Where this matters in civil engineering:**

| Application | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Pipe friction** | Cold water is more viscous → **lower Reynolds number** → higher friction factor in laminar and transitional flow |
| **Bitumen** in road works | Heated to reduce viscosity for spraying and mixing; the viscosity grade is temperature-specified |
| **Concrete admixtures** and grouts | Temperature affects flow and set |
| **Groundwater flow** | **Permeability k = K γ/μ** — so permeability measured in a cold laboratory differs from field behaviour; results are **corrected to 27 °C** by IS 2720 |
| Laboratory permeability tests | Same correction |

**The permeability correction deserves note** because it is a real procedural requirement: the coefficient of permeability depends on the fluid as well as the soil, and since μ varies by nearly a factor of two between 10 °C and 30 °C, the test result must be corrected to a standard temperature before it can be compared or used.

**Sutherland's formula** for gases and an **exponential or Andrade relation** for liquids describe the variation quantitatively, but for examination purposes the **direction** of each effect and the **reason** for it are what is tested.

examTip.trap: "Both decrease" feels right because everyday experience is of liquids. Gases behave the **opposite** way.
examTip.trick: Different mechanisms: a liquid's viscosity is **cohesion** (heat weakens it), a gas's is **molecular momentum exchange** (heat increases it).
examTip.mnemonic: **Hot oil runs; hot air drags.** Practical consequence: permeability depends on μ, so laboratory k values are corrected to **27 °C** before use.

questions.stem: The excess pressure inside a spherical liquid droplet of diameter d is:
questions.solution:
**4σ/d.**

**The three standard cases, which must be kept apart:**

| Case | Excess pressure | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Liquid DROPLET** | **Δp = 4σ/d** | **ONE** surface |
| **SOAP BUBBLE** | **Δp = 8σ/d** | **TWO** surfaces — inner and outer |
| **Cylindrical JET** | **Δp = 2σ/d** | Curved in **ONE** direction only |

**Derivation for the droplet** — equate the pressure force on a diametral plane to the surface tension force around its circumference:

> Pressure force = **Δp × (πd²/4)**
> Surface tension force = **σ × πd**
> Equating: **Δp = 4σ/d** ✓

**The soap bubble doubles it** because a bubble is a thin **film with two surfaces** in contact with air — inner and outer — each contributing σπd. **The jet halves it** because a cylinder is curved in only one plane, so only one radius of curvature contributes.

> The general statement is the **Young–Laplace equation**: **Δp = σ(1/R₁ + 1/R₂)**. For a sphere R₁ = R₂ = d/2 giving 4σ/d; for a cylinder R₂ = ∞ giving 2σ/d.

**Note the inverse relation with diameter:**

> **The SMALLER the droplet, the GREATER the internal pressure.**

That is why a fine mist is harder to produce than a coarse spray (more surface energy per unit volume), why small bubbles dissolve into large ones, and why a droplet's pressure rises as it evaporates.

**Surface tension** itself:

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **Definition** | Force per unit length at a liquid surface, or energy per unit area |
| **Unit** | **N/m** |
| **Water at 20 °C** | **0.073 N/m** |
| Mercury | 0.51 N/m |
| Effect of **temperature** | **DECREASES** — it vanishes at the critical point |
| Effect of a **detergent** | **DECREASES** sharply — which is how detergents work |

**Its cause**: a molecule in the **interior** is pulled equally in all directions; one at the **surface** has no neighbours above, so it feels a **net inward pull**. The surface therefore behaves as a **stretched membrane**, and the liquid minimises its surface area — which is why a free droplet is **spherical**, the sphere having the least surface area for a given volume.

**Where it matters in civil engineering:**

| Application | Effect |
|---|---|
| **CAPILLARY rise** in soil and in fine tubes | **h = 4σ cos θ/(γ d)** — the mechanism of soil suction and capillary fringe |
| **Apparent cohesion** in moist sand | Surface tension at the menisci binds the grains — why a sandcastle stands |
| **Manometer** readings in fine tubes | A capillary correction is needed |
| Formation of **spray and droplets** | Sprinklers, aerators |
| **Weir flow** at very low heads | Surface tension distorts the nappe, so weir formulae have a minimum head |

**Apparent cohesion is worth emphasis** because it explains a real and sometimes dangerous phenomenon: **moist** sand appears to have cohesion and will stand in a vertical cut, but the cohesion is **entirely due to capillary menisci between grains**. **Saturate it or dry it completely and the cohesion vanishes** — which is why trench collapses in sand so often follow rain or, equally, the drying of a previously damp face.

examTip.trap: 8σ/d is the bubble and 2σ/d is the jet. All three are offered together and the set is easy to scramble.
examTip.trick: Count what differs: a **jet** curves in one direction (2σ/d); a **droplet** curves in two (4σ/d); a **bubble** has two surfaces as well (8σ/d).
examTip.mnemonic: **Jet 2, drop 4, bubble 8** — each factor of two has a physical reason. Smaller means higher pressure, which is why small bubbles empty into large ones.

questions.stem: The capillary rise of water in a clean glass tube of diameter 1 mm is approximately (σ = 0.073 N/m, θ = 0):
questions.solution:
**About 30 mm.**

> **h = 4σ cos θ / (γ d) = 4 × 0.073 × 1 / (9810 × 0.001) = 0.292/9.81 = 0.0298 m ≈ 30 mm**

**Derivation** — equate the vertical component of the surface tension force around the circumference to the weight of the raised column:

> **σ cos θ × πd = γ × (πd²/4) × h**
> **h = 4σ cos θ/(γ d)** ✓

**The key relation:**

> **h ∝ 1/d** — the capillary rise is **inversely proportional to the diameter**.

So a **10× finer** tube gives **10× the rise**. In a 0.1 mm tube the water would rise **300 mm**; in a 0.01 mm tube, **3 m**. This is why capillary effects are negligible in a pipe and dominant in a fine-grained soil.

**The contact angle θ** determines whether the liquid rises or falls:

| Liquid and surface | θ | Behaviour | Meniscus |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Water on clean glass** | **≈ 0°** | **RISES** — wetting | **Concave** up |
| **MERCURY on glass** | **≈ 130°** | **DEPRESSES** — non-wetting | **CONVEX** up |
| Water on a greasy surface | > 90° | Depresses | Convex |

**Mercury is depressed** because cos 130° is **negative** — its cohesion (mercury to mercury) exceeds its adhesion to glass, so it pulls away from the wall. This matters for mercury manometers, where the correction is downward rather than upward, and it is why mercury forms beads on a surface while water spreads.

**The soil mechanics application is the important one:**

| Effect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Capillary FRINGE** above the water table | Soil is **saturated but under NEGATIVE pore pressure** |
| **Negative pore pressure → INCREASED effective stress** | **σ′ = σ − u**, and u is negative, so σ′ **exceeds** σ |
| **Apparent cohesion** in moist sand | Menisci bind the grains — the sandcastle effect |
| **Frost heave** | Capillary action draws water up to a growing ice lens |
| Rise of damp in masonry | Capillary rise through fine pores in brick and mortar |

**Approximate capillary rise in soils**, using an effective pore diameter:

| Soil | Capillary rise |
|---|---|
| Coarse sand | 0.1 – 0.15 m |
| Fine sand | 0.3 – 2 m |
| **Silt** | **1 – 10 m** |
| **Clay** | **10 m and more** |

**Silt's high capillary rise combined with reasonable permeability makes it the most FROST-SUSCEPTIBLE soil** — it can draw water up fast enough and far enough to feed a growing ice lens. Clay has a greater potential rise but is too impermeable to supply water quickly; sand is permeable but has too little rise. Silt is the unfortunate combination of both, which is why frost-susceptible subgrade criteria are written in terms of the silt fraction.

**A practical note on the calculation**: the capillary rise in soil is often written **h = C/(e d₁₀)** (Hazen), with C from 10 to 50 mm², recognising that the effective pore size relates to the grain size and the void ratio rather than to any measurable tube diameter.

examTip.trick: **h = 4σcosθ/(γd) = 4(0.073)/(9810 × 0.001) ≈ 0.030 m.** The relation is **h ∝ 1/d**, so a ten-times finer tube gives ten times the rise.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fine pores, big rise.** In soils: sand 0.1–2 m, **silt 1–10 m**, clay 10 m+. Silt's combination of high rise and workable permeability is exactly what makes it the most **frost-susceptible** soil.

questions.stem: The bulk modulus of elasticity of a fluid is defined as:
options: −dp/(dV/V), the ratio of pressure increase to volumetric strain
The product of density and gravity
questions.solution:
**K = −dp/(dV/V)** — the ratio of the pressure increase to the resulting **volumetric strain**.

**The negative sign** is there because an **increase** in pressure produces a **decrease** in volume, so dV is negative; K is thereby made a positive quantity.

> **Compressibility = 1/K** — the reciprocal.

**Typical values:**

| Fluid | K |
|---|---|
| **Water** | **2.1 × 10⁹ Pa = 2.1 GPa** |
| Oil | ~1.5 GPa |
| Mercury | 26 GPa |
| **Air (isothermal)** | **= p**, about **10⁵ Pa** — twenty thousand times less |
| Steel (for comparison) | 160 GPa |

**Water's bulk modulus is high enough that it is treated as INCOMPRESSIBLE for almost all civil engineering:**

> A pressure of **1 MPa (100 m head)** compresses water by only **1 MPa/2100 MPa ≈ 0.05%** — entirely negligible.

**But there are two situations where the compressibility of water is essential**, and both are examinable:

| Situation | Why compressibility matters |
|---|---|
| **WATER HAMMER** | The **pressure wave** travels at the **speed of sound in water**, which depends on K: **c = √(K/ρ)** ≈ **1440 m/s**. Without compressibility the wave speed would be infinite and the pressure rise unbounded |
| **Acoustics / sonar / very deep ocean** | Sound propagation |

**Water hammer** is the practical one:

> **Joukowsky's equation**: **Δp = ρ c ΔV** for a sudden valve closure

For water at 2 m/s stopped instantly: **Δp = 1000 × 1440 × 2 = 2.88 MPa ≈ 288 m of head**. That is an enormous pressure rise from a modest velocity, and it is what bursts pipes and wrecks valves.

**The wave speed in a real pipe is LESS than 1440 m/s**, because the **pipe wall also stretches**, adding to the effective compressibility:

> **c = √(K/ρ) / √(1 + K D/(E t))**

where D is the pipe diameter, t the wall thickness and E the pipe material's modulus. A **flexible pipe (plastic) gives a much lower wave speed and hence a much lower pressure rise** — which is one reason plastic pipes are less vulnerable to water hammer than steel or cast iron.

**Controlling water hammer:**

| Measure | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **SLOW valve closure** | If the closure time **exceeds 2L/c**, the reflected wave returns before closure is complete and the pressure rise is much reduced |
| **Surge tank** | Provides a free surface for the water column to rise into |
| Air vessel / accumulator | A compressible cushion |
| Pressure relief valve | Vents the surge |
| Flywheel on a pump | Slows the deceleration on power failure |

**The 2L/c criterion is the central design rule**: L/c is the time for the wave to travel to the reservoir, and 2L/c the time for it to return. A closure slower than that is a **"slow" closure**, and the pressure rise is reduced roughly in the ratio (2L/c)/T. Closure faster than 2L/c gives the **full Joukowsky rise**, however fast the valve actually moves beyond that.

**For a GAS, K depends on the process**: **K = p** for an isothermal change and **K = γp** for an adiabatic one — which is why the speed of sound in air uses the adiabatic value, **c = √(γRT)** ≈ 340 m/s at 20 °C.

examTip.trick: The minus sign is there because pressure **up** means volume **down**; it makes K positive. **Compressibility is 1/K.**
examTip.mnemonic: **K_water = 2.1 GPa — treat water as incompressible EXCEPT for water hammer.** There the finite K is everything: **c = √(K/ρ) = 1440 m/s**, and Joukowsky gives Δp = ρcΔV. Assume true incompressibility and the wave speed is infinite and the analysis collapses.

questions.stem: Cavitation in a hydraulic system occurs when the local pressure falls to:
options: The vapour pressure of the liquid
questions.solution:
**The VAPOUR PRESSURE of the liquid at the prevailing temperature.**

**The mechanism:**

> Where the local pressure falls to the **vapour pressure**, the liquid **BOILS at ambient temperature**, forming **vapour bubbles**. Carried into a region of higher pressure, these bubbles **COLLAPSE VIOLENTLY** — and the collapse is what does the damage.

**Vapour pressure of water:**

| Temperature | Vapour pressure |
|---|---|
| **20 °C** | **2.34 kPa** (0.24 m of water) |
| 40 °C | 7.4 kPa |
| 60 °C | 19.9 kPa |
| **100 °C** | **101.3 kPa** — which is why water boils at 100 °C at sea level |

> Note the last line: **boiling is simply the condition vapour pressure = ambient pressure.** Water boils at 100 °C because that is where its vapour pressure reaches one atmosphere — and at altitude, where the atmospheric pressure is lower, **it boils cooler**. On a Himalayan pass at 5000 m, water boils at about **83 °C**.

**Why the collapse is so damaging:**

| Effect | Magnitude |
|---|---|
| Local pressure at collapse | Up to **1000 MPa** in a microjet |
| **Pitting and erosion** of metal surfaces | Pits the hardest steels |
| **Noise** — a characteristic gravel-in-the-pipe rattle | The audible warning |
| **Vibration** | — |
| **Loss of efficiency** and head | The vapour occupies volume that should carry water |

**Where cavitation occurs:**

| Location | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Pump SUCTION side** | The lowest pressure in the system |
| **Impeller and turbine runner blades** | High local velocity → low pressure by Bernoulli |
| **Downstream of a partly closed valve** | Vena contracta |
| **Spillways** — at surface irregularities and on steep chutes | Very high velocity |
| Venturi throat | The point of minimum pressure |
| Draft tube of a reaction turbine | — |

**Preventing it in a PUMP** — the governing quantity is **NPSH**:

> **NPSH_available = (p_atm − p_vapour)/γ − h_suction − h_losses**
> Required: **NPSH_available > NPSH_required** (a property of the pump, from its manufacturer)

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **REDUCE the suction lift** — place the pump **LOWER**, ideally below the water level | The single most effective measure |
| **Shorten and enlarge the suction pipe**; minimise fittings | Reduces h_losses |
| Reduce the pumped liquid's temperature | Lowers p_vapour |
| Choose a pump with a lower NPSH_required | — |
| Avoid throttling on the suction side | Never throttle a suction line |

**Placing the pump below the water level (a flooded suction) eliminates the problem entirely** by making the suction head positive, and it is the standard solution wherever the site permits.

**A note for Nepal**: at altitude the **atmospheric pressure is lower**, so **NPSH_available is reduced** — roughly 1.1 m of water head less for every 1000 m of elevation. A pump installation that works at Terai elevations may cavitate at Kathmandu's 1400 m, and one designed for Kathmandu may fail at 3000 m. Pump selection must use the **site's atmospheric pressure**, not the sea-level value.

**On SPILLWAYS**, cavitation is prevented by **AERATION**: an aerator ramp entrains air into the flow, and the compressible air cushions the bubble collapse. Surface irregularities are also strictly limited — an offset of a few millimetres into a 30 m/s flow is enough to initiate cavitation damage.

examTip.trap: "Atmospheric pressure" is the intuitive wrong answer — but a liquid boils when its pressure reaches its **vapour** pressure, which at 20 °C is only 2.34 kPa.
examTip.trick: Boiling is simply p = p_vapour. Water boils at 100 °C at sea level because that is where its vapour pressure reaches one atmosphere — and at **83 °C on a 5000 m pass**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cavitation calculations must be done in ABSOLUTE pressure.** And in Nepal, subtract for altitude: NPSH available falls about **1.1 m per 1000 m** of elevation, so a pump that works in the Terai may cavitate in Kathmandu.

questions.stem: Fresh concrete, drilling mud and toothpaste behave as:
options: Bingham plastics, requiring a yield stress before flow begins
questions.solution:
**Bingham plastics — they require a YIELD STRESS before flow begins.**

> **τ = τ_y + μ_p (du/dy)** — no flow at all until **τ exceeds τ_y**

**The classification of fluids by their τ – du/dy relationship:**

| Type | Relationship | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Ideal** | **τ = 0** always; μ = 0 | Hypothetical; a useful idealisation |
| **NEWTONIAN** | **τ = μ(du/dy)** — straight line **through the origin** | **Water, air, most oils** |
| **Dilatant** (shear-thickening) | τ = k(du/dy)ⁿ, **n > 1** | Starch suspension, **wet sand** |
| **Pseudoplastic** (shear-thinning) | τ = k(du/dy)ⁿ, **n < 1** | **Paint, blood**, polymer solutions |
| **BINGHAM PLASTIC** | **τ = τ_y + μ_p(du/dy)** — an **intercept** on the τ axis | **Fresh CONCRETE, drilling mud, toothpaste, sewage sludge** |
| Thixotropic | Viscosity **decreases with TIME** under shear | Some gels, **sensitive clays** |
| Rheopectic | Viscosity increases with time under shear | Rare |

**Why the yield stress matters practically** — for fresh concrete it explains almost everything about its handling:

| Observation | Explained by |
|---|---|
| Concrete **holds its shape** after the slump cone is lifted | Below τ_y, it does not flow |
| It can be placed on a **slope** without running off | Same |
| **VIBRATION** makes it flow into the formwork | Vibration **temporarily reduces τ_y** to near zero |
| **Over-vibration causes SEGREGATION** | With τ_y removed, the heavy aggregate **sinks** through the paste |
| The **slump test** measures something meaningful | Slump correlates with the yield stress |
| Self-compacting concrete needs no vibration | It is formulated with a **very low τ_y** |

**Vibration is the engineering exploitation of the yield stress**: it converts a material that will not flow into one that will, for exactly as long as the vibrator runs, then lets it stiffen again in place. But because it removes the very property that holds the aggregate in suspension, **over-vibration segregates the mix** — which is why vibration is specified by duration and spacing rather than applied until the concrete looks convenient.

**Paint is the pseudoplastic example worth carrying**, because it shows why shear-thinning is useful:

> Paint is **thin under the brush** (high shear rate — it spreads easily) and **thick on the wall** (low shear rate — it does not run). A Newtonian paint of the same average viscosity would either be hard to brush or would sag.

**Thixotropy** deserves separate note because it appears in soil mechanics:

> A **sensitive clay** remoulded by pile driving loses much of its strength, then **regains it with time at constant water content**. That is thixotropy, and it is why a driven pile's capacity **increases over days or weeks** — the **set-up** effect — and why a pile load test done too soon understates the capacity.

**The distinction between thixotropic and shear-thinning** is the variable: **pseudoplastic** viscosity depends on the **shear RATE**; **thixotropic** viscosity depends on the **TIME** for which shear has been applied, and recovers when shearing stops.

examTip.trick: A Bingham plastic will not move at all until the stress exceeds **τ_y** — which is why concrete holds its shape after the slump cone lifts and can be placed on a slope.
examTip.mnemonic: **Vibration temporarily destroys the yield stress** — that is exactly how a poker works. And it is why **over-vibration segregates**: remove τ_y and the heavy aggregate sinks through the paste.

questions.stem: The kinematic viscosity of a fluid is:
options: The product of dynamic viscosity and density
The ratio of dynamic viscosity to density, μ/ρ
The same as the dynamic viscosity
The ratio of density to dynamic viscosity
questions.solution:
**ν = μ/ρ**, the ratio of dynamic viscosity to density.

| | **Dynamic viscosity μ** | **Kinematic viscosity ν** |
|---|---|---|
| **Definition** | From **τ = μ du/dy** | **μ/ρ** |
| **SI unit** | **Pa·s** = N·s/m² | **m²/s** |
| **CGS unit** | **poise** (1 Pa·s = 10 P) | **stokes** (1 m²/s = 10⁴ St) |
| **Water at 20 °C** | **1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s** | **1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s** |
| **Air at 20 °C** | 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ Pa·s | **1.5 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s** |
| Governs | The **shear STRESS** | The **DIFFUSION of momentum** |

**Note the striking comparison between air and water:**

> Air is about **55 times LESS viscous than water in DYNAMIC terms**, but about **15 times MORE viscous in KINEMATIC terms** — because its density is 800 times lower.

That is not a contradiction but a reminder that the two viscosities answer different questions. **Dynamic** viscosity tells you the shear stress for a given velocity gradient. **Kinematic** viscosity tells you how fast momentum **diffuses** through the fluid — and it is the quantity that appears in the **Reynolds number**:

> **Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν**

**Why ν has units of m²/s** — the same as a diffusion coefficient or a thermal diffusivity — is the physical clue: **kinematic viscosity IS the diffusivity of momentum**, exactly as thermal diffusivity α = k/(ρc) is the diffusivity of heat. A fluid with high ν spreads a velocity disturbance quickly through itself.

**Which one to use:**

| Problem | Use |
|---|---|
| Shear force on a plate, torque in a bearing | **μ** (dynamic) |
| **Reynolds number**, boundary layer thickness | **ν** (kinematic) |
| Head loss in laminar pipe flow (Hagen–Poiseuille) | Either — **h_f = 32μVL/(γD²) = 32νVL/(gD²)** |
| Terminal velocity, Stokes' law | **μ** |

**Measurement.** Kinematic viscosity is what most viscometers actually measure, because they time the flow of a fixed volume of liquid under gravity — and gravity-driven flow depends on μ/ρ:

| Instrument | Principle |
|---|---|
| **Capillary tube (Ostwald, Cannon–Fenske)** | Time for a volume to drain through a capillary; **Hagen–Poiseuille** |
| **Saybolt / Redwood / Engler** | Time for 60 ml to drain through a standard orifice — an empirical scale |
| **Rotating cylinder** | Torque on an inner cylinder in a rotating outer one — measures **μ** directly |
| **Falling sphere** | **Stokes' law**: μ = (γ_s − γ_f)d²/(18V) — good for very viscous liquids |

**The falling-sphere method is the one with the neat derivation**: at terminal velocity the drag balances the submerged weight, and Stokes' drag 3πμVd applies for Re < 1. It is the same relation used in the **hydrometer analysis** of soil grain size — which is a nice cross-connection between fluid mechanics and soil mechanics.

examTip.trick: Check the units: **Pa·s ÷ kg/m³ = m²/s** ✓ — the units of a diffusivity, because ν IS the diffusivity of momentum.
examTip.mnemonic: **Air is 55× less viscous than water in DYNAMIC terms but 15× MORE in KINEMATIC terms**, because its density is 800× lower. Use **μ** for shear force, **ν** for Reynolds number.

questions.stem: An ideal fluid is one which is:
questions.solution:
**Inviscid (μ = 0) and incompressible.**

**An ideal fluid does not exist** — it is an **idealisation**, and a very useful one. Its properties:

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **Viscosity μ** | **ZERO** — no shear stress, ever |
| **Density** | **Constant** — incompressible |
| **Surface tension** | Zero |
| Shear stress | **None**, even in motion |
| At a boundary | **SLIPS freely** — no no-slip condition |

**Why the idealisation is useful:**

| Benefit | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Bernoulli's equation** applies exactly | No friction loss term needed |
| **Potential flow theory** becomes available | The flow is **irrotational**, and powerful mathematics follows |
| Flow **outside the boundary layer** is well modelled by it | Viscous effects are confined to a thin layer near surfaces |
| Pressure distributions can be computed analytically | For aerofoils, weirs, bends |

**The essential insight — Prandtl's boundary layer concept:**

> In a **real** fluid of low viscosity, the viscous effects are **confined to a THIN LAYER near solid boundaries** (the boundary layer). **Outside** that layer the flow behaves very nearly as an **ideal fluid**.

That division is what makes practical fluid mechanics possible: solve the **outer** flow by ideal (potential) theory, and the **thin boundary layer** by viscous theory, then match them. Before Prandtl (1904), the two branches of the subject — mathematical hydrodynamics, which predicted no drag at all, and practical hydraulics, which measured plenty — could not be reconciled.

**D'Alembert's paradox** is the classic illustration of the idealisation's limit:

> Ideal flow theory predicts **ZERO DRAG** on any body moving steadily through an ideal fluid — because the pressure distribution is perfectly symmetric fore and aft.

Real bodies obviously experience drag. The resolution is that **real flow SEPARATES** from the rear of a bluff body, destroying the pressure recovery and leaving a low-pressure wake — a phenomenon that has no counterpart in ideal flow, and which accounts for most of the drag on a bluff body.

**Real fluid effects that an ideal fluid cannot represent:**

| Effect | Requires |
|---|---|
| **Head loss / friction** in pipes | Viscosity |
| **Drag** on bodies | Viscosity, separation |
| **Boundary layer** | Viscosity and no-slip |
| **Separation and wake** | Viscosity |
| **Turbulence** | Viscosity (for its dissipation) |
| **Water hammer** wave speed | Compressibility |

**Where ideal fluid analysis is nevertheless used successfully:**

| Application | Why it works |
|---|---|
| Flow through **short converging** sections — nozzles, venturi throats, orifices | **Accelerating** flow has a **thin** boundary layer and **no separation** |
| **Flow over a weir** or through a sluice | Short, accelerating |
| Wave motion | Viscosity negligible over the wave scale |
| Pressure distribution on a **streamlined** body | Boundary layer stays attached |

**Note the pattern in the first row**: ideal flow works well in **accelerating (converging)** flow and poorly in **decelerating (diverging)** flow — because an **adverse pressure gradient** thickens the boundary layer and causes **separation**. That is why a venturi's converging cone can be short and steep (20°) while its diverging cone must be long and gentle (5–7°): the converging flow is well behaved, the diverging flow is on the edge of separating.

examTip.trick: Ideal means **no viscosity and constant density** — so no shear stress ever, no boundary layer, and free slip at a wall.
examTip.mnemonic: **No viscosity, no drag — which is D'Alembert's paradox**, resolved only by real flow SEPARATING. Ideal theory works well in **accelerating (converging)** flow and badly in **decelerating (diverging)** flow — hence a venturi's steep 20° inlet and gentle 6° outlet.

questions.stem: The specific weight of water at 4 °C in SI units is:
questions.solution:
**9810 N/m³**, or **9.81 kN/m³**.

> **γ = ρg = 1000 kg/m³ × 9.81 m/s² = 9810 N/m³**

**The four related properties, kept distinct** — and confusing them is the commonest source of error in fluid mechanics arithmetic:

| Property | Symbol | Definition | Water at 4 °C | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Density** | **ρ** | **Mass** per unit volume | **1000** | **kg/m³** |
| **Specific weight** (unit weight) | **γ** | **WEIGHT** per unit volume = **ρg** | **9810** | **N/m³** |
| **Specific gravity** (relative density) | **S** or G | Ratio to water — **DIMENSIONLESS** | **1.0** | — |
| **Specific volume** | **v** | Volume per unit mass = **1/ρ** | **0.001** | **m³/kg** |

**Density is mass-based; specific weight is force-based.** The distinction matters because pressure is a force per area:

> **p = γh** — uses the **specific weight**, giving N/m² directly
> **p = ρgh** — the same thing written out

Using ρ where γ belongs gives an answer **9.81 times too small**, and it is a very common slip.

**Water's density anomaly** is worth knowing, and it is why the question specifies 4 °C:

> **Water is DENSEST at 4 °C**, not at 0 °C. Below 4 °C it **expands** as it cools, and **ice is LESS dense than water** — which is why ice floats.

| Temperature | Density (kg/m³) |
|---|---|
| 0 °C (ice) | **917** |
| 0 °C (water) | 999.8 |
| **4 °C** | **1000.0 — maximum** |
| 20 °C | 998.2 |
| 100 °C | 958.4 |

**The consequences of that anomaly are considerable:**

| Consequence | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Lakes freeze from the TOP down** | The 4 °C water sinks; the colder water stays on top and freezes there, insulating the depths — so **aquatic life survives the winter** |
| **Frost damage to concrete and rock** | Water expands about **9% on freezing**, and the pressure **cracks** the material |
| Frost heave | Ice lenses grow and lift the ground |
| Burst pipes | The same expansion |

**Specific gravity** is dimensionless and therefore the same in every unit system, which is why soil and rock properties are usually tabulated that way:

| Material | S |
|---|---|
| **Water** | **1.0** |
| **Mercury** | **13.6** |
| Oil | 0.8 – 0.9 |
| **Soil solids (G_s)** | **2.65 – 2.75** |
| Concrete | 2.4 |
| Steel | 7.85 |

**For any fluid: γ = S × 9810 N/m³.** So mercury's specific weight is 13.6 × 9810 = **133 400 N/m³**, which is why a mercury manometer measures a large pressure with a short column — a metre of mercury being worth 13.6 m of water.

**A note on g**: taking **g = 9.81 m/s²** is standard, and the variation over the earth's surface (9.78 at the equator to 9.83 at the poles) is well below the precision of any hydraulic calculation. Some texts use 9.807 or simply 9.8; the difference never matters.

examTip.trap: 1000 is the **density in kg/m³**, not the specific weight. Mixing ρ and γ gives an answer 9.81 times out, and it is the single commonest arithmetic error in hydrostatics.
examTip.trick: **γ = ρg = 1000 × 9.81 = 9810 N/m³.** Pressure is a force per area, so it needs γ, not ρ: **p = γh**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water is densest at 4 °C, not 0 °C** — which is why lakes freeze from the top down and why ice (917 kg/m³) floats.

questions.stem: The no-slip condition at a solid boundary means that:
options: The fluid slides freely over the surface
The pressure is zero at the surface
The shear stress is zero at the surface
The fluid velocity relative to the boundary is zero
questions.solution:
**The fluid velocity RELATIVE to the boundary is zero** — the fluid adheres to the surface.

**It is an experimental fact, not a derived result**, and it holds for every real (viscous) fluid on every solid surface. An **ideal** fluid, having no viscosity, would slip freely — which is one of the ways the idealisation departs from reality.

**Everything about viscous flow follows from it:**

| Consequence | Chain of reasoning |
|---|---|
| A **velocity GRADIENT** must exist near the wall | Velocity goes from 0 at the wall to the free-stream value |
| Hence a **SHEAR STRESS** τ = μ(du/dy) at the wall | The gradient is largest there |
| Hence **DRAG** on every surface | The wall shear integrated over the area |
| Hence **HEAD LOSS** in every pipe | The drag must be overcome by a pressure drop |
| Hence the **BOUNDARY LAYER** | The region over which the velocity adjusts |

> **Without no-slip there would be no friction, no boundary layer, no head loss, and no need for pumps.** The whole practical subject of hydraulics rests on it.

**The everyday demonstration**: dust remains on a fan blade however fast it spins, and a car does not clean itself by driving fast. The air immediately at the surface is **not moving relative to it**, so it exerts no sweeping force on the dust.

**Option (c) is exactly backwards** and worth correcting explicitly: the shear stress at the wall is not zero but is **at its MAXIMUM** there, because the velocity gradient is steepest at the wall. In pipe flow the shear stress varies **linearly** from **τ₀ at the wall to zero at the centreline**:

> **τ = τ₀ (r/R)**, with **τ₀ = (γ h_f D)/(4L) = ρ g R S**

**The velocity profile** correspondingly:

| Flow | Wall shear | Profile |
|---|---|---|
| **Laminar pipe flow** | Maximum at wall | **PARABOLIC**; **V_mean = V_max/2** |
| **Turbulent pipe flow** | Maximum at wall | **Logarithmic** — much **flatter**; **V_mean ≈ 0.82 V_max** |

**The turbulent profile is flatter** because turbulent mixing transports momentum across the section far more effectively than molecular viscosity, evening out the velocity — but it is **steeper right at the wall**, within the thin **viscous sublayer**, which is why turbulent friction is higher.

**The viscous sublayer** is the key to the smooth/rough pipe distinction:

| Condition | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Roughness **submerged** in the viscous sublayer | Pipe behaves as **HYDRODYNAMICALLY SMOOTH** — f depends on **Re only** |
| Roughness **projecting through** it | **Fully rough** — f depends on **k/D only**, not on Re |
| Between | Transitional — f depends on both (the Colebrook–White region) |

> So **"smooth" and "rough" are not properties of the pipe alone** but of the pipe **and the flow**: the same pipe is smooth at low Reynolds number and rough at high, because the sublayer thins as the flow accelerates. That is why the Moody diagram's curves become horizontal at high Re — the flow has gone fully rough and the Reynolds number no longer matters.

examTip.trap: "Shear stress is zero at the surface" is exactly backwards — the wall is where the shear is **maximum**, because the velocity gradient is steepest there.
examTip.trick: No-slip creates the velocity gradient, which creates the wall shear, which creates the drag and the head loss. Everything in viscous flow follows from it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dust stays on a spinning fan blade.** Shear stress in a pipe varies **linearly from τ₀ at the wall to zero at the centreline** — in both laminar and turbulent flow.

questions.stem: The excess pressure inside a soap bubble of diameter d is:
questions.solution:
**8σ/d — twice that of a droplet of the same size.**

**Because a soap bubble has TWO surfaces** — an inner and an outer face of the thin liquid film — each contributing a surface tension force σπd around the circumference:

> Pressure force = **Δp × πd²/4**
> Surface tension force = **2 × σ × πd**
> **Δp = 8σ/d** ✓

**The three cases side by side:**

| Case | Surfaces | Curvature | Δp |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cylindrical JET** | 1 | One direction only | **2σ/d** |
| **Liquid DROPLET** | 1 | Two directions | **4σ/d** |
| **SOAP BUBBLE** | **2** | Two directions | **8σ/d** |

**The pattern is systematic**: each factor of two comes from a distinct cause — the second direction of curvature doubles the jet's value to the droplet's, and the second surface doubles the droplet's to the bubble's.

> The unifying statement is the **Young–Laplace equation**: **Δp = σ(1/R₁ + 1/R₂)** per surface. A cylinder has R₂ = ∞ (2σ/d); a sphere has R₁ = R₂ = d/2 (4σ/d); a bubble is two spherical surfaces (8σ/d).

**A consequence worth knowing**: connect a **small** bubble to a **large** one and the **small one EMPTIES INTO THE LARGE**, because its internal pressure is higher. That is counter-intuitive — one expects them to equalise at an intermediate size — and it explains why a foam **coarsens** over time, small bubbles disappearing into larger ones.

**The same argument applies to alveoli in the lung**, where it would be disastrous — the small alveoli would collapse into the large. Nature's solution is a **surfactant** whose surface tension **falls as the surface contracts**, stabilising the small alveoli. It is a nice illustration that the physics is real enough to have driven a biological adaptation.

**Surface tension values and influences:**

| Factor | Effect on σ |
|---|---|
| **Temperature increase** | **DECREASES** — reaching zero at the critical point |
| **Detergent / surfactant** | **DECREASES sharply** — the mechanism by which detergents work |
| Dissolved salts | Slight increase |
| Contamination | Usually decreases |

**Water at 20 °C: σ = 0.073 N/m.** Mercury, at 0.51 N/m, is much higher — which is why mercury beads up so tightly.

**Where surface tension matters in civil engineering:**

| Application | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Capillary rise** in soils and fine tubes | **h = 4σcos θ/(γd)** |
| **Apparent cohesion** in moist sand | Menisci bind the grains |
| **Manometer** readings in fine-bore tubes | A capillary correction is needed — which is why manometer tubes are specified at 6 mm or more |
| **Weir flow at very low heads** | Surface tension distorts the nappe, so weir formulae specify a **minimum head** (typically 30 mm) |
| Droplet formation in sprinklers and aerators | — |
| Flotation of fine particles | — |

**The weir point is a practical one**: below about 30 mm head the nappe clings to the weir plate and the discharge coefficient departs from its tabulated value — so a weir cannot be used to measure very small flows accurately, and a V-notch (which concentrates a small flow into a greater head) is used instead.

examTip.trick: A bubble is a **film with two surfaces**, inner and outer, so the surface tension force is doubled: **8σ/d** against the droplet's 4σ/d.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two surfaces, twice the pressure.** Consequence: connect a small bubble to a large one and the **small one empties into the large**, because its pressure is higher. That is why foam coarsens over time.

questions.stem: An oil has specific gravity 0.8 and dynamic viscosity 0.04 Pa·s. Its kinematic viscosity is:
questions.solution:
**5 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s.**

> **ρ = S × ρ_water = 0.8 × 1000 = 800 kg/m³**
> **ν = μ/ρ = 0.04 / 800 = 5 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s**

**The trap in this question** is option (a), 0.032 — which is **μ × S**, or equivalently what you get by **multiplying instead of dividing**, and by using the specific gravity in place of the density. Two errors that happen to combine into a plausible-looking number.

**Check the units**, which settles it immediately:

> **μ/ρ = (Pa·s)/(kg/m³) = (N·s/m²)/(kg/m³) = (kg·m/s²·s/m²)/(kg/m³) = m²/s** ✓

And the magnitude is a further check: **oil is more viscous than water**, whose ν is 1 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s — so an answer of 5 × 10⁻⁵ (fifty times water's) is sensible for a light oil, while 0.032 m²/s would be **32 000 times** water's, which is the viscosity of a heavy grease.

**Developing a feel for the magnitudes** is worth the effort, because it catches errors that unit checks do not:

| Fluid | ν (m²/s) | Relative to water |
|---|---|---|
| **Water (20 °C)** | **1.0 × 10⁻⁶** | **1** |
| **Air (20 °C)** | 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ | 15 |
| Light oil | 5 × 10⁻⁵ | 50 |
| SAE 30 engine oil | 1 × 10⁻⁴ | 100 |
| Glycerine | 1.2 × 10⁻³ | 1200 |
| **Honey** | ~1 × 10⁻² | 10 000 |

**Why kinematic viscosity is the useful one here** — it feeds directly into the Reynolds number:

> **Re = VD/ν**

For this oil flowing at 1 m/s in a 50 mm pipe:

> **Re = 1 × 0.05 / (5 × 10⁻⁵) = 1000** — **LAMINAR** (Re < 2000)

Whereas water in the same pipe at the same speed gives **Re = 50 000** — firmly turbulent. That difference of regime changes everything about the flow: the velocity profile, the friction factor, the mixing, and the head loss relationship.

**The head loss comparison makes the point:**

| Regime | Head loss varies as |
|---|---|
| **Laminar** | **h_f ∝ V** — directly with velocity; **f = 64/Re** |
| **Turbulent** | **h_f ∝ V^1.75 to V²** |

So doubling the flow in the oil pipe doubles the head loss; doubling it in the water pipe roughly quadruples it. **Oil pipelines are laminar and water pipelines turbulent**, which is why they are analysed with different tools and why the friction factor for an oil line depends only on Re, not on the pipe roughness at all.

**A word on the CGS units**, still met in oil specifications: **1 stokes = 1 cm²/s = 10⁻⁴ m²/s**, and **1 centistokes = 10⁻⁶ m²/s** — which happens to be exactly the kinematic viscosity of water at 20 °C. So a viscosity quoted in **centistokes is a direct multiple of water's**, which is a convenient scale and the reason it persists.

examTip.trap: 0.032 is what you get by **multiplying** by the specific gravity instead of dividing by the density — two errors that combine into a plausible-looking number.
examTip.trick: **ρ = 0.8 × 1000 = 800; ν = 0.04/800 = 5 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s.** Sanity check the magnitude: water is 1 × 10⁻⁶, so a light oil at 50× water is sensible; 0.032 would be 32 000× water — a heavy grease.
examTip.mnemonic: **Always sanity-check ν against water's 10⁻⁶.**

questions.stem: A fluid at rest cannot sustain:
questions.solution:
**Shear stress.**

**This follows directly from the definition of a fluid:**

> A fluid **deforms continuously under ANY shear stress, however small**. So if a shear stress existed in a fluid at rest, the fluid would **flow** — and it would no longer be at rest. The two conditions are incompatible.

**Therefore in a static fluid the only stress is the NORMAL stress**, which is the **pressure** — and that leads immediately to the foundational result of hydrostatics:

> **PASCAL'S LAW: the pressure at a point in a fluid at rest is the SAME IN ALL DIRECTIONS.**

**Why Pascal's law follows.** Consider a small wedge-shaped element of fluid at rest. With no shear stresses on any face, only the normal (pressure) forces act. Resolving in two directions and letting the element shrink to a point, the weight term (proportional to volume) vanishes faster than the pressure terms (proportional to area) — and the pressures on all faces are found to be **equal**, whatever the orientation of the wedge.

**The consequences are the whole of hydrostatics:**

| Consequence | Statement |
|---|---|
| Pressure acts **PERPENDICULAR** to any surface | Because there is no shear component |
| **p = γh** — pressure increases **linearly** with depth | From the equilibrium of a vertical column |
| Pressure is the **same at all points on a horizontal plane** in a connected fluid | The basis of the **manometer** and of communicating vessels |
| **Hydrostatic paradox** | The force on a base depends on the **DEPTH and AREA only** — not on the shape of the vessel or the weight of liquid it holds |
| Pascal's principle of transmission | An applied pressure is transmitted **undiminished** throughout — the **hydraulic jack** |

**The hydrostatic paradox deserves its name** and is worth stating because it surprises people every time:

> Three vessels — one cylindrical, one flaring outward, one narrowing to a thin neck — with the **same base area** and the **same depth of water** exert **exactly the same force on the base**, even though they contain **utterly different weights of water**.

The resolution is that the **walls** carry the difference: in the flaring vessel the walls push down on the liquid, in the narrowing one they push up. The base force depends only on **p = γh** and the area.

**Options (b), (c) and (d) are all things a static fluid CAN sustain**, and each is worth a word:

| Option | Why it is wrong |
|---|---|
| **Normal stress** | A static fluid sustains it perfectly well — that **is** the pressure |
| **Pressure** | Same |
| **Its own weight** | It sustains it; the weight is precisely what **creates** the pressure variation with depth, p = γh |

**A refinement worth noting**: a fluid at rest cannot sustain shear, but it **can sustain TENSION** in principle — water can be put under a small negative absolute pressure in very clean, carefully prepared conditions. In practice **cavitation intervenes** at the vapour pressure, so for engineering purposes the absolute pressure in a liquid cannot fall below its vapour pressure, and negative gauge pressures are limited to about −10 m of water.

**And for a fluid IN MOTION**, shear stresses do exist — τ = μ(du/dy) — so the pressure at a point is no longer strictly equal in all directions. In practice the differences are tiny for ordinary flows, and the **mean** of the three normal stresses is what is called the pressure.

examTip.trick: If a fluid at rest could sustain shear it would flow, and then it would not be at rest. The two conditions are incompatible.
examTip.mnemonic: **No shear at rest → pressure acts EQUALLY IN ALL DIRECTIONS (Pascal) and PERPENDICULAR to every surface.** From that single fact follow p = γh, the manometer, and the hydrostatic paradox.

questions.stem: A liquid is generally regarded as incompressible in civil engineering because:
options: Its bulk modulus is very large, so the volume change under working pressures is negligible
questions.solution:
**Because its bulk modulus is very large, so the volume change under ordinary working pressures is negligible.**

> **K_water = 2.1 GPa.** A pressure of **1 MPa (about 100 m of head)** compresses water by **1/2100 ≈ 0.05%**.

That is far below the accuracy of any hydraulic calculation, so treating the density as constant introduces no meaningful error.

**The simplification is enormous**, and it is worth seeing what it buys:

| Simplification | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **ρ constant** | Continuity becomes **A₁V₁ = A₂V₂** — a simple volumetric statement |
| Bernoulli in **head** form | **p/γ + V²/2g + z = constant** — every term a length |
| No thermodynamic coupling | Temperature and pressure need not be solved together |
| **Free surface** problems tractable | Open channel flow, weirs, reservoirs |

**But there are situations where the compressibility of water is essential**, and they are examinable:

| Situation | Why |
|---|---|
| **WATER HAMMER** | The pressure wave travels at **c = √(K/ρ) = 1440 m/s**. Treat water as truly incompressible and the wave speed is **infinite** and the pressure rise **unbounded** — the analysis fails completely |
| Underwater acoustics, sonar | Sound is a compression wave |
| Very deep ocean | Density increases measurably with depth |
| Hydraulic transients generally | Surge analysis |

**Water hammer** is the one that matters in practice:

> **Joukowsky: Δp = ρ c ΔV.** Water at 2 m/s stopped instantly gives **Δp = 1000 × 1440 × 2 = 2.88 MPa ≈ 288 m of head** — enough to burst a pipe designed for 100 m.

**And when is a GAS incompressible?** The criterion is the **Mach number**:

> **M = V/c**, and a gas flow may be treated as **incompressible when M < 0.3** — for which the density change is under about 5%.

For air (c ≈ 340 m/s) that means velocities **below about 100 m/s**, which covers essentially all civil engineering: wind loading (design wind speeds up to 55 m/s), ventilation, and air in ducts. So **air is treated as incompressible in civil engineering too**, despite being a gas — which surprises candidates who assume the distinction is between liquids and gases.

> The distinction is **not liquid versus gas** but **whether the density changes appreciably in the flow**. A liquid essentially never does; a gas does only at high speed.

**Where compressible flow does matter**: gas pipelines over long distances (where the pressure drop is large enough to change the density substantially), compressed air systems, and high-speed aerodynamics — none of them core civil engineering, but the gas pipeline case does arise.

**A cautionary note about the word "incompressible"**: it describes an **assumption about the flow**, not an absolute property of the fluid. Water is not literally incompressible — as water hammer proves conclusively — and the assumption must be dropped whenever the phenomenon of interest depends on the compressibility itself.

examTip.trick: 1 MPa (100 m of head) compresses water by **0.05%** — far below the precision of any hydraulic calculation.
examTip.mnemonic: **Incompressible describes the FLOW, not the fluid.** Drop the assumption for **water hammer** and acoustics. And note **air is treated as incompressible too** below M = 0.3 (about 100 m/s), which covers all civil engineering wind loading.

questions.stem: Mercury in a glass tube shows a convex meniscus and is depressed below the outside level because:
options: Its cohesion exceeds its adhesion to glass, giving a contact angle greater than 90°
questions.solution:
**Because its COHESION (mercury to mercury) exceeds its ADHESION to glass, giving a contact angle greater than 90°.**

**The competition between two forces determines the behaviour:**

| Force | Between |
|---|---|
| **COHESION** | Molecules of the **liquid and each other** |
| **ADHESION** | Molecules of the **liquid and the solid surface** |

| Relationship | Contact angle θ | Meniscus | Capillary effect | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Adhesion > cohesion** | **θ < 90°** — **WETTING** | **CONCAVE** up | **RISES** | **Water on clean glass** (θ ≈ 0) |
| **Cohesion > adhesion** | **θ > 90°** — **non-wetting** | **CONVEX** up | **DEPRESSES** | **MERCURY on glass** (θ ≈ 130°) |

**In the capillary formula the sign takes care of itself:**

> **h = 4σ cos θ/(γ d)**

> For water, **cos 0° = +1** → **h positive, a rise**.
> For mercury, **cos 130° = −0.64** → **h negative, a depression**.

**The magnitude for mercury** in a 1 mm tube, with σ = 0.51 N/m and γ = 133 400 N/m³:

> **h = 4 × 0.51 × (−0.64)/(133 400 × 0.001) = −0.0098 m ≈ −10 mm**

So mercury is depressed about 10 mm in a 1 mm tube, against water's 30 mm rise — smaller in magnitude despite mercury's much higher surface tension, because its specific weight is 13.6 times greater.

**Note that option (a), while a true statement about mercury, is not the CAUSE.** Density determines how far the meniscus moves, not whether it rises or falls. The **direction** is set entirely by the **contact angle**, which is a property of the liquid–solid **pair**. Mercury on a clean **copper** surface, for instance, wets it and would rise.

**Practical consequences:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Mercury manometer** readings need a **downward** capillary correction | The reverse of a water manometer's |
| The correction is **reduced by using a wider tube** | h ∝ 1/d, so a 10 mm tube has a tenth the error of a 1 mm one |
| **Mercury does not wet glass** | So it leaves a clean tube behind as it falls — an advantage for a manometer |
| Mercury beads on a surface | The same non-wetting behaviour |
| **Mercury intrusion porosimetry** | Non-wetting means mercury must be **FORCED** into pores, and the pressure required measures the pore size |

**The porosimetry application is a neat inversion** of the usual view of capillarity as a nuisance: because mercury does **not** enter a pore spontaneously, the pressure needed to drive it in is a direct measure of the pore diameter — **p = −4σ cos θ/d** — and sweeping the pressure gives the pore size distribution of a concrete, rock or ceramic specimen.

**A note on why mercury is used in manometers at all**, despite its toxicity: its **high density** (13.6) means a large pressure produces a **short, manageable column** — 1 bar is 760 mm of mercury against 10.3 m of water — and it **does not wet the tube**, so the meniscus is clean and repeatable. Modern practice has largely replaced mercury manometers with electronic transducers on health grounds, but the mmHg unit and the physics survive.

examTip.trap: "Mercury is denser" is a true statement and the wrong reason. Density fixes **how far** the meniscus moves, never **which way**.
examTip.trick: Direction is set entirely by the **contact angle**, a property of the liquid–solid **pair**. cos 130° is negative, so h comes out negative — a depression.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water wets glass and climbs; mercury does not wet and sinks.** Use a **wider tube** to shrink the correction, since h ∝ 1/d.

questions.stem: The gauge pressure at a depth of 5 m in water is:
questions.solution:
**49.05 kPa** — commonly rounded to **49 kPa** or, loosely, **50 kPa**.

> **p = γh = 9810 × 5 = 49 050 Pa = 49.05 kPa**

**Option (b), 50 kPa**, is what you get with **g = 10 m/s²** — a legitimate rough approximation, but where an exact option is offered it is the one to take. Read the options before rounding.

**The fundamental hydrostatic relation:**

> **p = γh = ρgh**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| Pressure increases **LINEARLY** with depth | The pressure diagram is a **triangle** for a liquid open to atmosphere |
| It depends **ONLY on the depth** | Not on the shape of the container, nor on the volume of liquid |
| It is the **same at every point on a horizontal plane** in a connected fluid | The basis of the manometer |
| It acts **PERPENDICULAR** to any surface | Because a static fluid sustains no shear |

**Useful conversions to have by heart:**

| Head of water | Pressure |
|---|---|
| **1 m** | **9.81 kPa** |
| **10 m** | **98.1 kPa ≈ 1 atmosphere** |
| **10.33 m** | **101.3 kPa = 1 atm exactly** |
| 100 m | 981 kPa ≈ 1 MPa |

> The relation **10 m of water ≈ 1 bar ≈ 1 atmosphere** is the single most useful number in hydraulics, and it should be instant. It tells you that a 30 m building needs about 3 bar at its base, that a suction lift can never exceed about 10 m, and that a pipeline rated at 10 bar can take 100 m of head.

**Gauge versus absolute pressure:**

| Term | Datum | Relation |
|---|---|---|
| **GAUGE pressure** | **Atmospheric** | What a gauge reads; can be **negative** |
| **ABSOLUTE pressure** | **Perfect vacuum** | **p_abs = p_gauge + p_atm**; **never negative** |
| **Vacuum pressure** | Below atmospheric | **p_vac = −p_gauge** |

> **p_atm = 101.3 kPa = 10.33 m of water = 760 mm of mercury** at sea level.

**Which to use:**

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| Structural design — force on a dam, tank wall, gate | **GAUGE** — atmospheric pressure acts on both sides and cancels |
| **CAVITATION** and pump suction (NPSH) | **ABSOLUTE** — vapour pressure is an absolute quantity |
| Gas laws | **ABSOLUTE** |
| Most hydraulic calculations | Gauge |

**Using gauge pressure in a cavitation calculation is a real error**, because the criterion is that the **absolute** pressure must not fall to the **absolute** vapour pressure. Mixing the datums gives an answer wrong by a full atmosphere.

**And a note for Nepal**: atmospheric pressure falls with altitude — about **89 kPa at Kathmandu's 1400 m** against 101.3 at sea level. That reduces the available suction lift and the NPSH for every pump, and it must be taken from the **site elevation**, not from a table's sea-level value.

examTip.trick: **p = γh = 9810 × 5 = 49.05 kPa.** The 50 kPa option comes from g = 10, which is a fine approximation until an exact option is on the list.
examTip.mnemonic: **10 m of water ≈ 1 bar ≈ 1 atmosphere** — the single most useful number in hydraulics. Use **gauge** pressure for structural design (atmosphere cancels on both faces) and **absolute** for cavitation.

questions.stem: The total hydrostatic force on one face of a vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide and 3 m deep, with its top edge at the water surface, is:
questions.solution:
**88.3 kN.**

> **F = γ h̄ A**, where **h̄** is the depth of the **CENTROID**
> **h̄ = 3/2 = 1.5 m**, **A = 2 × 3 = 6 m²**
> **F = 9810 × 1.5 × 6 = 88 290 N = 88.3 kN** ✓

**The formula in words:**

> **Total force = (pressure at the CENTROID) × (area)**

which is exactly the volume of the pressure diagram — a triangular prism of base pressure γH = 29.43 kPa, height 3 m and width 2 m: **½ × 29.43 × 3 × 2 = 88.3 kN** ✓ — the same answer by a different route, and a useful check.

**Option (b), 58.9 kN**, is **γ(H/3)A** — it takes the depth of the resultant's line of action (H/3 above the base, so 2H/3 down) and misuses it as the centroid depth. The centroid and the centre of pressure are different points, and only the **centroid** belongs in F = γh̄A. Option (c), 176.6 kN, is **γHA** — the full base pressure applied over the whole area, forgetting that the pressure varies from zero at the surface.

**The CENTRE OF PRESSURE** — where the force acts — is the second half of the problem, and it is **not** at the centroid:

> **h_cp = h̄ + I_G/(A h̄)**

For this gate: **I_G = bd³/12 = 2 × 27/12 = 4.5 m⁴**
> **h_cp = 1.5 + 4.5/(6 × 1.5) = 1.5 + 0.5 = 2.0 m** below the surface

**The centre of pressure is ALWAYS BELOW the centroid**, because **I_G/(Ah̄) is always positive**. Physically: the pressure is greater at greater depth, so the lower part of the surface carries more than its share of the force, and the resultant is pulled downward.

**For a vertical rectangle with its top at the surface**, the result is a standard one worth memorising:

> **Centroid at H/2; centre of pressure at 2H/3 from the surface — that is, H/3 above the base.**

**Note what happens as the surface is submerged deeper:**

| Depth of the plate | h̄ | I_G/(Ah̄) | Centre of pressure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Top at surface | Small | **Large** | Well below the centroid |
| Deeply submerged | **Large** | **Small** | **Approaches the centroid** |

> As the plate goes deeper the pressure variation across it becomes **relatively** smaller — the pressure is nearly uniform — so the centre of pressure **converges on the centroid**. A gate 50 m down has its centre of pressure within millimetres of its centroid.

**For an INCLINED plane surface** at angle θ, the same formulae hold with distances measured **along the plane**:

> **F = γ h̄ A** (h̄ still the **vertical** depth of the centroid)
> **y_cp = ȳ + I_G/(A ȳ)** (distances **along the plane**)

**Common values of I_G:**

| Shape | I_G about the horizontal centroidal axis |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle b × d** | **bd³/12** |
| **Circle diameter D** | **πD⁴/64** |
| Triangle base b, height h (apex up) | bh³/36 |

**A note on the direction of the force**: it acts **perpendicular to the surface**, because a static fluid exerts no shear. For a vertical gate it is therefore horizontal, and it must be resisted by the gate's supports and transmitted to the structure.

examTip.trap: 58.9 kN is γ(H/3)A — it uses the depth of the resultant's **line of action** as though it were the centroid depth. Those are different points.
examTip.trick: **F = γh̄A** uses the **CENTROID** (1.5 m here). Cross-check with the pressure prism: ½ × 29.43 × 3 × 2 = 88.3 kN ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Centroid for the FORCE, centre of pressure for its LOCATION.** For a vertical rectangle with its top at the surface, those are H/2 and **2H/3** respectively.

questions.stem: The centre of pressure on a submerged plane surface always lies:
questions.solution:
**Below the centroid — always.**

> **h_cp = h̄ + I_G/(A h̄)**

The correction term **I_G/(Ah̄)** is a **second moment of area divided by two positive quantities**, so it is **always positive**. The centre of pressure therefore always lies **deeper** than the centroid, with no exception.

**The physical reason:**

> **Pressure INCREASES with depth.** The lower portion of the surface therefore experiences greater pressure and contributes more to the total force. The resultant is consequently **pulled downward** from the centroid, which is the centre of **area** alone.

**The distinction is between two different "centres":**

| | Depends on | Location |
|---|---|---|
| **Centroid** | The **AREA** distribution only | The geometric centre |
| **Centre of pressure** | The **FORCE** distribution, which is area × pressure | **Deeper**, weighted toward the high-pressure region |

**How the separation varies:**

| Situation | I_G/(Ah̄) | Separation |
|---|---|---|
| Surface **at the free surface** | Large (h̄ small) | **Greatest** |
| Surface **deeply submerged** | Small (h̄ large) | **Approaches zero** |
| As **h̄ → ∞** | → 0 | Centre of pressure **→ centroid** |

> A deeply submerged plate has nearly **uniform** pressure across it, so the centre of pressure converges on the centroid. A plate at the surface has the pressure varying from zero to its maximum, and the separation is at its largest.

**The standard result** for a **vertical rectangle with its top edge at the water surface**:

> **Centroid at H/2. Centre of pressure at 2H/3 from the surface — that is, H/3 above the base.**

That **H/3 above the base** is worth committing to memory, because it appears in every dam and retaining wall calculation: the water thrust acts at one third of the depth from the bottom, and its moment about the base is therefore **F × H/3**.

**Why it matters:**

| Application | Use of the centre of pressure |
|---|---|
| **Dam stability** | The **overturning moment** is F × (lever arm from the base) |
| **Retaining wall** | The same, for the earth and water thrusts |
| **Sluice gate** | Position of the **hinge** and the **operating force** |
| **Lock gate** | Reaction distribution |
| **Tank wall** | The bending moment diagram |

**A useful cross-check.** For a triangular pressure distribution on a vertical surface, the resultant acts at the **centroid of the triangle** — one third of the height from the base. That is the same H/3 result, obtained by thinking about the **pressure diagram** rather than the formula, and it generalises: **the resultant acts through the centroid of the pressure VOLUME.**

**For a curved surface** the concept still applies but is handled by components:

| Component | Magnitude | Line of action |
|---|---|---|
| **Horizontal F_H** | Force on the **vertical PROJECTION** of the surface | Through the centre of pressure of that projection |
| **Vertical F_V** | **WEIGHT of the fluid** above the surface (real or imaginary) | Through the **centroid of that volume** |

and the resultant is **√(F_H² + F_V²)** at **tan⁻¹(F_V/F_H)** to the horizontal.

**For a circular curved surface**, one further simplification: since every pressure force acts **normal to the surface** and therefore **passes through the centre of the circle**, the **resultant must also pass through the centre** — which locates its line of action without any integration at all. That is the standard trick for a radial (Tainter) gate.

examTip.trick: **h_cp = h̄ + I_G/(Ah̄)**, and the correction term is a positive quantity divided by two positive quantities — so it can never be negative.
examTip.mnemonic: **Pressure grows with depth, so the resultant is dragged downward.** As the plate is submerged deeper the pressure becomes nearly uniform and the centre of pressure **converges on the centroid**. For a surface-piercing rectangle it sits at **H/3 above the base** — the number every dam calculation uses.

questions.stem: In a simple U-tube manometer connected to a pipe, the pressure is determined by:
options: Equating pressures at a common horizontal level in the connected fluid
questions.solution:
**By equating the pressures at a common horizontal level in the connected fluid.**

**The principle** rests on a result of hydrostatics established earlier:

> In a **connected body of the SAME fluid at rest**, the pressure is **equal at all points on the same horizontal plane**.

So a horizontal line is drawn through the manometer at a level where the fluid is continuous and of one kind, and the pressures computed down each limb must be equal.

**The systematic procedure:**

1. **Choose a datum level** — usually the **lower** of the two manometer fluid surfaces, so the line lies in continuous manometer fluid.
2. **Start at one end** with a known pressure (often atmospheric, so gauge zero).
3. Move to the datum, **ADDING γh going DOWN** and **SUBTRACTING γh going UP**.
4. **Equate** to the same walk from the other end.
5. Solve.

**The sign rule is the whole method**: **down adds, up subtracts** — because pressure increases with depth.

**A worked example.** A pipe carrying water is connected to a U-tube containing mercury (S = 13.6). The mercury in the far limb stands **h = 200 mm** above the level in the near limb, and the near mercury level is **300 mm below** the pipe centreline.

> Starting at the pipe centreline at pressure **p**:
> **p + 9810 × 0.3 − (13.6 × 9810) × 0.2 = 0** (atmosphere at the open surface)
> **p = 26 683 − 2943 = 23 740 Pa ≈ 23.7 kPa**

**Types of manometer:**

| Type | Measures | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Piezometer** | **Gauge pressure** in a liquid | Simplest; a vertical tube. Only for **positive, moderate** pressures, and **liquids** |
| **Simple U-tube** | Gauge pressure, positive or negative | Uses a heavier manometer fluid |
| **DIFFERENTIAL U-tube** | **Pressure DIFFERENCE** between two points | The workhorse — used with a venturi or orifice meter |
| **INVERTED U-tube** | **Small** differences in liquids | Uses a **lighter** fluid (air or oil) above |
| **Inclined tube** | Very small pressure differences | **Magnifies** the reading: the length along the tube is **L = h/sin θ** |
| Micromanometer | Minute differences | — |

**The differential manometer relation** for a venturi, which is the connection to flow measurement:

> **h = x(S_m/S_f − 1)**

where x is the manometer deflection, S_m the manometer fluid's specific gravity and S_f the flowing fluid's. For mercury under water: **h = x(13.6 − 1) = 12.6x** — so a 100 mm mercury deflection represents **1.26 m** of water head.

**Choosing the manometer fluid** is a real design decision:

| Requirement | Choice |
|---|---|
| **Large** pressure, want a **short** column | **Heavy** fluid — mercury (13.6) |
| **Small** pressure difference, want a **long, readable** column | **Light** fluid — carbon tetrachloride (1.6), or an **inverted** manometer with air |
| Must not **mix** with the flowing fluid | **Immiscible**, and of clearly different density |

**Practical cautions:**

| Caution | Reason |
|---|---|
| Use tubes of **6 mm bore or more** | To keep the **capillary** correction negligible |
| **Purge all air bubbles** | An unnoticed bubble makes the reading meaningless |
| Both limbs the **same bore** | So capillary effects cancel |
| Read the meniscus **consistently** | Bottom for water, top for mercury |

examTip.trick: The whole method is one sign rule: walk from a known pressure to the datum, **ADD γh going DOWN, SUBTRACT going UP**, then equate the two walks.
examTip.mnemonic: **Down adds, up subtracts.** Choose the datum in **continuous manometer fluid**, usually at the lower of the two mercury surfaces.

questions.stem: The vertical component of the hydrostatic force on a curved surface equals the:
options: Weight of the fluid volume vertically above the surface, real or imaginary
Force on the horizontal projection of the surface
Force on the vertical projection of the surface
Product of pressure at the centroid and the curved area
questions.solution:
**The WEIGHT of the fluid volume vertically above the surface — whether that fluid is really there or is imaginary.**

**Forces on a curved surface are resolved into two components**, because the pressure acts normal to a surface whose direction changes from point to point:

| Component | Equals | Acts through |
|---|---|---|
| **HORIZONTAL F_H** | The force on the **VERTICAL PROJECTION** of the surface | The **centre of pressure of that projection** |
| **VERTICAL F_V** | The **WEIGHT of the fluid volume** vertically above the surface, up to the free surface | The **CENTROID of that volume** |

> **Resultant R = √(F_H² + F_V²)**, at **θ = tan⁻¹(F_V/F_H)** to the horizontal.

**The "real or imaginary" qualification is the crux**, and it is where the concept is usually misunderstood:

| Case | Fluid above? | Direction of F_V |
|---|---|---|
| Surface **concave upward**, fluid resting on it | **REAL** fluid above | **DOWNWARD** |
| Surface **convex upward**, fluid pressing from below | **IMAGINARY** — the volume that *would* lie above | **UPWARD** |

> In the second case the fluid is **below** the surface and pushes **up** on it. The magnitude of that upward force is still the weight of the volume between the surface and the free surface level — the volume of fluid that is **not** there. This is often called the **imaginary** or **virtual** volume, and the result is exact.

**Why it works** — consider the equilibrium of the fluid volume bounded by the curved surface, the free surface, and vertical planes. Its weight must be balanced by the vertical forces on its boundaries; the only vertical force available on the curved boundary is F_V, so F_V equals the weight. The argument runs identically whether the fluid is present or the volume is imagined.

**The special case of a CIRCULAR curved surface** — a Tainter (radial) gate, a pipe wall, a circular arch dam:

> Every pressure force acts **NORMAL to the surface**, and a normal to a circle **passes through its centre**. So **every elemental force passes through the centre**, and therefore **so does the resultant**.

That locates the line of action with no integration whatever, and it is why the **radial gate** is such an elegant design: the entire water thrust passes through the trunnion pin, so the **hoisting force is independent of the water pressure** — the gate needs only to overcome its own weight and friction. A vertical lift gate of the same size needs a hoist sized for the full hydrostatic thrust times the seal friction coefficient.

**A worked illustration.** A quadrant-shaped gate of radius R = 2 m and width b = 3 m, with water to the top of the quadrant:

> **F_H** = force on the vertical projection (a 2 m × 3 m rectangle, top at the surface)
> = γ h̄ A = 9810 × 1 × 6 = **58.9 kN**
> **F_V** = weight of the volume above the surface = γ × (¼πR²) × b = 9810 × (¼π × 4) × 3 = **92.4 kN**
> **R = √(58.9² + 92.4²) = 109.6 kN** at **tan⁻¹(92.4/58.9) = 57.5°** to the horizontal, passing through the centre of the circle.

**The applications:**

| Structure | Curved surface |
|---|---|
| **Radial (Tainter) gate** | The skin plate |
| **Arch dam** | The upstream face |
| **Pipe wall** | Hoop tension: **T = pD/2t** |
| Storage tank shell | The same hoop relation |
| Ship's hull, submerged pipeline | — |

examTip.trap: "Real fluid only" is the misconception. Where the fluid is **below** the surface and pushing up, the volume is **imaginary** — and the rule still gives the exact answer.
examTip.trick: **Horizontal component** = force on the **vertical projection**. **Vertical component** = weight of the fluid volume above, **real or imaginary**.
examTip.mnemonic: **For a CIRCULAR surface the resultant passes through the CENTRE** — every pressure force is normal to the surface, hence radial. That is why a **radial (Tainter) gate's hoist force is independent of the water pressure**.

questions.stem: Archimedes' principle states that the buoyant force on a submerged body equals the:
questions.solution:
**The WEIGHT of the fluid displaced.**

> **F_B = γ_fluid × V_displaced**, acting **vertically UPWARD** through the **CENTRE OF BUOYANCY** — the **centroid of the displaced volume**.

**Why it is true.** The buoyant force is simply the **net vertical pressure force** on the body: the pressure on the **bottom** surface is greater than on the **top**, because the bottom is deeper. Integrating that difference over the body gives exactly the weight of the displaced fluid — a result that holds for any shape.

**The centre of buoyancy is the centroid of the DISPLACED VOLUME, not of the body.** For a uniform fully submerged body the two coincide; for a **floating** body or a body of non-uniform density they do not, and the distinction is what governs stability.

**The three conditions for a body in a fluid:**

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| **W > F_B** | **SINKS** |
