| **W = F_B** | **Neutral** — floats at any depth, fully submerged |
| **W < F_B** | **RISES** to the surface, then **FLOATS** with part above |

**For a FLOATING body, equilibrium requires:**

> **Weight of body = Weight of fluid displaced** — the **PRINCIPLE OF FLOTATION**

so the body sinks until it has displaced its own weight. A steel ship floats because its **average** density, including the enclosed air, is less than water's, even though steel itself is 7.85 times denser.

**STABILITY** is the second and more interesting question, and it differs between submerged and floating bodies:

**Fully SUBMERGED body** — a submarine, a balloon, a submerged pipeline:

| Relative positions | Stability |
|---|---|
| **B ABOVE G** | **STABLE** — a tilt creates a **restoring** couple |
| **B below G** | **UNSTABLE** — a tilt creates an **overturning** couple |
| B coincides with G | Neutral |

> For a submerged body the criterion is simply that the **centre of buoyancy must be ABOVE the centre of gravity**. B and G both stay fixed in the body as it tilts, so the couple they form does the work.

**FLOATING body** — the criterion is different, and this is the point candidates most often confuse:

> For a floating body, **B MOVES as the body tilts**, because the shape of the displaced volume changes. So B may be **below** G and the body still stable — which is the case for virtually every ship.

> The criterion becomes the **METACENTRE M**: **stable if M is ABOVE G**, that is if the **metacentric height GM is POSITIVE**.

> **GM = BM − BG**, where **BM = I/V** — I being the second moment of area of the **waterline plane** about the axis of tilt, and V the displaced volume.

**BM = I/V is the key relation**, and it shows why a **wide** vessel is stable: I varies as the **cube of the beam** (I = LB³/12 for a rectangular waterplane), so widening a vessel increases BM very rapidly. That is why a raft is stable and a log rolls.

**Applications in civil engineering:**

| Application | Use |
|---|---|
| **UPLIFT on submerged structures** | An **empty basement or tank BELOW the water table will FLOAT** — a real and recurring failure |
| **Caisson and well** sinking | The buoyancy **reduces** the effective sinking weight, so kentledge may be needed |
| **Floating docks, pontoon bridges, dredgers** | Direct application |
| **Hydrometer** — for specific gravity, and for the soil grain-size analysis | Floats at a depth set by the fluid density |
| **Effective stress** in soil below water | **σ′ = σ − u** is the same physics: the buoyant unit weight **γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w** |

**The flotation check on an empty structure** is the one worth naming as a design requirement: an empty basement, a swimming pool, or a sewage tank, complete but unloaded, with the water table at its seasonal high, must be checked against uplift with a factor of safety of about 1.2 — and the remedies are added dead weight, tension piles, anchors, or a controlled relief valve.

examTip.trick: It is just the net vertical pressure force: the bottom is deeper than the top, so it feels more pressure, and the difference integrates to the displaced weight.
examTip.mnemonic: **Buoyant force acts through the centroid of the DISPLACED VOLUME, not of the body.** Civil application: an **empty basement or tank below the water table will FLOAT** — check uplift with the structure complete but unloaded.

questions.stem: A floating body is in stable equilibrium when its metacentric height GM is:
questions.solution:
**Positive — the metacentre M lying ABOVE the centre of gravity G.**

> **GM = BM − BG**, with **BM = I/V**

| GM | M relative to G | Stability | Behaviour on tilting |
|---|---|---|---|
| **POSITIVE** | **M above G** | **STABLE** | A **RESTORING** couple returns the body upright |
| **Zero** | M at G | **Neutral** | Stays in the tilted position |
| **NEGATIVE** | M below G | **UNSTABLE** | An **OVERTURNING** couple capsizes it |

**What the metacentre is.** When a floating body tilts through a small angle, the shape of the displaced volume changes and the **centre of buoyancy B shifts sideways** to B′. The **METACENTRE M** is the point where the **new line of buoyant force** crosses the body's original **centreline**.

> The **restoring moment = W × GM × sin θ**, so a positive GM gives a moment that rights the vessel.

**Why a floating body can be stable with B BELOW G** — the point that distinguishes it from a submerged body:

| | **Submerged body** | **Floating body** |
|---|---|---|
| Does B move on tilting? | **NO** — the displaced volume is the whole body, unchanged | **YES** — the waterplane shape changes |
| Stability criterion | **B must be above G** | **M must be above G** (GM > 0) |
| Can it be stable with B below G? | **No** | **YES** — and almost all ships are |

**BM = I/V is the relation that makes it possible**, where **I** is the second moment of area of the **WATERLINE PLANE** about the tilting axis and **V** the displaced volume. For a rectangular waterplane of length L and beam B:

> **I = L B³/12**, so **BM ∝ B³**

**Beam cubed** — so widening a vessel raises the metacentre very rapidly. That is why a **raft or pontoon is extremely stable** and a **log rolls**: the log's tiny waterplane gives a negligible I, hence a negligible BM, and its metacentre falls below its centre of gravity.

**A worked example.** A rectangular pontoon 6 m long, 3 m wide, drawing 0.8 m, with G at 1.0 m above the base:

> **V = 6 × 3 × 0.8 = 14.4 m³**
> **I = 6 × 3³/12 = 13.5 m⁴**
> **BM = 13.5/14.4 = 0.94 m**
> **B (centre of buoyancy) = 0.8/2 = 0.4 m above the base**
> **BG = 1.0 − 0.4 = 0.6 m**
> **GM = 0.94 − 0.6 = +0.34 m — STABLE** ✓

**The design tension in GM** is worth understanding, because bigger is not simply better:

| GM | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Large GM** | **Very stable**, but a **SHORT, JERKY rolling period** — uncomfortable, and hard on cargo and structure |
| **Small positive GM** | A **slow, easy roll** — comfortable, but a **small margin** against capsize |

> **Rolling period T = 2π k/√(g × GM)**, where k is the radius of gyration.

So the naval architect chooses GM as a **compromise** between safety and seakeeping — typically **0.3 to 1.0 m** for a cargo ship, more for a vessel carrying deck cargo.

**Determining GM experimentally — the INCLINING EXPERIMENT:**

> A known weight **w** is moved a known distance **x** across the deck, and the resulting small angle of heel **θ** is measured by a pendulum.
> **GM = w x/(W tan θ)**

It is performed on every new vessel before it enters service, and it is the only reliable way to establish the actual position of G for a real, complicated structure.

**Civil engineering applications**: **pontoon bridges**, **floating docks and jetties**, **dredgers**, **caissons being floated to position**, and **barge-mounted plant** — all require the GM check, and the caisson case is the one where a civil engineer is most likely to perform it personally.

examTip.trap: Applying the submerged-body rule (B above G) to a floating body is the standard error — **almost every ship has B below G and is perfectly stable.**
examTip.trick: For a floating body **B MOVES** as it heels, so the criterion shifts to the metacentre: **GM = BM − BG** with **BM = I/V**.
examTip.mnemonic: **BM = I/V, and I ∝ beam³** — which is why a raft is stable and a log rolls. Design tension: a **large GM is stable but rolls harshly**; a small positive GM is comfortable but marginal.

questions.stem: For a fully submerged body, stable equilibrium requires that the centre of buoyancy be:
questions.solution:
**Above the centre of gravity.**

**Why the criterion differs from a floating body's** — the essential difference:

> For a **fully submerged** body, the **displaced volume is the whole body and does NOT change shape** when it tilts. So **B stays fixed in the body**, and the metacentre coincides with B (BM = I/V = 0, since there is no waterline plane).

> The criterion therefore reduces to the simple one: **B must be ABOVE G**.

| | **SUBMERGED** | **FLOATING** |
|---|---|---|
| Displaced volume on tilting | **Unchanged** | **Changes shape** |
| Does B move? | **No** | **Yes** |
| BM = I/V | **0** (no waterplane) | **Positive** |
| Criterion | **B above G** | **M above G**, i.e. **GM > 0** |
| Can be stable with B below G? | **No** | **Yes** |

**The tilting couple.** Both W (down through G) and F_B (up through B) are equal in magnitude. If **B is above G**, tilting separates them into a couple that **rotates the body back upright** — restoring. If **B is below G**, the couple **increases the tilt** — the body turns over until B is above G again.

**Which is why a submarine carries ballast LOW**: the heavy batteries, machinery and ballast tanks are in the bottom of the hull, pulling **G down below B**. It is not an incidental arrangement but the condition of the vessel's survival.

**And why a hot-air balloon is stable**: the heavy basket and burner hang well below the envelope's centre of buoyancy, so G is far below B and the assembly is very stable indeed.

**Civil engineering cases of submerged bodies:**

| Case | Stability consideration |
|---|---|
| **Submerged pipeline** | Must be **weighted (concrete coated)** so it does not float — and ballasted to stay upright |
| **Immersed tube tunnel** sections | Floated to position, then sunk; stability during the sinking operation is critical |
| **Caisson** during flotation and sinking | The transition from floating to submerged is the dangerous phase |
| Submerged tanks and chambers | **UPLIFT** check |
| Diving bells, subsea equipment | — |

**The immersed tube tunnel is the most demanding of these**: a tunnel element is floated out with just a few hundred millimetres of freeboard, then sunk by admitting ballast water. During that transition it passes through a state of **near-neutral buoyancy with a very small waterplane** — which means **BM = I/V is small** while the element is still partly afloat, and the stability margin is at its minimum precisely when the element is least controllable. The operation is therefore planned around maintaining adequate GM throughout, using ballast distribution and temporary buoyancy towers to keep the waterplane area up.

**The uplift check on submerged structures** is the everyday application, and it is the same physics stated as a design requirement:

> **Factor of safety against flotation = (downward forces) / (uplift force) ≥ 1.2**

with the uplift taken as **γ_w × displaced volume** at the **highest credible water table**, and the downward forces counting only the **reliable dead load** — never the live load, which may be absent, and never the weight of a superstructure not yet built.

**A note on partly submerged bodies**: a body floating with only a small part above the surface has a **small waterplane area**, hence a small I, hence a small BM — so it is close to the submerged criterion and needs B above G, or nearly so. This is the **"low freeboard" instability** that makes a nearly-swamped boat so dangerous: as the freeboard falls, the effective waterplane shrinks and the metacentric height collapses.

examTip.trick: A fully submerged body's displaced volume **cannot change shape**, so B stays fixed in the body and BM = I/V = 0. The metacentre collapses onto B, and the criterion reduces to B above G.
examTip.mnemonic: **Submerged: B above G. Floating: M above G.** A submarine keeps its batteries in the keel for exactly this reason. The dangerous case is the transition — an **immersed tube tunnel element** being sunk passes through minimum GM precisely when it is least controllable.

questions.stem: The hydrostatic paradox states that the force on the base of a vessel depends on:
options: The total weight of liquid in the vessel
The depth of liquid and the base area only
questions.solution:
**The DEPTH of liquid and the BASE AREA only** — not on the shape of the vessel or the weight of liquid it contains.

> **F = p × A = γ h A**

**The paradox stated concretely.** Three vessels have the **same base area** and hold liquid to the **same depth**, but differ in shape:

| Vessel | Shape | Weight of liquid | Force on the base |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cylindrical** | Straight sides | W | **γhA** |
| **Flaring outward** | Wider at top | **Much MORE than W** | **γhA — the same** |
| **Narrowing to a thin neck** | Narrow at top | **Much LESS than W** | **γhA — the same** |

> A vessel holding a **thimbleful** of water in a thin tube above a wide base exerts the **same force on that base** as a vessel holding **many litres** — provided the depth is the same.

**The resolution is in the WALLS**, and it is worth working through because it dissolves the apparent contradiction:

| Vessel | The walls | Vertical force from the walls on the liquid |
|---|---|---|
| **Flaring outward** | Slope outward, so the liquid presses **outward and up** on them; by reaction they press **DOWN** on the liquid | **Downward** — but the base force is unchanged, so the extra weight is carried by the walls |
| **Narrowing (thin neck)** | Slope inward, so the walls press **UP** on the liquid | **Upward** — supplying the apparent deficit |

In every case **vertical equilibrium of the whole liquid body holds exactly**: base force + wall vertical components = weight. The base force is set by γh, and the walls take up whatever difference the shape creates.

**A cleaner way to see it**: the pressure at the base is **γh**, and pressure depends only on **depth**, by p = γh. There is nowhere for the shape to enter. It follows immediately.

**Practical consequences:**

| Consequence | Explanation |
|---|---|
| A **DAM's** water thrust depends on **DEPTH**, not on the **size of the reservoir** | A small deep pond and a vast lake of the same depth exert the same pressure on the face |
| **Standpipe** pressure testing | A thin standpipe generates full test pressure with very little water |
| **Water supply pressure** depends on the reservoir's **LEVEL**, not its capacity | Which is why service reservoirs are placed high, not made large, to get pressure |
| **Formwork pressure** from fresh concrete | Depends on the depth of the pour (and the rate), not the total volume |

**The dam point is the one worth emphasising** because it surprises people:

> The **entire Indian Ocean** pressing on a 10 m deep sea wall exerts **exactly the same pressure** as a 10 m deep swimming pool would. The size of the water body behind is irrelevant; only the **depth** counts.

What the reservoir's size **does** affect is quite different things: the **duration** of a flood, the **energy** available, the **sediment** load, and the **consequences of failure** — but not the hydrostatic pressure on the structure.

**A related result — the force on the base of a vessel need not equal the weight it stands on the ground with.** Put a narrow-necked flask on a balance: the balance reads the true total weight (liquid + vessel), while the base of the liquid experiences γhA, which may be much greater. There is no contradiction; the vessel's own walls transmit the difference to the balance.

**Pascal's demonstration** of this — the **barrel-bursting experiment** — is the historical illustration: a long thin vertical tube fitted to a sealed barrel and filled with a few litres of water generated enough pressure to burst the barrel, because the **head** was several metres even though the **weight** added was trivial.

examTip.trap: "The weight of liquid" is the intuitive answer and is decisively wrong — three vessels of wildly different contents give identical base forces.
examTip.trick: **p = γh** contains no term for shape or volume. There is nowhere for them to enter.
examTip.mnemonic: **The WALLS carry the difference** — sloping walls push down or lift up on the liquid, and equilibrium holds exactly. Consequence: a dam's thrust depends on **DEPTH, not reservoir size**. A 10 m pond loads a wall exactly as a 10 m ocean would.

questions.stem: In a hydraulic jack, a force of 100 N on a piston of area 10 cm² can lift a load on a piston of area 500 cm² equal to:
questions.solution:
**5000 N.**

> **Pascal's principle**: pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted **UNDIMINISHED** throughout.
> **p = F₁/A₁ = 100/(10 × 10⁻⁴) = 100 000 Pa = 100 kPa**
> **F₂ = p A₂ = 100 000 × (500 × 10⁻⁴) = 5000 N** ✓

**Or simply by the area ratio:**

> **F₂/F₁ = A₂/A₁ = 500/10 = 50**, so **F₂ = 50 × 100 = 5000 N**

**Mechanical advantage = the area ratio.** That is the whole principle of the hydraulic jack, press, brake and lift.

**But energy is conserved, and the price is DISTANCE:**

> The **volume displaced is the same on both sides**: **A₁ d₁ = A₂ d₂**
> So **d₂ = d₁ × (A₁/A₂) = d₁/50**

> To raise the load **1 mm**, the small piston must travel **50 mm**. The **work done is identical** on both sides (100 N × 50 mm = 5000 N × 1 mm = 5 J) — as it must be, since the fluid stores no energy.

**This is exactly analogous to a lever, a pulley system or a gear train**: force is multiplied and distance divided, with the product — the work — unchanged. The hydraulic jack is a lever made of fluid, and its advantage is that the two "ends" need not be rigidly connected or even near each other.

**Which is the real engineering benefit:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Force multiplied** by the area ratio | Very large ratios are easy to achieve |
| **Force transmitted around corners** | Through flexible hoses — no linkage geometry required |
| **One pump can drive several rams** | Distributed force, synchronised |
| **Smooth, controllable** force | No backlash |
| **Compact** for the force delivered | High pressures give high force in a small cylinder |

**Applications:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Hydraulic jack and press** | The direct case |
| **Vehicle brakes** | One master cylinder, four slave cylinders |
| **Excavator and crane** hydraulics | — |
| **Prestressing JACKS** | Tensioning tendons in post-tensioned concrete |
| **Bridge bearing replacement** | Synchronised jacks lifting a whole span |
| Hydraulic gates and hoists | — |
| **Compression testing machine** | The load is measured from the hydraulic pressure |

**The prestressing jack** is the one a civil engineer handles directly, and the pressure-to-force relation is how the tendon force is actually controlled: the jack has a calibrated pressure gauge, and the specified tendon force is applied by pumping to the corresponding **gauge pressure** — cross-checked against the measured **elongation** of the tendon. Agreement between the two within about 5% is the standard acceptance criterion, and a discrepancy indicates friction losses, a slipping anchorage or a jack out of calibration.

**Practical requirements** for the principle to hold:

| Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|
| The fluid must be **CONFINED** | Otherwise it simply flows away |
| **No air** in the system | Air is compressible, so the stroke is absorbed in squashing it — hence **bleeding** the brakes |
| Both pistons at the **same level**, or the γh difference allowed for | The pressure differs with elevation |
| Seals must hold the working pressure | Leakage loses force |

**The air-in-the-system point is the practical one**: a spongy brake pedal or a jack that sinks under load is almost always air, not a seal failure — because air's bulk modulus (10⁵ Pa) is **twenty thousand times** lower than oil's, so even a small bubble absorbs the entire stroke.

examTip.trick: **Mechanical advantage = area ratio = 500/10 = 50**, so 100 N lifts 5000 N.
examTip.mnemonic: **Force multiplied, distance divided — work unchanged.** To raise the load 1 mm the small piston travels 50 mm. Practical corollary: **air in the system ruins it**, because air's bulk modulus is 20 000× lower than oil's, so the whole stroke is absorbed squashing the bubble. That is a spongy brake pedal.

questions.stem: A differential mercury manometer connected across a venturi shows a deflection of 150 mm. The equivalent head of water is:
questions.solution:
**1890 mm = 1.89 m of water.**

> **h = x (S_m/S_f − 1) = 0.150 × (13.6/1 − 1) = 0.150 × 12.6 = 1.89 m** ✓

**Option (b), 2040 mm**, is the trap: it is **x × 13.6**, omitting the **−1**. That omission is the single commonest error in manometry, and it is worth understanding why the term is there.

**Why subtract 1.** The mercury deflection x displaces mercury **up one limb and down the other**, but in doing so it **also displaces the water** that was occupying those spaces. The net pressure difference is therefore the weight of the mercury column **minus** the weight of the water column it replaced:

> **Δp = x γ_m − x γ_f = x γ_f (S_m/S_f − 1)**
> Expressed as a head of the **flowing** fluid: **h = x (S_m/S_f − 1)** ✓

**The general relation:**

> **h = x (S_m/S_f − 1)**

where **x** is the manometer deflection, **S_m** the manometer fluid's specific gravity and **S_f** the flowing fluid's. The result **h** is a head **of the flowing fluid**.

**Common combinations:**

| Manometer fluid | Flowing fluid | Multiplier (S_m/S_f − 1) |
|---|---|---|
| **Mercury (13.6)** | **Water (1.0)** | **12.6** |
| Mercury | Oil (0.8) | 16.0 |
| Carbon tetrachloride (1.6) | Water | 0.6 |
| **Air (inverted)** | Water | ≈ **−1** — the inverted manometer, where **h = x(1 − S_m/S_f)** |

**Choosing the manometer fluid** is a genuine design decision, and this table shows why:

> For a **LARGE** pressure difference, use a **HEAVY** fluid (mercury) so the column stays short and manageable.
> For a **SMALL** difference, use a **LIGHT** fluid (carbon tetrachloride, or an **INVERTED** manometer with air) so the deflection is **magnified** and readable.

A 1.89 m water head shown as 150 mm of mercury is a 12.6-fold **compression** of the reading — convenient for a large head, useless for a small one. The same head shown on an inverted air manometer would be 1.89 m of deflection, which is why inverted manometers are used for the small differences across a filter or a short pipe run.

**Then the venturi discharge:**

> **Q = C_d × (A₁A₂/√(A₁² − A₂²)) × √(2gh)**

with **C_d ≈ 0.98** for a well-made venturi. Note that h here is the **head difference in metres of the flowing fluid** — which is exactly what the manometer relation delivers, and why the −1 term matters: using 2.04 m instead of 1.89 m would overstate the discharge by **√(2.04/1.89) = 3.9%**.

**An important property of the venturi–manometer combination:**

> The relation **h = x(S_m/S_f − 1)** holds **whatever the INCLINATION of the venturi** — horizontal, vertical or sloping. The elevation terms in the Bernoulli equation and in the manometer reading **cancel exactly**.

So a venturi meter can be installed in any orientation and calibrated identically. That is a genuinely useful practical result, and it follows from the fact that the manometer connections are themselves subject to the same elevation difference as the flow.

**A final check on the arithmetic**: 12.6 × 0.15 — a useful mental shortcut is 12.6 × 0.15 = 12.6 × 0.1 + 12.6 × 0.05 = 1.26 + 0.63 = **1.89** ✓

examTip.trap: 2040 mm is **x × 13.6** — the classic error of **omitting the −1**. It appears on almost every manometer question.
examTip.trick: The rising mercury **displaces the water** that was there, so the net effect is the *difference* in weights: **h = x(S_m/S_f − 1) = 0.15 × 12.6 = 1.89 m.**
examTip.mnemonic: **Mercury under water: multiply by 12.6, not 13.6.** Useful property: the relation holds **whatever the venturi's inclination** — the elevation terms cancel exactly.

questions.stem: The pressure distribution on the vertical upstream face of a dam retaining water of depth H is:
options: Triangular, from zero at the surface to γH at the base
questions.solution:
**Triangular — zero at the water surface, increasing linearly to γH at the base.**

> **p = γ z**, where z is the depth below the surface — a **linear** relation, so the diagram is a **triangle**.

**The resultant thrust per metre length of dam:**

> **P = ½ γ H²** (the area of the pressure triangle)
> acting at **H/3 above the base** (the centroid of the triangle)

**For H = 20 m**: **P = ½ × 9810 × 400 = 1962 kN/m** — nearly 2000 kN for every metre of dam length, acting 6.67 m above the base. The **overturning moment about the toe** is then **1962 × 6.67 = 13 086 kN·m/m**.

**Note the H² dependence**, which is the dominating fact of dam design:

> **DOUBLING the depth QUADRUPLES the thrust — and the overturning moment increases EIGHTFOLD** (since the moment is P × H/3 ∝ H³).

That is why dam sections grow so rapidly with height, and why the base width of a gravity dam is roughly proportional to its height.

**The forces on a gravity dam** and their directions:

| Force | Direction | Magnitude |
|---|---|---|
| **Self weight W** | **Down**, through the section's centroid | The **stabilising** force |
| **Water thrust P** | **Horizontal**, at H/3 above the base | **½γH²** per metre |
| **UPLIFT U** | **UP**, on the base | The most treacherous |
| Silt pressure | Horizontal, near the base | Using the submerged unit weight |
| Earthquake forces | Horizontal and vertical | Inertia plus **hydrodynamic** (Westergaard) |
| Ice, wave, tailwater | Various | Site-specific |

**UPLIFT deserves emphasis** because it is the force most often underestimated and it acts in the worst possible direction:

> Water penetrates the **foundation and the dam–rock interface**, exerting an **UPWARD** pressure over the base area. It **REDUCES the effective weight** of the dam — reducing both the sliding resistance (which depends on the normal force) and the overturning resistance.

**Controlling uplift:**

| Measure | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **DRAINAGE GALLERY** with relief holes near the heel | **Intercepts and relieves** the seepage — the single most effective measure |
| **GROUT CURTAIN** at the heel | Reduces the seepage entering |
| Foundation treatment, consolidation grouting | Reduces permeability generally |
| Impervious upstream blanket | Lengthens the seepage path |

> A **grout curtain plus a drainage gallery** typically reduces the uplift at the drain line to about **one third** of the reservoir head, and the assumed uplift diagram becomes a broken line rather than a straight one from heel to toe. The drainage is more reliable than the grouting, which is why both are used and why the drains are inspected and re-drilled over the dam's life.

**The stability checks on a gravity dam:**

| Check | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **OVERTURNING** | FS = (righting moments)/(overturning moments) ≥ **2.0** |
| **SLIDING** | FS = μ(ΣV − U)/ΣH ≥ **1.5**; with shear–friction factor ≥ 4 |
| **NO TENSION** at the heel | The resultant must stay within the **MIDDLE THIRD** of the base |
| **Compressive stress** within the allowable | At the toe, which carries the greatest stress |

**The no-tension requirement is the one that shapes the section**: concrete and, more importantly, the **rock joint at the base** cannot carry tension, and any crack at the heel **admits full reservoir pressure into the crack**, which then propagates. So the resultant of all forces must fall within the middle third of the base, and the section is proportioned to ensure it — for both the reservoir-full and reservoir-empty conditions.

examTip.trick: p = γz is **linear in depth**, so the diagram must be a triangle: zero at the surface, γH at the base.
examTip.mnemonic: **P = ½γH² acting at H/3 above the base.** Note **P ∝ H²** and the **moment ∝ H³** — doubling the depth quadruples the thrust and multiplies the overturning moment eightfold. That is why dam sections grow so fast with height, and why **UPLIFT** (relieved by a drainage gallery) is the force most often underestimated.

questions.stem: A tank of water is accelerated horizontally at a m/s². The free surface makes an angle with the horizontal whose tangent is:
questions.solution:
**tan θ = a/g.**

**Relative equilibrium** — a fluid accelerating uniformly moves **as a rigid body**, with no relative motion between its particles and therefore **no shear stress**, so the hydrostatic methods still apply with gravity replaced by the resultant of gravity and the acceleration.

**Derivation.** Consider a fluid particle at the free surface. The forces on it are its weight **mg** downward and the pressure gradient force. For it to accelerate horizontally at **a**, the resultant must be horizontal of magnitude **ma**. Since the free surface must be **perpendicular to the resultant body force**:

> **tan θ = a/g** ✓

**The free surface tilts DOWN in the direction of acceleration** — the water piles up at the **rear**. Anyone who has carried a full bucket, or watched a tanker accelerate, has seen it.

**The pressure at any point** is still found from the depth measured **perpendicular to the tilted free surface**, or equivalently:

> **p = ρ(g z − a x)** taking x in the direction of acceleration

**The consequences for design:**

| Situation | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Road tanker** braking or accelerating | The **surge** loads the end bulkhead; a full tanker's surge can jack-knife the vehicle |
| **Baffle plates** in tankers | Fitted specifically to **limit the surge** by breaking up the free surface |
| **Water tank on a building** in an earthquake | **SLOSHING** — and the tank must have freeboard for it |
| Lift/elevator carrying liquid | Vertical acceleration case |

**The VERTICAL acceleration case** is the companion result:

> **p = ρ(g ± a)h** — **plus** for upward acceleration, **minus** for downward.

> In **FREE FALL (a = g downward), the pressure everywhere becomes ZERO** — the fluid is weightless, and a bucket of water dropped from a height exerts no pressure on its base. That is a striking result and a good check on the formula.

**ROTATION about a vertical axis** — the third standard case:

> The free surface becomes a **PARABOLOID of revolution**: **z = ω²r²/(2g)**
> The **rise at the wall equals the depression at the centre**, each being **ω²R²/(4g)** from the original level.

**That equal rise and fall** follows from conservation of volume, and it is the quick way to locate the new surface without integrating: the vertex of the paraboloid drops by exactly as much as the rim rises.

**Applications of the rotating case:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Centrifugal pump** — pressure rise in the impeller | The same ω²r²/2g term |
| **Rotating (centrifugal) casting** of concrete pipes | Compacts the concrete against the mould |
| Centrifuge testing of soil models | Simulates prototype stresses at small scale |
| Vortex flow, free and forced | — |

**The distinction between forced and free vortex** is worth adding here since it belongs with the rotating case:

| | **FORCED vortex** | **FREE vortex** |
|---|---|---|
| Velocity | **v = ωr** — increases outward | **v = c/r** — decreases outward |
| Driven by | An **external torque** (an impeller, a rotating vessel) | **No external torque** — angular momentum conserved |
| Free surface | **Paraboloid rising outward** | **Hyperbolic, dropping steeply at the centre** |
| Example | Water in a rotating bucket; pump impeller | **Water draining from a bath**; a whirlpool; flow in a scroll casing |

A real vortex — a bathtub drain, or a **vortex drop shaft** — is usually a **combination**: a forced vortex core surrounded by a free vortex, called a **Rankine vortex**.

examTip.trick: The free surface must be **perpendicular to the resultant body force** — the vector sum of g downward and a backward. Hence **tan θ = a/g**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water piles up at the BACK when you accelerate.** Companion results: **vertical** acceleration gives p = ρ(g ± a)h — so in **free fall the pressure is zero everywhere**. **Rotation** gives a paraboloid, with the rim rising exactly as much as the centre falls.

questions.stem: The hoop tension in a thin circular pipe of internal diameter D under internal pressure p, per unit length, is:
questions.solution:
**pD/2** per unit length of pipe, giving a hoop **stress** of **σ = pD/(2t)**.

**Derivation** — consider a half-pipe of unit length cut along a diameter:

> The pressure force on the projected area: **p × D × 1**
> Resisted by tension in **two** wall sections: **2T**
> **2T = pD**, so **T = pD/2** ✓
> **σ_hoop = T/t = pD/(2t)**

**The LONGITUDINAL stress** in a closed pipe or cylinder is **half** the hoop stress:

> **σ_long = pD/(4t)**

**Derivation**: the pressure acts on the end area **πD²/4**, resisted by the wall of area **πDt**, giving **σ = pD/(4t)** ✓

**So the hoop stress is TWICE the longitudinal stress** — which is why:

| Consequence | Explanation |
|---|---|
| A **pressurised pipe splits LENGTHWISE**, not around its circumference | The hoop stress reaches the limit first |
| A **sausage splits along its length** when cooked | The same physics |
| **Spiral welds** in a pipe are efficient | The weld is not aligned with the maximum stress |
| A **spherical** vessel is more efficient than a cylinder | **σ = pD/(4t)** in **all** directions — half the cylinder's hoop stress for the same p, D, t |

**The spherical vessel result is why gas storage spheres are spherical**: for the same pressure and diameter, a sphere needs **half the wall thickness** of a cylinder. Cylinders are used where the shape suits the application (pipes must be long) or where fabrication is simpler.

**Design of a penstock or pressure pipe:**

> **t = pD/(2σ_allowable) + corrosion allowance**

with the **pressure p taken as the maximum**, including:

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **Static head** | γH from the reservoir level |
| **WATER HAMMER surge** | Can **double or triple** the static pressure — often the governing case |
| Test pressure | Usually 1.5 × working |

**The water hammer allowance is essential**: a penstock designed for the static head alone will fail on the first emergency shutdown. **Joukowsky: Δp = ρcΔV**, and for water at 3 m/s in a steel pipe (c ≈ 1200 m/s) that is **3.6 MPa ≈ 360 m** of additional head — frequently more than the static head itself.

**Where the relation is used:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Penstocks** in hydropower | Both hoop and longitudinal; often with stiffener rings |
| **Water supply mains** | Class of pipe selected by pressure rating |
| **Prestressed concrete cylinder pipe** | The prestress puts the concrete into compression so the hoop tension never develops as net tension |
| **Storage tank shells** | The hoop force varies with depth: **T = γ h D/2** |
| Boilers, gas cylinders | The same theory |

**For a TANK, the hoop force varies with depth** because the pressure does:

> **T(h) = γ h D/2** — **maximum at the base**, zero at the top

which is why a steel tank's plates are **thicker at the bottom** and get progressively thinner up the shell — a stepped design that follows the pressure diagram.

**The thin-cylinder assumption** behind all of this is **D/t > 20**, so that the stress may be taken as uniform through the wall thickness. For a thick cylinder (D/t < 20) the stress varies radially and **Lamé's equations** are needed — relevant for high-pressure hydraulic cylinders and gun barrels, but rarely for civil engineering pipework.

examTip.trick: Hoop from a diametral cut: pressure force **pDL** resisted by **two** wall thicknesses **2tL**, so **σ = pD/2t**. Longitudinal from an end cut gives **pD/4t** — exactly half.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hoop is twice longitudinal — so a pipe SPLITS LENGTHWISE.** A **sphere** is pD/4t in every direction, needing **half** a cylinder's thickness, which is why gas storage vessels are spherical. Always design a penstock for static head **plus water hammer**, which often exceeds it.

questions.stem: A body weighs 500 N in air and 300 N when fully immersed in water. Its volume is:
questions.solution:
**0.0204 m³.**

> **Buoyant force = loss of weight in water = 500 − 300 = 200 N**
> **F_B = γ_w V**, so **V = 200/9810 = 0.02039 m³ ≈ 0.0204 m³** ✓

**And the body's other properties follow at once:**

> **Density: ρ = m/V = (500/9.81)/0.0204 = 50.97/0.0204 = 2499 kg/m³**
> **Specific gravity: S = 2499/1000 = 2.5**

A specific gravity of 2.5 is about right for **concrete, stone or glass** — a sensible cross-check on the arithmetic.

**A shortcut worth knowing:**

> **S = W_air/(W_air − W_water) = 500/200 = 2.5** ✓

The same result without computing the volume at all, and it works because both weights scale with the same volume.

**This is the principle of the HYDROSTATIC WEIGHING method** for specific gravity, and it is used in real testing:

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Specific gravity of AGGREGATE** | IS 2386 Part 3 — the standard method, weighing in air and in water |
| **Specific gravity of soil solids G_s** | By pycnometer, the same principle |
| **Density of hardened concrete** cores | — |
| **Water absorption** of aggregate and brick | The saturated surface-dry weight enters the calculation |
| Archimedes' original problem | Testing the goldsmith's crown |

**The aggregate test is the one specified**, and its arithmetic is exactly this question's:

> **Specific gravity = A/(A − C)** where A is the oven-dry weight in air and C the weight in water
> **Apparent specific gravity = A/(B − C)** where B is the saturated surface-dry weight in air
> **Water absorption % = 100(B − A)/A**

**Note the different definitions**, which trip people up: **bulk** specific gravity uses the total volume including the accessible pores; **apparent** specific gravity excludes them. For a dense aggregate the two are nearly equal; for a porous one they differ appreciably, and specifying which is meant matters.

**A variation on the question worth being ready for — a body immersed in a fluid OTHER than water:**

> **V = (W_air − W_fluid)/(S_fluid × 9810)**

So the same body weighed in oil of S = 0.8 would lose only **0.8 × 200 = 160 N**, weighing **340 N**.

**And the case where the body FLOATS**, which is a different calculation:

> A floating body displaces its **own weight**, not its own volume. **V_displaced = W/γ_fluid**, and the **submerged fraction = S_body/S_fluid**.

So a body of S = 0.9 floats with **90%** of its volume submerged in water. **Ice (S = 0.917) floats with about 92% submerged** — the origin of the expression about the tip of the iceberg, and a number that is nine tenths rather than the one tenth people often assume.

**A caution on the method**: the body must be **fully immersed and free of trapped air bubbles**, and the suspension wire's own buoyancy must be negligible or corrected for. An air bubble adhering to a rough specimen adds spurious buoyancy and understates the specific gravity — which is why the standard requires the specimen to be **soaked and the surface bubbles brushed off** before weighing.

examTip.trick: **Loss of weight = buoyant force = 200 N; V = 200/9810 = 0.0204 m³.** Shortcut for the specific gravity: **S = W_air/(W_air − W_water) = 500/200 = 2.5** — no volume needed.
examTip.mnemonic: **S = 2.5 means concrete or stone** — a sanity check on the arithmetic. This is exactly the IS 2386 method for aggregate specific gravity; brush the bubbles off the specimen or the result reads low.

questions.stem: In a rotating cylindrical vessel of radius R spinning at angular velocity ω, the rise of the liquid at the wall above the original level is:
questions.solution:
**ω²R²/(4g).**

**The free surface becomes a PARABOLOID of revolution:**

> **z = ω²r²/(2g)** — the height of the surface above its **vertex** (the lowest point, at the centre)

So the **total height difference** between the centre and the wall is:

> **z_total = ω²R²/(2g)**

**But that is measured from the vertex, not from the original level.** By **conservation of volume**, since the paraboloid's volume is exactly **half** that of the enclosing cylinder, the original level lies **midway**:

> **Rise at the wall = ω²R²/(4g)**
> **Depression at the centre = ω²R²/(4g)** — **equal and opposite** ✓

**The equal rise and fall is the memorable result**, and it is the quick way to locate the new surface: the vertex drops by exactly as much as the rim rises, each being **half** the total height difference.

**A worked example.** A vessel of R = 0.3 m spun at 60 rpm (ω = 2π rad/s = 6.283 rad/s):

> **Total difference = ω²R²/(2g) = (6.283)² × (0.3)²/(2 × 9.81) = 39.48 × 0.09/19.62 = 0.181 m**
> **Rise at wall = 0.091 m; depression at centre = 0.091 m**

**Two conditions worth being able to handle:**

| Condition | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Liquid **just touches the rim** without spilling | The rise at the wall equals the **freeboard** |
| The **vertex just reaches the base** — liquid clears the centre | The depression equals the **original depth** |

Beyond the second condition a **dry circle** is exposed at the centre of the base, and its radius follows from setting z = 0 there.

**FORCED versus FREE vortex** — the distinction this case introduces:

| | **FORCED vortex** | **FREE vortex** |
|---|---|---|
| Velocity distribution | **v = ωr** — **increases** outward | **v = c/r** — **decreases** outward |
| Cause | An **external TORQUE** — a rotating vessel, a pump impeller | **NO external torque**; **angular momentum conserved** |
| Free surface | **Paraboloid**, rising outward | **Hyperbolic**, plunging steeply at the centre |
| Energy | **Increases** outward (torque adds energy) | **Constant** — Bernoulli applies throughout |
| Examples | Water in a spun bucket; **centrifugal pump impeller** | **Bathtub drain**; whirlpool; **flow in a spiral casing**; a tornado's outer region |

**The energy distinction is the important one**: in a **forced** vortex, external work is being done, so the total energy **increases with radius** and Bernoulli's equation cannot be applied between different radii. In a **free** vortex no work is done, so the **total head is constant** and Bernoulli applies — which is what makes the free vortex analytically tractable.

**A real vortex is usually both** — a **Rankine vortex**, with a **forced-vortex core** (where viscosity forces the fluid to rotate together) surrounded by a **free-vortex outer region**. The bathtub drain, the tornado and the vortex drop shaft all have this structure, and it resolves the free vortex's unphysical prediction of infinite velocity at r = 0.

**Engineering applications:**

| Application | Vortex type |
|---|---|
| **Centrifugal pump** pressure rise in the impeller | Forced — the **ω²r²/2g** term is the pressure head generated |
| **Spiral (volute) casing** of a pump or turbine | Free — designed for **vr = constant** |
| **VORTEX DROP SHAFT** in a spillway or sewer | Free — the swirl **dissipates energy** against the shaft wall |
| **Air-entraining vortex at a pump intake** | A nuisance — prevented by adequate **submergence** and anti-vortex baffles |
| Centrifugal casting of concrete pipe | Forced |

**The intake vortex is the practical problem** most often met: insufficient submergence at a pump or turbine intake lets a free vortex form and draw air down into the suction, causing loss of capacity, vibration and cavitation. The remedy is **greater submergence** (a rule of thumb being S > D + 0.23V/√D) or **anti-vortex devices** — a floating raft, a splitter plate, or a curtain wall.

examTip.trap: ω²R²/(2g) is the **total** height difference between centre and rim. The question asks the rise **above the original level**, which is half of it.
examTip.trick: Conservation of volume: a paraboloid holds exactly **half** its enclosing cylinder, so the original level sits midway — the **rim rises exactly as much as the vertex falls**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Half up, half down.** Distinguish **forced** vortex (v = ωr, driven by torque, paraboloid) from **free** vortex (v = c/r, no torque, Bernoulli applies throughout) — a bathtub drain is free, a spun bucket is forced.

questions.stem: Atmospheric pressure at sea level corresponds to a head of water of about:
questions.solution:
**10.33 m of water.**

> **p_atm = 101.325 kPa**
> **h = p/γ = 101 325/9810 = 10.33 m of water** ✓
> **= 760 mm of mercury** (since 101 325/(13.6 × 9810) = 0.760 m)

**The standard equivalences, worth knowing cold:**

| Expression | Value |
|---|---|
| **1 atmosphere** | **101.325 kPa** |
| | **10.33 m of water** |
| | **760 mm of mercury** |
| | **1.01325 bar** |
| Approximately | **≈ 100 kPa ≈ 10 m of water ≈ 1 bar** |

> The working approximation **10 m of water ≈ 1 bar ≈ 1 atmosphere** is the most useful number in hydraulics, and it should be instant.

**Option (a), 1.033 m**, is the trap: 1.033 is the atmosphere expressed in **kgf/cm²**, an older unit still met on gauges — not a head in metres at all. Option (b), 76 m, confuses metres with the **760 mm** of mercury.

**The single most important consequence — the LIMIT ON SUCTION LIFT:**

> A pump can only lift water by suction because **ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE PUSHES IT UP** into the evacuated space. The **theoretical maximum lift is therefore 10.33 m**, and no pump of any design can exceed it.

**In practice the limit is much lower**, and it is worth seeing why:

| Deduction | Typical value |
|---|---|
| Theoretical maximum | **10.33 m** |
| Less **vapour pressure** of water (2.34 kPa at 20 °C) | **−0.24 m** |
| Less **friction losses** in the suction pipe | −0.5 to −1.5 m |
| Less **NPSH required** by the pump | −2 to −4 m |
| Less a **safety margin** | −0.5 m |
| **Practical maximum suction lift** | **about 6 to 7 m** |

**And at ALTITUDE it is less still**, which matters directly in Nepal:

| Elevation | p_atm | Head of water | Practical suction lift |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sea level** | 101.3 kPa | **10.33 m** | ~7 m |
| **Kathmandu (1400 m)** | **86 kPa** | **8.8 m** | **~5.5 m** |
| 3000 m | 70 kPa | 7.1 m | ~4 m |
| 5000 m | 54 kPa | 5.5 m | ~2.5 m |

> A pump installation designed on sea-level assumptions **will fail at altitude**. The atmospheric pressure must be taken from the **site elevation** — a rule of thumb being a reduction of about **1.1 m of water head per 1000 m** of elevation.

**The barometer** is the direct application: **Torricelli's** mercury barometer stands at 760 mm because that is the column of mercury the atmosphere supports. A **water** barometer would need a tube over **10.33 m** tall — which is why mercury is used, quite apart from its non-wetting behaviour.

**Absolute versus gauge, restated with these numbers:**

> **p_absolute = p_gauge + 101.3 kPa** (at sea level)

| Situation | Gauge | Absolute |
|---|---|---|
| Open water surface | **0** | 101.3 kPa |
| 10 m below the surface | **98.1 kPa** | 199.4 kPa |
| A **perfect vacuum** | **−101.3 kPa** | **0** |
| Water at its vapour point, 20 °C | −99 kPa | **2.34 kPa** |

**The last row is the cavitation condition**, and it shows why the calculation must be done in **absolute** terms: the criterion is that the absolute pressure must not reach the absolute vapour pressure, and a gauge-pressure calculation has no way to express that.

examTip.trap: 1.033 is the atmosphere in **kgf/cm²**, an older gauge unit — not a head in metres. 76 confuses metres with the **760 mm** of mercury.
examTip.mnemonic: **10.33 m water = 760 mm mercury = 1 atm.** This is the **absolute ceiling on suction lift** — and practically only 6–7 m after vapour pressure, friction and NPSH. At Kathmandu's 1400 m it falls to about **5.5 m**.

questions.stem: The continuity equation for steady incompressible flow in a pipe of varying section states that:
questions.solution:
**A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ = Q = constant.**

**It is a statement of the CONSERVATION OF MASS.** For a steady flow, whatever mass enters a control volume must leave it:

> **ρ₁A₁V₁ = ρ₂A₂V₂**

and for an **incompressible** fluid (ρ constant) this reduces to the **volumetric** statement **A₁V₁ = A₂V₂**.

**The consequence:**

> **Velocity is INVERSELY proportional to area.** Where the pipe **narrows, the flow SPEEDS UP**; where it widens, it slows.

**A worked example.** Water flows at 2 m/s in a 200 mm pipe that reduces to 100 mm:

> **A₁ = π(0.2)²/4 = 0.0314 m²**, **A₂ = π(0.1)²/4 = 0.00785 m²**
> **V₂ = V₁A₁/A₂ = 2 × (0.0314/0.00785) = 8 m/s**

**Note that HALVING the diameter QUADRUPLES the velocity**, since area varies as D². For a circular pipe the relation is conveniently:

> **V₂/V₁ = (D₁/D₂)²**

**Continuity is used constantly, and often as the first step:**

| Application | Use |
|---|---|
| **Venturi and orifice meters** | Combined with Bernoulli to relate the pressure drop to Q |
| **Pipe networks** | At each junction, **inflow = outflow** (Kirchhoff's first law for pipes) |
| **Open channel flow** | **Q = AV** at every section |
| **Reservoir routing** | **Inflow − Outflow = dS/dt** — the unsteady form |
| Nozzles and jets | The jet velocity from the supply pipe velocity |

**The UNSTEADY form** is the general one and is worth stating, because it underlies flood routing:

> **Inflow − Outflow = rate of change of STORAGE**
> **I − O = dS/dt**

When storage is constant (steady flow) it reduces to I = O. When a reservoir is filling, the difference accumulates — and that single equation, solved step by step, is the whole of reservoir flood routing.

**Why continuity and Bernoulli are used TOGETHER.** Continuity relates the **velocities**; Bernoulli relates the **pressures and velocities**. Neither alone solves a varying-section problem:

> **Continuity:** A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ — two unknowns, one equation
> **Bernoulli:** p₁/γ + V₁²/2g + z₁ = p₂/γ + V₂²/2g + z₂
> **Together:** the venturi discharge formula

**The physical pairing they express** is worth stating, because it explains the venturi:

> Flow through a **contraction ACCELERATES** (continuity), and where it accelerates the **pressure FALLS** (Bernoulli). So a throat is a region of **high velocity and low pressure** — which is why a venturi can measure flow from a pressure reading, and also why cavitation occurs at throats.

**A caution about the mass form.** For a **compressible** flow, ρ₁A₁V₁ = ρ₂A₂V₂ must be used, and the volumetric statement fails. In civil engineering the volumetric form is essentially always adequate for water, and for air below about 100 m/s — but a long gas pipeline, where the density falls appreciably along its length, requires the mass form.

examTip.trick: It is conservation of mass. For constant density it reduces to a purely **volumetric** statement, so the flow rate through every section is the same.
examTip.mnemonic: **V ∝ 1/A, and for a pipe V₂/V₁ = (D₁/D₂)² — halve the diameter and the velocity QUADRUPLES.** Continuity gives velocities, Bernoulli gives pressures; a varying-section problem needs both.

questions.stem: Flow in which the velocity at a given point does not change with time, but does change from point to point along the flow, is:
questions.solution:
**Steady and non-uniform.**

**Two independent classifications**, and confusing them is the point of the question:

| Classification | Question asked | Mathematically |
|---|---|---|
| **STEADY / UNSTEADY** | Does it change with **TIME** at a fixed point? | **∂V/∂t = 0** for steady |
| **UNIFORM / NON-UNIFORM** | Does it change with **POSITION** along the flow? | **∂V/∂s = 0** for uniform |

**They are independent, so all four combinations exist:**

| Combination | Example |
|---|---|
| **Steady uniform** | **Constant** flow in a **long straight pipe of constant diameter** |
| **Steady NON-uniform** | **Constant** flow through a **TAPERING** pipe or a venturi; flow over a weir at constant discharge |
| **Unsteady uniform** | Flow in a constant-diameter pipe during a **valve closure** — same at every section, changing with time |
| **Unsteady non-uniform** | A **FLOOD WAVE** in a river; the general case |

> **Steady is about TIME; uniform is about SPACE.** Holding that distinction is the whole of the question.

**Most real flows are unsteady and non-uniform**, and are analysed by **assuming** steadiness where the change with time is slow enough to be neglected. That assumption is what makes routine hydraulic design tractable, and knowing when it fails matters:

| Assumption fails | Because |
|---|---|
| **Water hammer** | The flow changes in **milliseconds** |
| **Flood routing** | The discharge changes over hours; storage must be tracked |
| **Surge in a channel** | A moving wave front |
| Reservoir filling and drawdown | Storage changes |

**In OPEN CHANNEL flow the same terms are used but the classification is applied to the DEPTH**, which is the more useful variable:

| Flow | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Uniform flow** | **Depth CONSTANT along the channel** — the **normal depth**; the water surface is **parallel to the bed** |
| **Gradually varied flow (GVF)** | Depth changes **slowly** — **backwater curves**, computed by the GVF equation |
| **Rapidly varied flow (RVF)** | Depth changes **abruptly** — a **HYDRAULIC JUMP**, flow over a weir, a sluice gate |

**Uniform flow in a channel requires** a prismatic channel of constant slope, roughness and discharge, long enough for the depth to settle — and then the **gravity component driving the flow exactly balances the boundary friction resisting it**, which is the condition **Manning's equation** expresses.

**Other kinematic classifications** worth having:

| Pair | Distinction |
|---|---|
| **LAMINAR / TURBULENT** | Orderly layers versus chaotic mixing — decided by **Reynolds number** |
| **ROTATIONAL / IRROTATIONAL** | Do fluid elements **spin** about their own axes? Irrotational if **∂v/∂x = ∂u/∂y** |
| **Compressible / incompressible** | Does the density change? |
| **One-, two-, three-dimensional** | How many coordinates the velocity depends on |

**Irrotational flow matters** because it permits a **VELOCITY POTENTIAL φ** to be defined, from which the whole flow field follows — the basis of **flow nets** and potential flow theory. Real flow is irrotational outside the boundary layer, which is why the flow net is a good model of seepage and of flow around structures.

examTip.trap: The two words are independent and are constantly conflated. **Steady is about TIME; uniform is about SPACE.**
examTip.trick: Constant discharge through a taper: nothing changes with time (steady) but velocity changes along the pipe (non-uniform).
examTip.mnemonic: **Steady = ∂/∂t = 0. Uniform = ∂/∂s = 0.** All four combinations exist. In open channels the same words describe the DEPTH: uniform = normal depth, GVF = backwater, RVF = hydraulic jump.

questions.stem: A streamline is a line such that:
options: The velocity vector is tangential to it at every point
The pressure is constant along it
The velocity is constant along it
It marks the path of a single particle over time
questions.solution:
**A line to which the VELOCITY VECTOR is TANGENTIAL at every point.**

**The immediate consequence:**

> Since the velocity is tangential, there is **NO FLOW ACROSS a streamline**. Streamlines act as though they were solid boundaries — which is what makes them so useful.

**The related lines**, which are distinct but coincide in steady flow:

| Line | Definition |
|---|---|
| **STREAMLINE** | Velocity is **tangential** at every point, at **one instant** |
| **PATHLINE** | The **actual path** traced by **one particle** over time |
| **STREAKLINE** | The line joining all particles that have **passed through one point** — what a dye injection shows |
| Streamtube | A tube whose walls are made of streamlines |

> **In STEADY flow all three COINCIDE.** In **unsteady** flow they differ, and the distinction matters for flow visualisation — a dye trace shows the **streakline**, which in unsteady flow is not the streamline.

**Option (d) describes a PATHLINE**, and it is the most tempting wrong answer for exactly that reason.

**A STREAMTUBE** is a bundle of streamlines forming a tube. Since no flow crosses its walls, it behaves as a **pipe with imaginary walls** — and **continuity applies to it**:

> **A₁V₁ = A₂V₂** along a streamtube

> So where streamlines **CONVERGE** (the tube narrows) the **velocity INCREASES**, and where they diverge it decreases. A streamline diagram is therefore a **velocity map**: closely spaced streamlines mean fast flow.

**That reading of a streamline plot is genuinely useful** — it lets you see at a glance where a flow is accelerating (and by Bernoulli, where the pressure is low) without any calculation.

**FLOW NETS** combine streamlines with **equipotential lines**, and are the classical graphical solution for two-dimensional potential flow:

| Property | Statement |
|---|---|
| Streamlines and equipotentials are **ORTHOGONAL** | They cross at **right angles** everywhere |
| The mesh consists of approximate **SQUARES** | Which is the criterion for a correctly drawn net |
| No flow **crosses** a streamline | — |
| **Boundaries** are streamlines | An impervious boundary is a flow line |
| A **free surface / water surface** is a streamline | With atmospheric pressure on it |

**The seepage application** is the one a civil engineer uses:

> **q = k H (N_f/N_d)**

where **N_f** is the number of **flow channels**, **N_d** the number of **equipotential drops**, k the permeability and H the total head loss. The **shape factor N_f/N_d** depends only on the geometry, so one flow net serves any permeability and any head.

**And the flow net gives more than the discharge:**

| Quantity | From the net |
|---|---|
| **Seepage quantity** | q = kH(N_f/N_d) |
| **Pore pressure** at any point | From the number of drops to that point |
| **UPLIFT** on a structure | Integrating the pore pressure over the base |
| **EXIT GRADIENT** | **i_exit = Δh/Δl** at the **downstream exit**, where the field is smallest — checked against the critical gradient for **PIPING** |

**The exit gradient is the safety-critical output**: **piping** occurs when the upward seepage force lifts the soil grains, and the check is **i_exit < i_critical/F** with **i_critical = (G−1)/(1+e) ≈ 1** and F between 4 and 7. It is why the downstream end of the net is drawn most carefully, and why cutoff walls and filters are placed where they are.

examTip.trap: "The path of a single particle" describes a **PATHLINE**, and it is the most tempting distractor. The three coincide only in **steady** flow.
examTip.trick: Because the velocity is tangential, **no flow crosses a streamline** — so a bundle of them behaves as a pipe with imaginary walls, and continuity applies to it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Streamlines converging = flow accelerating = pressure falling.** A streamline plot is a velocity map you can read at a glance.

questions.stem: Bernoulli's equation in the form p/γ + V²/2g + z = constant is valid for:
options: Steady, incompressible, frictionless flow along a streamline
questions.solution:
**Steady, incompressible, frictionless flow along a streamline.**

**The assumptions in full:**

| Assumption | If violated |
|---|---|
| **STEADY** flow | An unsteady term is needed |
| **INCOMPRESSIBLE** | ρ must stay inside the integral |
| **FRICTIONLESS (inviscid)** | A **head loss term h_f** must be added |
| **Along a STREAMLINE** | Unless the flow is **irrotational**, in which case it holds throughout the field |
| No **energy added or removed** | Otherwise pump/turbine head terms are needed |
| Along a **single** streamline (constant density) | — |

**The three terms are all HEADS — that is, LENGTHS:**

| Term | Name | Physical meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **p/γ** | **Pressure head** | The height a column of the fluid would rise under that pressure |
| **V²/2g** | **VELOCITY (kinetic) head** | The height a jet of that velocity would rise |
| **z** | **Elevation (potential) head** | Height above the datum |
| **Sum** | **TOTAL head** | **Constant** for ideal flow |

> Because every term is a length, the equation can be **drawn**: the **hydraulic grade line (HGL)** plots p/γ + z, and the **energy grade line (EGL)** plots the total head. That graphical representation is one of the most useful tools in hydraulics.

**HGL and EGL properties:**

| Property | Statement |
|---|---|
| **EGL is always ABOVE the HGL** by **V²/2g** | The vertical gap is the velocity head |
| **EGL always FALLS** in the direction of flow | Because of friction — unless a pump adds energy |
| **HGL may RISE** | Where the pipe **expands** and the velocity falls |
| The HGL **coincides with the water surface** in an open channel | Since p = 0 at the surface |
| **HGL below the pipe** means **NEGATIVE pressure** | A siphon; a risk of cavitation and air release |

**The extended (real-fluid) form** is what is actually used:

> **p₁/γ + V₁²/2g + z₁ + h_pump = p₂/γ + V₂²/2g + z₂ + h_turbine + h_L**

**Applications:**

| Application | Use |
|---|---|
| **VENTURI meter** | Pressure drop at the throat → discharge |
| **Orifice and nozzle** | **Torricelli: V = √(2gh)** |
| **PITOT tube** | Stagnation minus static head → velocity |
| **Siphon** | Whether the flow will run, and where cavitation threatens |
| Pump and turbine systems | Sizing the head required |
| Flow over a weir | — |

**Torricelli's result** is Bernoulli at its simplest: applying it from a reservoir surface (V ≈ 0, p = 0) to a jet issuing at depth h (p = 0),

> **V = √(2gh)**

which is exactly the velocity a body would reach falling freely through h — the potential energy of the head converted entirely to kinetic energy.

**The commonest misuse** is applying Bernoulli **across a region of high loss**, where the frictionless assumption fails badly:

| Where Bernoulli fails | Why | Use instead |
|---|---|---|
| Across a **sudden EXPANSION** | Large eddy losses | The **momentum** equation, or **h_L = (V₁−V₂)²/2g** |
| Across a **HYDRAULIC JUMP** | Violent turbulent dissipation | The **momentum** equation |
| Through a long pipe | Friction accumulates | Bernoulli **with h_f** from Darcy–Weisbach |
| Across a pump or turbine | Energy added or removed | Include the machine head |

**The rule of thumb** worth carrying:

> Use **ENERGY (Bernoulli)** where the **losses are small or known**. Use **MOMENTUM** where the **losses are large or unknown** but the **forces** are what you need — because the momentum equation does not require the losses to be quantified.

examTip.trick: Every term is a **length**, which is what lets the equation be drawn as the **HGL and EGL**. The EGL always falls (friction); the HGL may **rise** where the pipe expands.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use ENERGY where losses are small or known; use MOMENTUM where they are large or unknown.** So Bernoulli fails across a sudden expansion or a hydraulic jump — use momentum there instead.

questions.stem: The velocity head of water flowing at 4 m/s is:
questions.solution:
**0.82 m.**

> **Velocity head = V²/2g = 4²/(2 × 9.81) = 16/19.62 = 0.815 m ≈ 0.82 m** ✓

**Option (a), 0.41 m**, is V²/4g — a factor-of-two slip. Option (d), 0.20 m, is V/2g, forgetting to square.

**A useful mental shortcut**: **V²/2g ≈ V²/20**, which for V = 4 gives 16/20 = 0.8 — close enough to identify the right option instantly.

**Typical velocity heads**, worth having a feel for:

| Velocity | V²/2g |
|---|---|
| **1 m/s** | **0.05 m** |
| **2 m/s** | **0.20 m** |
| **3 m/s** | 0.46 m |
| **4 m/s** | **0.82 m** |
| 6 m/s | 1.83 m |
| 10 m/s | 5.10 m |

**The quadratic growth is the point**: the velocity head is **negligible at low speeds and dominant at high ones**. At 1 m/s it is 50 mm and can often be ignored; at 10 m/s it is over 5 m and dominates the energy balance.

**Which is why design velocities are limited:**

| System | Typical design velocity | Reason for the limit |
|---|---|---|
| **Water supply mains** | **0.6 – 2.0 m/s** | Below: **sedimentation**. Above: **erosion, noise, water hammer** and excessive head loss |
| **Sewers (self-cleansing)** | **min 0.6 – 0.75 m/s** | To keep solids in suspension |
| Sewers (maximum) | 3 m/s | Erosion of the invert |
| **Penstocks** | 3 – 6 m/s | Economic balance between pipe cost and head loss |
| Pump suction lines | **< 1.5 m/s** | To protect **NPSH** |
| Irrigation canals (unlined) | 0.6 – 1.0 m/s | Erosion of the bed |

**The economic optimum for a pipeline** is worth understanding, because it explains the ranges above:

> A **larger** pipe costs more to buy but has a **lower velocity, hence lower head loss**, hence lower **pumping cost** over its life. A **smaller** pipe is cheaper but costs more to pump through. The **economic diameter** minimises the sum of capital and running costs.

Since **h_f ∝ V² ∝ 1/D⁴** and pumping power ∝ Q h_f, the running cost falls very steeply with diameter — which is why the optimum usually lies at a lower velocity than intuition suggests, and why undersized rising mains are such a common and expensive mistake.

**The velocity head in an open channel** carries an extra refinement — the **kinetic energy correction factor α**:

> **Velocity head = α V²/2g**

because the velocity is **not uniform** across the section, and the mean of the cubes exceeds the cube of the mean:

| Channel | α |
|---|---|
| Regular channel, turbulent | **1.03 – 1.10** |
| Natural river with a flood plain | **1.5 – 2.0** |
| Laminar pipe flow | **2.0** exactly |

> For a **river with a flood plain**, where the deep channel flows fast and the shallow overbank slowly, **α can reach 2** — so the velocity head is **double** what the mean velocity suggests. Ignoring α in a flood level calculation is then a real error.

**The companion is the MOMENTUM correction factor β** (1.01–1.05 for regular channels, 2.0 for laminar pipe flow), used in the momentum equation for the same reason.

examTip.trick: **V²/2g = 16/19.62 = 0.82 m.** Mental shortcut: **V²/20** gets you close enough to pick the option instantly.
examTip.mnemonic: **1 m/s → 0.05 m; 4 m/s → 0.82 m; 10 m/s → 5.1 m.** The quadratic growth is why design velocities are capped: water mains 0.6–2.0 m/s, sewers minimum 0.6–0.75 for self-cleansing. In an open channel add **α**, which reaches **2.0 on a river with a flood plain**.

questions.stem: The force exerted by a flowing fluid on a pipe bend is best calculated using:
options: The momentum equation, applied to a control volume enclosing the bend
questions.solution:
**The MOMENTUM equation, applied to a control volume enclosing the bend.**

> **ΣF = ρQ(V_out − V_in)** — a **VECTOR** equation, applied **component by component**

**For a bend in the horizontal plane turning through angle θ:**

> **F_x = p₁A₁ − p₂A₂cos θ − ρQ(V₂cos θ − V₁)**
> **F_y = −p₂A₂ sin θ − ρQ(V₂ sin θ − 0)**
> **Resultant R = √(F_x² + F_y²)**

where F_x and F_y are the force components the **bend exerts on the fluid**; the force **on the bend** is equal and opposite.

**Why the momentum equation and not Bernoulli** — the reason is fundamental:

| | **ENERGY (Bernoulli)** | **MOMENTUM** |
|---|---|---|
| Gives | **Pressures and velocities** | **FORCES** |
| Requires losses to be | **Known and small** | **Not known at all** |
| A scalar or vector? | **Scalar** | **VECTOR** — direction matters |
| Use where | Losses are small or quantified | **Forces are wanted**, or losses are large/unknown |

> **The momentum equation does NOT require the energy losses to be known.** It relates the net force to the change in momentum flux, and whatever turbulence and dissipation occur inside the control volume are irrelevant to it. That is exactly why it works across a hydraulic jump, a sudden expansion, or a complicated bend where Bernoulli would fail.

**The standard applications of the momentum equation:**

| Application | Force found |
|---|---|
| **Force on a pipe BEND** | The **thrust block** design load |
| **Force on a REDUCER or nozzle** | Anchorage |
| **Jet striking a plate** — flat, curved, moving | Turbine and Pelton bucket theory |
| **HYDRAULIC JUMP** | Relates the conjugate depths |
| **Sudden expansion** loss | Combined with energy: **h_L = (V₁−V₂)²/2g** |
| **Sluice gate** force | — |
| Propulsion, thrust | — |

**THRUST BLOCKS** are the practical outcome for a civil engineer:

> An unrestrained pipe bend will **move** under the resultant force, pulling the joints apart. A **concrete thrust block** transfers that force to the surrounding soil by **passive resistance**.

**A worked scale.** A 300 mm main carrying 0.15 m³/s at 8 bar through a 90° bend:

> **A = 0.0707 m², V = 2.12 m/s**
> Pressure terms dominate: **pA = 800 000 × 0.0707 = 56.6 kN** in each direction
> Momentum terms: **ρQV = 1000 × 0.15 × 2.12 = 0.32 kN** — small by comparison
> **Resultant ≈ √(56.9² + 56.9²) = 80 kN**, bisecting the bend angle

**The lesson from that arithmetic**: for a normal water main the **PRESSURE term dominates** and the momentum term is almost negligible. It is the **static pressure**, not the flow, that pushes the bend outward — which is why a thrust block must be sized for the **test pressure** with the pipe full and **not flowing**, and why capping a dead end needs a thrust block just as a bend does.

**Where the momentum term does dominate**: high-velocity, low-pressure flows — a **free jet** striking a Pelton bucket, or the nappe from a spillway hitting a stilling basin floor.

**A caution on applying it**: the control volume must be drawn so that the **inlet and outlet sections are in regions of known, reasonably uniform flow**, and **all** external forces must be counted — pressure forces on the inlet and outlet faces, the weight of the fluid, and the reaction from the pipe wall. Omitting the pressure force on a face is the commonest error.

examTip.trap: Bernoulli is offered and is the wrong tool — it gives pressures and velocities, never forces, and it is a **scalar** equation.
examTip.trick: **ΣF = ρQ(V_out − V_in)** is a **vector** equation applied component by component. Crucially, it does **not require the losses to be known**.
examTip.mnemonic: **For a normal water main the PRESSURE term dominates and the momentum term is tiny** — so size a thrust block for the **test pressure with the pipe not flowing**, and remember a **dead end needs one just as a bend does**.

questions.stem: Flow in a circular pipe is generally taken as laminar when the Reynolds number is below:
questions.solution:
**2000.**

> **Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν**

| Reynolds number | Regime |
|---|---|
| **Re < 2000** | **LAMINAR** |
| **2000 – 4000** | **TRANSITIONAL** — unpredictable |
| **Re > 4000** | **TURBULENT** |

**What the Reynolds number is:**

> **Re = INERTIA forces / VISCOUS forces**

| Re | Which dominates | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **Low** | **VISCOUS** | Disturbances are **damped out** — orderly, layered flow |
| **High** | **INERTIA** | Disturbances **grow** — chaotic mixing |

**The two regimes compared:**

| | **LAMINAR** | **TURBULENT** |
|---|---|---|
| Motion | **Orderly layers**, no mixing | **Chaotic**, strong mixing |
| **Velocity profile** | **PARABOLIC** | **Logarithmic** — much **flatter** |
| **V_mean/V_max** | **0.5** | **≈ 0.82** |
| **Friction factor** | **f = 64/Re** — depends on **Re ONLY** | Depends on **Re AND roughness** |
| **Head loss** | **h_f ∝ V** | **h_f ∝ V^1.75 to V²** |
| Shear stress | Purely **viscous** | Viscous **plus** turbulent (Reynolds) stresses |
| Mixing, heat transfer | **Poor** | **Excellent** |

**Almost all civil engineering water flow is TURBULENT.** Check: water at 1 m/s in a 100 mm pipe gives **Re = 1 × 0.1/10⁻⁶ = 100 000** — a hundred times the laminar limit. Laminar flow in water requires either a very small pipe or a very low velocity.

**Where laminar flow does occur:**

| Case | Note |
|---|---|
| **Groundwater seepage** | Very low velocity — which is why **Darcy's law is LINEAR** (v = ki) |
| **Oil pipelines** | High viscosity |
| Capillary and micro-channel flow | — |
| Lubricating films | Very thin |
| Blood in capillaries | — |

**Darcy's law being linear is a direct consequence of laminar seepage**, and it is worth seeing the connection: **v = ki** holds because the flow is viscous-dominated, so resistance is proportional to velocity. At high gradients through coarse gravel or rockfill the flow **becomes turbulent and Darcy's law FAILS** — which is why rockfill drains and gabions are analysed with non-linear resistance laws.

**Laminar pipe flow — Hagen–Poiseuille:**

> **Q = πΔp D⁴/(128 μL)**, or **h_f = 32μVL/(γD²)**

**Note the D⁴** — the discharge varies as the **fourth power of the diameter**. Halving a pipe's diameter cuts the flow to **one sixteenth** at the same pressure. That extreme sensitivity is why a partly blocked capillary, filter or artery loses capacity so dramatically.

**The CRITICAL Reynolds number is not a sharp constant.** The **lower critical value (~2000)** is reasonably reproducible — below it, flow is laminar however much it is disturbed. The **upper** value depends on the care taken: in a very smooth pipe with an undisturbed inlet, laminar flow has been maintained to **Re = 40 000** or beyond. So 2000 is the value **below which laminar flow is guaranteed**, not the point at which turbulence must begin.

**Other Reynolds numbers** worth distinguishing, since the characteristic length changes:

| Situation | Characteristic length | Critical value |
|---|---|---|
| **Pipe** | **Diameter D** | 2000 |
| **Open channel** | **Hydraulic radius R** | **500** (since D ≈ 4R) |
| **Flat plate** boundary layer | Distance **x** from the leading edge | **5 × 10⁵** |
| Sphere | Diameter | 1 (for Stokes' law) |

**The open-channel value of 500 follows directly** from the pipe value: for a full circular pipe **R = D/4**, so Re based on R is one quarter of Re based on D — and 2000/4 = 500.

examTip.trick: **Re = VD/ν** compares inertia with viscosity. Below 2000 viscosity damps every disturbance; above 4000 disturbances grow.
examTip.mnemonic: **Almost all civil water flow is turbulent** — 1 m/s in a 100 mm pipe is already Re = 100 000. Laminar flow matters for **groundwater seepage** (which is exactly why **Darcy's law is LINEAR**) and for oil. Note the open-channel critical value is **500**, because R = D/4.

questions.stem: For an orifice, the coefficient of discharge C_d is related to the coefficients of velocity and contraction by:
questions.solution:
**C_d = C_v × C_c.**

**The three coefficients:**

| Coefficient | Definition | Typical value |
|---|---|---|
| **C_v** — velocity | **Actual velocity / theoretical velocity** at the vena contracta | **0.95 – 0.99** |
| **C_c** — contraction | **Area of the VENA CONTRACTA / area of the orifice** | **0.61 – 0.69** |
| **C_d** — discharge | **Actual discharge / theoretical discharge** | **0.60 – 0.65** |

> **Q_actual = C_d A √(2gh)**, where **A** is the **orifice** area and **h** the head above its centre.

**Why it is a product.** The actual discharge is the actual **velocity** times the actual **area**:

> **Q = (C_v V_theory) × (C_c A) = C_v C_c × (A V_theory) = C_d Q_theory** ✓

So each coefficient corrects one factor, and the corrections multiply.

**The VENA CONTRACTA** is the key physical feature:

> The jet **CONTINUES TO CONTRACT** after leaving the orifice, reaching its **minimum area about half a diameter downstream**. The streamlines converging toward the orifice **cannot turn a sharp corner**, so they carry on inward past the plane of the opening.

> At the vena contracta the streamlines are **parallel** and the pressure is **atmospheric** — which is the only section where Bernoulli can be applied cleanly, and why the coefficients are defined there.

**C_c ≈ 0.62 for a sharp-edged orifice** is the dominant loss: the discharge is reduced far more by the contraction of the jet than by any velocity loss. **C_v is close to 1** because a short, accelerating flow has very little friction.

> **Which is why C_d ≈ 0.62** — essentially the contraction coefficient, lightly reduced.

**Improving the coefficient** by controlling the contraction:

| Type | C_d | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Sharp-edged orifice** | **0.62** | Full contraction |
| **Bell-mouthed (rounded) entry** | **0.98** | The rounding **guides the streamlines**, so there is almost **no contraction** |
| **Borda's mouthpiece** (re-entrant, running full) | 0.707 | Theoretically derivable |
| **External cylindrical mouthpiece** running full | **0.855** | The jet contracts then **re-expands** to fill the tube |
| **Venturi** | **0.98** | Gradual convergence |

**The bell-mouth result is a genuinely useful design lesson**: simply **rounding an entry** raises the discharge coefficient from 0.62 to 0.98 — a **58% increase in capacity** for no extra opening size. That is why intakes, culvert entries and pump suction bells are rounded rather than square-cut.

**Torricelli's theoretical velocity** underlying all of it:

> **V_theory = √(2gh)** — from Bernoulli between the reservoir surface and the jet

**The trajectory method** for measuring C_v experimentally is worth knowing:

> The jet is a **projectile**. Measuring the horizontal distance **x** and the fall **y** from the orifice:
> **C_v = x/(2√(hy))**

which requires no velocity measurement at all — only a scale and a plumb line.

**Where orifice theory applies in practice:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Orifice plate flow meter** | Cheap; higher permanent head loss than a venturi |
| **Sluice gate discharge** | **Q = C_d b a √(2gh)** |
| **Reservoir outlet and draw-off** | — |
| **Tank emptying time** | Integrating Q = C_d A√(2gh) as h falls |
| Culvert under inlet control | — |
| Orifice-type flow restrictors | — |

**The orifice plate versus the venturi** is a standard comparison: the **orifice** is cheap, compact and easy to install, but its **permanent head loss is high** (perhaps 50–70% of the differential) because the jet expands abruptly and dissipates energy. The **venturi** costs more and is bulkier, but recovers most of its pressure (permanent loss ~10%) because its **gradual diffuser** decelerates the flow without separation.

examTip.trick: Actual discharge = actual **velocity** × actual **area**, so the two corrections **multiply**. C_v ≈ 0.98 (little friction in a short accelerating flow) and **C_c ≈ 0.62**, so C_d ≈ 0.62 — the contraction does nearly all the damage.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rounding the entry raises C_d from 0.62 to 0.98** — a 58% capacity gain for nothing but a radius. That is why intakes, culvert entries and pump suction bells are always belled.

questions.stem: A Pitot tube measures the velocity of flow by sensing the difference between:
options: The stagnation (total) pressure and the static pressure
The pressures upstream and downstream of a contraction
questions.solution:
**The STAGNATION (total) pressure and the STATIC pressure.**

> **V = C_v √(2g Δh)**, where **Δh** is the difference between the stagnation and static heads

**How it works.** A tube facing **into** the flow brings the fluid to **rest** at its opening — a **STAGNATION POINT**. By Bernoulli, all the velocity head there is converted to pressure head:

> **Stagnation head = static head + V²/2g**
> so **Δh = V²/2g**, giving **V = √(2gΔh)** ✓

**The two pressures and how they are sensed:**

| Pressure | Sensed by | Reads |
|---|---|---|
| **STATIC** | An opening **PARALLEL** to the flow (flush with the wall, or side holes) | **p/γ + z** |
| **STAGNATION (total)** | An opening **FACING INTO** the flow | **p/γ + z + V²/2g** |
| Difference | — | **V²/2g** — the **velocity head** |

**The PITOT-STATIC tube** combines both in one instrument: a central tube facing upstream for the stagnation pressure, and an annulus with side holes for the static — connected to a differential manometer that reads the difference directly. That combination is what makes it a practical field instrument.

**Its defining characteristic:**

> A Pitot tube measures the velocity at a **POINT**, not the discharge. To obtain Q, the velocity must be measured at **several points across the section** and **integrated**.

**Which distinguishes it from the other meters:**
