| Meter | Measures | Head loss | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PITOT tube** | **POINT velocity** | **Negligible** | Must traverse to get Q; blocks easily |
| **VENTURI** | **Discharge** | **Low (~10%)** | Accurate, C_d ≈ 0.98; bulky and costly |
| **Orifice plate** | Discharge | **High (50–70%)** | Cheap and compact; C_d ≈ 0.62 |
| Nozzle meter | Discharge | Medium | Between the two |
| **Electromagnetic** | Mean velocity | **None** | No obstruction; needs a conducting fluid |
| **Ultrasonic** | Mean velocity | **None** | Clamp-on types need no pipe entry |
| **Current meter** | Point velocity | — | The **river gauging** standard |

**In river gauging** the same point-measurement logic applies, and it is formalised as the **velocity–area method**:

> The cross-section is divided into **segments**; the mean velocity in each is measured with a **current meter**; and **Q = Σ(a_i v_i)**.

**The depth at which to measure** is standardised, and it is a genuinely useful piece of practice:

| Depth | Method |
|---|---|
| **Shallow water** | **One point at 0.6 × depth** from the surface — this reads close to the mean |
| **Deeper water** | **Two points, at 0.2 and 0.8 depth**, averaged |
| Very deep or irregular | Three points: 0.2, 0.6, 0.8, weighted |

> The **0.6-depth rule** works because a logarithmic velocity profile has its **mean value at about 0.6 of the depth below the surface** — a convenient accident of the profile shape that saves a great deal of fieldwork.

**Practical cautions with a Pitot tube:**

| Caution | Reason |
|---|---|
| Must be **aligned with the flow** | A yaw of more than about 10° gives a low reading |
| The **static holes must be far enough back** | Away from the disturbance of the nose |
| **Blocks easily** | Small openings; unsuitable for dirty water or sewage |
| **C_v ≈ 0.98** for a well-made tube | Not exactly 1 |
| Poor at **low velocities** | Δh varies as V², so at 0.5 m/s the reading is only 13 mm — hard to measure |

**The low-velocity limitation** is the practical constraint: because Δh ∝ V², halving the velocity **quarters** the reading. Below about 1 m/s a Pitot tube becomes unreliable, and an electromagnetic or ultrasonic meter is used instead.

examTip.trick: A tube facing the flow brings it to rest, converting the velocity head into pressure head. The **difference** between stagnation and static is therefore **V²/2g** exactly.
examTip.mnemonic: **A Pitot tube measures a POINT velocity, not a discharge** — you must traverse the section and integrate. It is also poor below about 1 m/s, since Δh ∝ V². In river gauging the same logic gives the **0.6-depth rule**: a logarithmic profile has its mean at 0.6 of the depth.

questions.stem: A flow is irrotational if:
options: The fluid elements do not rotate about their own axes, so ∂v/∂x = ∂u/∂y
questions.solution:
**If the fluid elements do not rotate about their own axes** — the condition being **∂v/∂x = ∂u/∂y**, that is, **zero vorticity**.

> **Rotation ω_z = ½(∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y)**, and the flow is **irrotational when ω_z = 0**.

**The distinction that trips people up:**

> A fluid element can travel along a **CURVED path** and still be **IRROTATIONAL**, provided it does not **spin about its own axis** as it goes. Conversely, a flow along **straight** streamlines can be **ROTATIONAL** if the velocity varies across them.

**The two classic illustrations:**

| Flow | Streamlines | Rotational? |
|---|---|---|
| **FREE vortex** (v = c/r) — a bathtub drain | **Circular** | **IRROTATIONAL** — an element goes round the centre without spinning |
| **FORCED vortex** (v = ωr) — a spun bucket | Circular | **ROTATIONAL** — the whole body rotates together |
| **Laminar pipe flow** | **Straight** | **ROTATIONAL** — the velocity gradient shears each element |
| Uniform flow | Straight | Irrotational |

**The free vortex is the memorable case**: think of a chair on a Ferris wheel — it travels in a circle but always faces the same way, so it does not rotate. That is irrotational circular motion. A chair welded to the rim would rotate with it — the forced vortex.

**Option (d) is a common confusion**: **laminar and irrotational are entirely unrelated.** Laminar pipe flow is **rotational** (the parabolic profile shears every element), while flow outside a boundary layer may be **turbulent yet effectively irrotational** in the mean.

**Why irrotationality matters** — it is what makes the mathematics tractable:

| Consequence | Explanation |
|---|---|
| A **VELOCITY POTENTIAL φ** can be defined | With **u = ∂φ/∂x, v = ∂φ/∂y** |
| φ satisfies **LAPLACE'S equation** | **∇²φ = 0** — for which a vast body of solutions exists |
| **Bernoulli applies THROUGHOUT the field**, not just along a streamline | A significant generalisation |
| **FLOW NETS** can be drawn | Streamlines and equipotentials, orthogonal, forming squares |
| Solutions can be **superposed** | Because Laplace's equation is linear — source + sink + uniform flow, and so on |

**The stream function ψ** is the companion, defined for any **two-dimensional incompressible** flow (rotational or not):

> **u = ∂ψ/∂y, v = −∂ψ/∂x**

| Function | Exists when | Constant along |
|---|---|---|
| **Stream function ψ** | Flow is **2-D and incompressible** | A **STREAMLINE** |
| **Velocity potential φ** | Flow is **IRROTATIONAL** | An **EQUIPOTENTIAL** line |

> **When BOTH exist** — 2-D, incompressible **and** irrotational — the flow is called **potential flow**, and both φ and ψ satisfy Laplace's equation. The **φ and ψ families are orthogonal**, which is exactly the flow-net property.

**A further useful property**: the **difference in ψ between two streamlines equals the discharge between them**. So a flow net's flow channels each carry an equal share of the total, which is why counting them (N_f) gives the discharge directly.

**Where potential flow is used in civil engineering:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **SEEPAGE** through and under dams | The Laplace equation governs, and the flow net solves it |
| **Well hydraulics** | A well is a **sink**; superposition handles well fields and image wells |
| Flow around bridge piers | Pressure distribution and scour |
| Groundwater contaminant transport | Flow paths and travel times |

**Seepage is the great civil engineering application**, and the connection is exact: Darcy's law plus continuity gives **∇²h = 0** for the head in an isotropic homogeneous soil — the same Laplace equation, so the same flow-net method applies with the head playing the role of the velocity potential.

examTip.trap: "Laminar" is a common confusion and is unrelated — **laminar pipe flow is ROTATIONAL**, because the parabolic profile shears every element.
examTip.trick: An element can travel a **curved** path and still be irrotational, provided it does not spin about its own axis — like a Ferris wheel chair.
examTip.mnemonic: **Free vortex (bathtub) is IRROTATIONAL; forced vortex (spun bucket) is ROTATIONAL.** Irrotationality is what permits a **velocity potential**, Laplace's equation, and hence **flow nets** — which is how seepage is solved.

questions.stem: In fully developed laminar flow in a circular pipe, the ratio of mean velocity to maximum velocity is:
questions.solution:
**0.5 — the mean velocity is exactly HALF the maximum.**

**Because the laminar velocity profile is PARABOLIC:**

> **u(r) = u_max[1 − (r/R)²]**

Integrating over the circular section gives **V_mean = u_max/2** exactly — a clean analytical result, not an empirical one.

**Compare with turbulent flow:**

| | **LAMINAR** | **TURBULENT** |
|---|---|---|
| Profile | **PARABOLIC** | **Logarithmic** (or a 1/7 power law) |
| **V_mean/V_max** | **0.5** exactly | **≈ 0.82** |
| Shape | Sharply peaked | **Much FLATTER** |
| Wall gradient | Moderate | **Steeper** — in the thin viscous sublayer |

**Why the turbulent profile is flatter:**

> **Turbulent MIXING transports momentum across the section** far more effectively than molecular viscosity can. Fast fluid from the core is continually swept toward the wall and slow fluid outward, **evening out the profile**.

**But it is STEEPER right at the wall**, within the **viscous sublayer** — and since the wall shear is τ₀ = μ(du/dy) at the wall, that is why **turbulent friction is higher** despite the flatter overall profile.

**The practical consequence of V_mean/V_max ≈ 0.82 in turbulent flow**: a **single centreline velocity measurement** (by Pitot tube) can be converted to a discharge with reasonable accuracy, since **Q ≈ 0.82 V_max × A**. In laminar flow the same trick gives **Q = 0.5 V_max × A**. Applying the wrong factor gives a 64% error.

**Other laminar pipe flow results**, all following from the parabolic profile:

| Quantity | Relation |
|---|---|
| **Discharge (Hagen–Poiseuille)** | **Q = πΔp D⁴/(128 μL)** |
| **Head loss** | **h_f = 32 μ V L/(γ D²)** |
| **Friction factor** | **f = 64/Re** |
| **Shear stress** | **Linear**: τ = τ₀(r/R) |
| Kinetic energy correction α | **2.0** |
| Momentum correction β | **1.33** |

**The D⁴ in the discharge relation** is worth noting again for its severity: **halving the diameter reduces the flow to one sixteenth** at the same pressure. That is why a partly blocked filter, capillary or small-bore pipe loses capacity so dramatically, and why fine-bore instrument lines must be kept scrupulously clean.

**The head loss relation h_f ∝ V** is the signature of laminar flow, and it distinguishes it experimentally:

| Regime | h_f varies as |
|---|---|
| **Laminar** | **V^1.0** |
| Transitional | V^1.75 |
| **Turbulent, smooth** | V^1.75 |
| **Turbulent, fully rough** | **V^2.0** |

> Plotting **log h_f against log V** and reading the slope identifies the regime directly — the classic **Reynolds experiment** result, and still the way a pipe friction rig is analysed in the laboratory.

**The shear stress distribution is LINEAR in BOTH regimes** — a point often missed. Force balance on a cylindrical element gives **τ = (Δp/2L)r** regardless of whether the flow is laminar or turbulent, so:

> **τ = τ₀(r/R)** — **maximum at the wall, ZERO at the centreline**, always.

What differs between the regimes is not the shear distribution but the **velocity** distribution, because in turbulent flow the shear is carried mostly by turbulent momentum exchange rather than by molecular viscosity.

examTip.trick: The laminar profile is **parabolic**, and integrating a paraboloid over the section gives exactly half the peak.
examTip.mnemonic: **Laminar 0.5, turbulent 0.82.** Turbulent mixing flattens the profile — but makes it **steeper right at the wall**, which is why turbulent friction is higher. Using the wrong factor to convert a centreline Pitot reading into a discharge gives a 64% error.

questions.stem: The head loss due to a sudden enlargement in a pipe is given by:
questions.solution:
**h_L = (V₁ − V₂)²/2g**, where V₁ is the velocity in the **smaller** pipe.

**It is derived by combining the MOMENTUM and ENERGY equations** — one of the few loss coefficients that can be derived rather than measured, and worth appreciating for that reason:

> **Momentum** across the enlargement gives the pressure rise, taking the pressure on the annular face as p₁.
> **Energy** (Bernoulli with a loss term) gives the head loss.
> Combining them eliminates the pressures and yields **h_L = (V₁ − V₂)²/2g**.

**Why the loss occurs.** The jet issuing from the small pipe **cannot expand instantly** to fill the large one. It separates, and the **annular region of EDDIES** between the jet and the wall dissipates energy as heat. The kinetic energy of the jet is destroyed rather than recovered.

**The special case of a SUDDEN EXIT into a large tank** — where V₂ → 0:

> **h_L = V₁²/2g** — the **ENTIRE velocity head is lost**

That is the largest single minor loss in most pipe systems, and it is unavoidable: water discharging into a reservoir loses all its kinetic energy. It is why a discharge pipe's velocity head must be counted in the system head calculation.

**The standard minor loss coefficients** (h_L = K V²/2g):

| Fitting | K |
|---|---|
| **Sharp (square) entrance** from a tank | **0.5** |
| **Bell-mouth (rounded) entrance** | **0.04 – 0.05** |
| Re-entrant (Borda) entrance | 0.8 – 1.0 |
| **EXIT into a tank** | **1.0** |
| Sudden enlargement | **(1 − A₁/A₂)²**, based on V₁ |
| Sudden contraction | 0.5(1 − A₂/A₁), roughly |
| **90° elbow, sharp** | **0.9** |
| **90° bend, long radius** | **0.2 – 0.3** |
| Gate valve, fully open | 0.2 |
| **Globe valve**, fully open | **10** |
| Swing check valve | 2.5 |
| Tee, through flow | 0.4 |

**Two of these deserve comment.**

**The bell-mouth entrance** reduces K from 0.5 to about 0.05 — a **tenfold reduction** — for nothing more than rounding the edge. It is one of the cheapest improvements available in hydraulic design, and it is why intakes, culvert entries and pump suction bells are always rounded.

**The globe valve's K of 10** against a gate valve's 0.2 explains their different roles: a **globe valve is for THROTTLING** (its tortuous path gives fine control), a **gate valve for ISOLATION** (fully open or fully shut, minimal loss). Using a globe valve as an isolating valve wastes a great deal of head.

**Minor versus major losses** — the terminology is misleading:

| | **Major (friction)** | **Minor (local)** |
|---|---|---|
| Cause | Wall friction along the pipe | Fittings, bends, valves, changes of section |
| Formula | **Darcy–Weisbach: h_f = fLV²/(2gD)** | **h_L = K V²/2g** |
| Dominates in | **LONG** pipelines | **SHORT** pipes with many fittings |

> **"Minor" losses are NOT always minor.** In a short pipe run — a pump house, a treatment plant's internal pipework, a domestic installation — the fittings can account for **most** of the total loss. The convention is that minor losses may be neglected when the pipe is longer than about **1000 diameters**, and must be counted otherwise.

**The equivalent length method** is the convenient way to combine them:

> **L_e = K D/f** — each fitting is replaced by an equivalent length of straight pipe, and the whole system treated as one long pipe.

examTip.trick: This is one of the few loss coefficients that can be **derived** rather than measured — by combining the momentum and energy equations across the expansion.
examTip.mnemonic: **Exit into a tank (V₂ → 0) loses the ENTIRE velocity head.** That is the largest single minor loss in most systems and is unavoidable. Note "minor" losses are **not minor in short pipework** — they dominate in a pump house.

questions.stem: Water issues from an orifice under a head of 5 m. The theoretical jet velocity is:
questions.solution:
**9.9 m/s.**

> **Torricelli: V = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 5) = √98.1 = 9.90 m/s** ✓

**Option (c), 49 m/s**, is **2gh** without the square root. Option (d), 7.0, is √(gh) — forgetting the 2.

**A useful mental shortcut**: **V ≈ 4.43√h**, since √(2 × 9.81) = 4.43. So for h = 5, V ≈ 4.43 × 2.24 = 9.9 ✓ — instant, and worth memorising.

| Head h | V = √(2gh) |
|---|---|
| **1 m** | **4.43 m/s** |
| 2 m | 6.26 m/s |
| **5 m** | **9.90 m/s** |
| **10 m** | **14.0 m/s** |
| 20 m | 19.8 m/s |
| 100 m | 44.3 m/s |

**Note the square-root relation**: **quadrupling the head only doubles the velocity**. That diminishing return is why very high heads are exploited by turbines (which extract the energy) rather than simply by faster jets.

**Derivation from Bernoulli**, between the reservoir surface (1) and the jet (2):

> At the surface: **p₁ = 0** (atmospheric), **V₁ ≈ 0** (large reservoir), **z₁ = h**
> At the jet: **p₂ = 0** (free jet at atmospheric pressure), **z₂ = 0**
> **0 + 0 + h = 0 + V₂²/2g + 0**, so **V₂ = √(2gh)** ✓

**Two assumptions worth naming:**

| Assumption | Note |
|---|---|
| **V₁ ≈ 0** at the surface | Valid when the **reservoir area ≫ orifice area**; otherwise a velocity-of-approach correction is needed |
| **p = 0 in the free jet** | Valid **at the vena contracta**, where the streamlines are parallel |

**The result is exactly the free-fall velocity** from a height h — which is the physical statement of what Bernoulli is doing here: the **potential energy of the head is converted entirely into kinetic energy**, exactly as for a body dropped from that height. A frictionless jet and a dropped stone arrive at the same speed.

**The ACTUAL velocity** is slightly less:

> **V_actual = C_v √(2gh)**, with **C_v ≈ 0.97 – 0.99**

and the **actual discharge** is much less, because of the **contraction**:

> **Q = C_d A √(2gh)**, with **C_d = C_v C_c ≈ 0.62** for a sharp-edged orifice

**TIME TO EMPTY A TANK** is the standard extension, and it requires integration because the head falls as the tank drains:

> **T = 2A_tank(√h₁ − √h₂)/(C_d A_orifice √(2g))**

For complete emptying (h₂ = 0): **T = 2A√h₁/(C_d a√(2g))**

**A useful consequence**: the time to empty is **twice** what it would be at the initial discharge rate — because the average discharge over the emptying is half the initial value, the √h relation making the flow slow as the tank drains.

**Practical applications of the orifice equation:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Reservoir outlets and draw-off works** | Sizing the opening |
| **Sluice gate** discharge | **Q = C_d b a √(2gh)** |
| **Tank emptying / dewatering** time | The integrated form |
| **Detention pond outlet** design | Controlling the release rate |
| **Culvert under inlet control** | The entry behaves as an orifice |
| Fire hydrant and nozzle discharge | — |

**The detention pond case** is a common modern application: a stormwater pond is designed to **release at a controlled rate**, and an orifice is the simplest device that does so — its √h characteristic giving a discharge that rises only slowly as the pond fills, which is exactly the attenuating behaviour wanted.

examTip.mnemonic: **Torricelli gives exactly the free-fall speed from height h** — all the potential energy of the head becomes kinetic. **Square root**, so quadrupling the head only doubles the velocity. Time to empty a tank is **twice** what the initial rate suggests.

questions.stem: Boundary layer separation occurs when the flow encounters:
options: An adverse pressure gradient, with pressure increasing in the flow direction
questions.solution:
**An ADVERSE pressure gradient — pressure INCREASING in the direction of flow (dp/dx > 0).**

**Why it separates.** Fluid in the boundary layer has already been **slowed by friction** and has little momentum left. An adverse pressure gradient **pushes against** the flow. The slow fluid near the wall cannot make headway, **stops**, and then **reverses** — and the main flow is lifted off the surface.

> At the **separation point**, **(∂u/∂y) = 0 at the wall** — the velocity gradient, and therefore the wall shear stress, vanishes. Beyond it the flow near the wall is **reversed**.

**The pressure gradient conditions:**

| Gradient | Flow | Boundary layer |
|---|---|---|
| **FAVOURABLE (dp/dx < 0)** — **converging**, accelerating flow | Pressure **falls** downstream | **THINS**; **NEVER separates** |
| **Zero** | Flat plate | Grows slowly; no separation |
| **ADVERSE (dp/dx > 0)** — **diverging**, decelerating flow | Pressure **rises** downstream | **THICKENS**; **may SEPARATE** |

> **Accelerating flow never separates; decelerating flow may.** That single statement governs an enormous amount of hydraulic design.

**The consequences of separation:**

| Consequence | Effect |
|---|---|
| A **WAKE** of recirculating fluid forms | Large energy dissipation |
| **Pressure (form) DRAG** increases sharply | Usually far exceeding friction drag on a bluff body |
| **Pressure recovery is LOST** | The diffuser stops working |
| **Vortex shedding** | Causing vibration — and, at resonance, failure |
| Reduced lift on an aerofoil | **Stall** |

**This is the resolution of D'Alembert's paradox**: ideal flow theory predicts **zero drag** because the pressure distribution is symmetric fore and aft. Real flow **separates** at the rear of a bluff body, destroying the downstream pressure recovery and leaving a low-pressure wake — which is where most of the drag on a bluff body comes from.

**Design consequences — the recurring one is the DIFFUSER:**

| Element | Angle | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Venturi CONVERGING cone** | **20 – 21°** — steep is fine | **Accelerating**; cannot separate; kept short to save length and friction |
| **Venturi DIVERGING cone** | **5 – 7°** — must be gentle | **Decelerating**; a steeper angle **SEPARATES**, losing the pressure recovery |
| Draft tube of a reaction turbine | Similarly gentle | Recovers the exit kinetic energy |
| Pump volute | Gradual expansion | — |

> That asymmetry — a short steep inlet and a long gentle outlet — is the visual signature of every well-designed venturi, diffuser and draft tube, and it exists entirely because of separation.

**Methods of controlling or delaying separation:**

| Method | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **STREAMLINING** the body | Gradual rear taper keeps the adverse gradient gentle |
| **TRIPPING the boundary layer to TURBULENT** | A turbulent layer has **more momentum near the wall** and resists separation longer |
| Suction through the surface | Removes the low-momentum fluid |
| Blowing / injecting high-momentum fluid | Re-energises the layer |
| Vortex generators | Mix high-momentum fluid down to the wall |
| Gentle diffuser angles | Avoids the adverse gradient becoming severe |

**The turbulent-tripping trick is counter-intuitive and worth understanding:**

> **A GOLF BALL is DIMPLED to force the boundary layer TURBULENT.** The turbulent layer separates **further back**, giving a **narrower wake and LESS pressure drag** — so a dimpled ball flies roughly **twice as far** as a smooth one.

The same effect appears as the **drag crisis** on a sphere or cylinder: at a critical Reynolds number (~3 × 10⁵) the boundary layer goes turbulent, the separation point jumps rearward, and **the drag coefficient FALLS abruptly** — one of the few cases in engineering where increasing the Reynolds number reduces the drag.

**In civil engineering** separation matters for **wind loading on buildings** (the leeward suction is a separated wake), **vortex shedding on chimneys, cables and bridge decks** (the Tacoma Narrows lesson), and **scour around bridge piers**, where the separated horseshoe vortex is what excavates the bed.

examTip.trick: Boundary-layer fluid has already been slowed by friction and has little momentum left. An adverse gradient pushes back against it, it stops, and it reverses.
examTip.mnemonic: **Accelerating flow NEVER separates; decelerating flow may.** That single rule explains the venturi's asymmetry — a steep **20°** inlet and a gentle **6°** diffuser. It also explains why a **golf ball is dimpled**: a turbulent layer carries more momentum near the wall and separates later, giving a narrower wake and less drag.

questions.stem: In a venturi meter, the pressure at the throat compared with that at the inlet is:
questions.solution:
**Lower.**

**The reasoning is the pairing of continuity and Bernoulli**, and it is the central idea of flow measurement by differential pressure:

> **CONTINUITY**: the throat is narrower, so **A₂ < A₁**, so **V₂ > V₁** — the flow **ACCELERATES**.
> **BERNOULLI**: the total head is constant, so if the velocity head **rises**, the pressure head must **FALL**.

> **Throat = high velocity = LOW pressure.**

**The venturi discharge equation** follows from combining them:

> **Q = C_d × (A₁A₂/√(A₁² − A₂²)) × √(2gh)**

where **h** is the **head difference** between inlet and throat, and **C_d ≈ 0.98** for a well-made venturi.

**The three parts of a venturi and why each is shaped as it is:**

| Part | Angle | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Converging cone** | **20 – 21°** — steep | Flow is **ACCELERATING**, so it **cannot separate**. Kept short to save length and friction |
| **THROAT** | Cylindrical, short | The measurement section; typically **D/3 to D/2** |
| **Diverging cone** | **5 – 7°** — gentle | Flow is **DECELERATING**; a steeper angle would **SEPARATE**, destroying the pressure recovery |

**That asymmetry is the signature of the design**, and it exists entirely because of boundary layer separation. The long gentle diffuser is what gives the venturi its great advantage — a **permanent head loss of only about 10%** of the differential, against **50–70%** for an orifice plate.

**Venturi versus orifice plate:**

| | **VENTURI** | **ORIFICE PLATE** |
|---|---|---|
| **C_d** | **0.98** | **0.62** |
| **Permanent head loss** | **~10%** | **50 – 70%** |
| Cost | **High** | **Low** |
| Length required | **Long** | **Negligible** — fits between flanges |
| Wear and fouling | Resistant | The **sharp edge WEARS**, changing C_d |
| Suits | Large flows, continuous duty, where **head is precious** | Small installations, where head is plentiful |

**The choice is an economic one**: a venturi's higher capital cost is recovered through **lower pumping energy** over its life. For a large continuously pumped main the venturi wins easily; for an intermittent or gravity-fed line the orifice is the sensible choice.

**The orifice plate's wearing edge** is its real operational weakness: **C_d depends on the edge remaining SHARP**, and erosion by grit rounds it over time, causing the meter to read progressively high without any obvious sign. Periodic inspection and replacement is required.

**Two important practical points about the venturi:**

**1. Orientation is immaterial.** The relation between the manometer deflection and the discharge holds **whatever the inclination** of the venturi — horizontal, vertical or sloping — because the elevation terms in the Bernoulli equation and in the manometer reading **cancel exactly**. So one calibration serves any installation.

**2. CAVITATION at the throat is the design limit.** Since the throat is the point of **minimum pressure** in the whole meter, an excessive throat velocity can drop the pressure to the **vapour pressure** and cause cavitation — which damages the meter and makes the reading meaningless. The throat diameter is therefore chosen so the throat pressure stays comfortably above vapour pressure at the maximum flow, which sets a lower limit on the throat size.

**Straight-pipe requirements** apply to both meters and are often neglected in practice: a swirling or asymmetric approach flow changes the coefficient. Standards require roughly **10 to 30 diameters of straight pipe upstream** and **5 downstream**, more if the upstream fitting is a bend out of plane. A meter installed immediately after an elbow can read several percent in error.

examTip.trick: Continuity says the throat is faster; Bernoulli says faster means lower pressure. The two together are the whole principle of differential-pressure flow measurement.
examTip.mnemonic: **Throat = fast = low pressure.** Which is also why the throat is where **cavitation** starts, and that sets a lower limit on throat size. Venturi C_d ≈ 0.98 with only ~10% permanent loss; an orifice plate is 0.62 with 50–70% loss — cheap to buy, expensive to run.

questions.stem: A jet of water of area 0.01 m² strikes a fixed flat plate normally at 20 m/s. The force on the plate is:
questions.solution:
**4000 N.**

> **F = ρ a V²** for a jet striking a **fixed flat plate normally**
> **= 1000 × 0.01 × 20² = 1000 × 0.01 × 400 = 4000 N** ✓

**Derivation from the momentum equation.** The jet arrives with momentum flux **ρaV × V** in the direction of the jet, and leaves **radially** — that is, with **zero momentum in the original direction**:

> **F = ρQ(V_initial − V_final) = ρ(aV)(V − 0) = ρaV²** ✓

**The standard cases**, which differ by the change in momentum achieved:

| Case | Force | Ratio to flat plate |
|---|---|---|
| **Fixed FLAT plate, normal** | **F = ρaV²** | **1.0** |
| Fixed **inclined** plate, angle θ | **F_normal = ρaV² sin θ** | sin θ |
| **Fixed CURVED vane**, deflecting through θ | **F = ρaV²(1 − cos θ)** | — |
| **Fixed HEMISPHERICAL cup (θ = 180°)** | **F = 2ρaV²** | **2.0** |
| **MOVING flat plate** at velocity u | **F = ρa(V − u)²** | — |
| **MOVING curved vane** (Pelton bucket) | **F = ρa(V − u)²(1 − cos θ)** | — |

**The hemispherical cup doubles the force** — the single most useful result in this family, and the reason the **PELTON turbine bucket** is shaped as it is:

> A flat plate stops the jet: momentum change **V**.
> A hemispherical cup **REVERSES** it: momentum change **2V**.

In practice the Pelton bucket deflects through about **165°, not 180°**, because a full reversal would send the outgoing water straight back into the incoming jet. The small sacrifice costs only **(1 − cos 165°)/2 = 0.983** — under 2% of the theoretical maximum, in exchange for a workable machine.

**Work is done only by a MOVING plate.** A fixed plate experiences a force but the point of application does not move, so:

> **Fixed plate: force but NO WORK — the jet's energy is entirely dissipated.**
> **Moving plate: Work = F × u = ρa(V − u)² u**

**The optimum vane speed** follows by differentiating:

> **dWork/du = 0 gives u = V/2**

> **A Pelton wheel runs at a bucket speed of HALF the jet velocity** — the condition of maximum power. And at that speed the **theoretical maximum efficiency** is:

> **η_max = (1 − cos θ)/2 = 100% for θ = 180°**, or about **98%** for the practical 165°

**Why u = V/2 is optimal** is worth grasping physically: if the bucket moves **too slowly**, the water hits hard but the bucket travels little (high force, low speed → moderate power). If it moves **too fast**, it runs away from the jet and the relative velocity — hence the force — collapses. Halfway between is the maximum, and at that speed the water leaves the bucket with **almost zero absolute velocity**, having given up virtually all its kinetic energy.

**That last observation is the design ideal for any turbine**: the water should leave with as little velocity as possible, since whatever velocity it retains is energy not extracted. It is why reaction turbines have **draft tubes** — to recover the exit kinetic energy that would otherwise be lost.

**A note on the arithmetic**: option (a), 2000 N, is **½ρaV²** — using the kinetic energy expression instead of the momentum one. That is a genuinely common error, and the check is dimensional reasoning: a **force** comes from a **momentum** balance (ρQV), not from an energy expression.

**Relevance to Nepal**: the **Pelton turbine is the workhorse of Nepali hydropower**, suited to the **high heads and modest flows** of Himalayan streams. Its jet velocity for a 300 m head is **√(2 × 9.81 × 300) ≈ 76 m/s**, and the runner runs at half that at the bucket pitch circle.

examTip.trap: 2000 N is **½ρaV²** — using a kinetic-energy expression where a momentum balance belongs. A **force** always comes from momentum.
examTip.trick: **F = ρaV² = 1000 × 0.01 × 400 = 4000 N**, because the jet's momentum in the original direction goes to zero.
examTip.mnemonic: **A hemispherical cup REVERSES the jet and DOUBLES the force** — which is why a Pelton bucket is shaped so, and why it runs at **u = V/2** for maximum power. At that speed the water leaves with almost no absolute velocity, having given up nearly all its energy.

questions.stem: In a flow net, streamlines and equipotential lines:
questions.solution:
**They intersect ORTHOGONALLY, forming approximate SQUARES.**

**Why orthogonal.** The velocity is **tangential to a streamline** by definition, and it is **normal to an equipotential line** (flow goes down the steepest gradient of head). A line tangential to one family and normal to the other requires the two families to cross at **right angles**.

**The square mesh** is the practical criterion for a correctly drawn net: when the flow channels each carry equal discharge and the equipotentials each represent an equal head drop, the resulting figures are **curvilinear squares** — their average width equalling their average length. Drawing a net is an iterative sketching process, and the squareness is what tells you when it is right.

**The seepage result:**

> **q = k H (N_f / N_d)**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **k** | Coefficient of permeability |
| **H** | **Total head loss** across the system |
| **N_f** | Number of **FLOW CHANNELS** (spaces between flow lines) |
| **N_d** | Number of **EQUIPOTENTIAL DROPS** |
| **N_f/N_d** | The **SHAPE FACTOR** — depends **only on the geometry** |

> Because the shape factor depends only on geometry, **one flow net serves any permeability and any head** for that geometry. That is what makes the method so economical.

**Count the SPACES, not the LINES** — the commonest error in the calculation. If there are 5 flow lines there are **4** flow channels; if 11 equipotential lines, **10** drops.

**What else the flow net yields:**

| Quantity | How |
|---|---|
| **Seepage discharge** | q = kH(N_f/N_d) |
| **Pore water pressure** at any point | Head at that point = H − (drops to that point) × H/N_d; then **u = γ_w × pressure head** |
| **UPLIFT** on a structure | Integrate the pore pressure over the base |
| **EXIT GRADIENT** | **i = Δh/Δl** in the **smallest field at the downstream exit** |

**The EXIT GRADIENT is the safety-critical output**, because it governs **PIPING**:

> **PIPING** (or **quick condition**) occurs when the **upward seepage force equals the submerged weight of the soil**, so the effective stress falls to **zero** and the grains are lifted.

> **Critical hydraulic gradient i_c = (G − 1)/(1 + e) ≈ 1.0** for typical soils.

> Required: **i_exit < i_c / F**, with **F = 4 to 7**.

**The factor of safety is high** — far higher than in most geotechnical design — because piping is **sudden, progressive and catastrophic**: once a pipe starts to form at the exit it **erodes backward** toward the reservoir, enlarging as it goes, and the process is self-accelerating. There is no warning and no opportunity to intervene.

**Controlling piping:**

| Measure | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Increase the seepage PATH LENGTH** | Cutoff walls, sheet piling, upstream impervious blanket — increases N_d, reducing the gradient |
| **FILTERS (inverted / graded)** at the exit | Let the **water out but hold the SOIL in** — the essential measure |
| **Relief wells and drainage** | Relieve the pressure |
| Loaded filter / weighted berm | Adds weight against the uplift |

**The graded filter is the classic solution** and its design rules are worth carrying:

> **D₁₅(filter) / D₈₅(soil) < 4 to 5** — **piping criterion**: the filter's pores are too small for the soil to wash through
> **D₁₅(filter) / D₁₅(soil) > 4 to 5** — **permeability criterion**: the filter is free-draining and does not itself build up pressure

> The filter must satisfy **BOTH simultaneously** — it must be **fine enough to retain the soil** and **coarse enough to drain freely**. Where a single layer cannot do both, a **graded filter of several layers** is used, each satisfying the criteria against the one before it.

**Anisotropy** is a common refinement: natural soils are usually more permeable **horizontally** than vertically. The net is drawn on a **transformed section** with the horizontal scale reduced by **√(k_v/k_h)**, and the discharge computed with an **equivalent permeability k_eq = √(k_h k_v)**.

examTip.trick: Velocity is **tangential** to a streamline and **normal** to an equipotential, so the two families must cross at right angles. The square mesh is the check that the net is drawn correctly.
examTip.mnemonic: **q = kH(N_f/N_d), and COUNT THE SPACES, NOT THE LINES.** The shape factor depends only on geometry, so one net serves any k and any head. Its safety-critical output is the **exit gradient**, checked against i_c ≈ 1 with a factor of **4 to 7** — high, because piping is sudden and self-accelerating.

questions.stem: The Darcy–Weisbach equation for friction head loss in a pipe is:
questions.solution:
**h_f = f L V² / (2 g D).**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **f** | **Darcy friction factor** — dimensionless |
| **L** | Pipe length |
| **V** | **Mean** velocity |
| **D** | Pipe **diameter** |

**Note the V² and the single power of L**, which is where the wrong options depart. A useful check: **h_f must be a LENGTH**, and (dimensionless × m × m²/s²)/(m/s² × m) = m ✓.

**In terms of discharge**, which is often more useful:

> **h_f = 8 f L Q²/(π² g D⁵) = 0.0826 f L Q²/D⁵**

**The D⁵ is the dominant fact of pipeline design:**

> **Doubling the diameter reduces the head loss by a factor of 32** at the same discharge.

That extreme sensitivity is why the **economic diameter** matters so much, and why an undersized rising main is such an expensive mistake — the pumping cost penalty is severe and permanent.

**A caution on the friction factor.** Two definitions are in circulation:

| Factor | Symbol | Relation |
|---|---|---|
| **Darcy (Moody) friction factor** | **f** | **f = 64/Re** laminar; used above |
| **Fanning friction factor** | f′ | **f′ = 16/Re** laminar; **f = 4f′** |

> Some older texts write the equation as **h_f = 4fLV²/(2gD)**, using the **Fanning** factor. A **factor-of-four error** results from mixing them, and the tell is the laminar value: if the text says f = 64/Re it is the Darcy factor and no 4 belongs.

**Determining f:**

| Regime | f |
|---|---|
| **Laminar (Re < 2000)** | **f = 64/Re** — depends on **Re only**, not on roughness |
| **Turbulent smooth** | Blasius: **f = 0.316/Re^0.25** for 4000 < Re < 10⁵ |
| **Turbulent transitional** | **Colebrook–White** — implicit; solved iteratively or read from the **MOODY diagram** |
| **Fully rough** | **f depends on k/D ONLY** — independent of Re |

**The Colebrook–White equation:**

> **1/√f = −2 log₁₀[k/(3.7D) + 2.51/(Re√f)]**

It is **implicit in f**, which is why the **Moody diagram** — a graphical solution — remains in use, and why explicit approximations (Swamee–Jain, Haaland) were developed for computer work.

**That roughness does not matter in laminar flow** is worth understanding: in laminar flow the fluid moves in **smooth layers that do not interact with the wall texture** — the roughness elements sit within a region of orderly flow and disturb nothing. Only when turbulence brings eddies into contact with the wall projections does roughness begin to cost energy.

**Typical roughness values k (mm):**

| Pipe | k |
|---|---|
| **Drawn tubing, PVC, glass** | **0.0015 – 0.0025** |
| **Commercial steel** | **0.045** |
| Galvanised iron | 0.15 |
| **Cast iron, new** | **0.26** |
| **Cast iron, old/tuberculated** | **1 – 3** |
| Concrete | 0.3 – 3 |
| Riveted steel | 0.9 – 9 |

**The ageing of cast iron is a real design issue**: **tuberculation** — the growth of corrosion nodules on the bore — can increase k by a factor of ten over decades, and simultaneously reduce the effective diameter. An old main can lose **half its capacity**, and the design must either allow for it or specify a lining. Cement mortar lining is the standard remedy, restoring both the roughness and the bore.

examTip.trap: Older texts write **h_f = 4fLV²/(2gD)** using the **FANNING** factor, where f = 16/Re. Mixing the two conventions gives a **factor-of-four error**.
examTip.trick: The tell is the laminar value: if the text says **f = 64/Re** it is the Darcy factor and no 4 belongs. Dimension check: (–)(m)(m²/s²)/((m/s²)(m)) = m ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **h_f = 0.0826 fLQ²/D⁵ — note the D⁵.** Doubling the diameter cuts the head loss **32-fold**, which is the dominant fact of pipeline economics.

questions.stem: For laminar flow in a pipe, the Darcy friction factor is:
questions.solution:
**f = 64/Re.**

**It is derived, not measured** — one of the few exact results in pipe hydraulics. Equating the **Hagen–Poiseuille** head loss to the **Darcy–Weisbach** form:

> **Hagen–Poiseuille: h_f = 32 μ V L/(γ D²)**
> **Darcy–Weisbach: h_f = f L V²/(2gD)**
> Equating and solving: **f = 64μ/(ρVD) = 64/Re** ✓

**Option (c), 16/Re**, is the **FANNING** friction factor — the same physics in the convention where **f_Darcy = 4 f_Fanning**. Option (d) is the **Blasius** equation, valid for **turbulent smooth** pipes (4000 < Re < 10⁵), not laminar.

**The critical property of f = 64/Re:**

> In laminar flow the friction factor depends on the **REYNOLDS NUMBER ONLY** — the **ROUGHNESS IS IRRELEVANT**.

**Why**: laminar flow moves in **smooth layers**. The roughness elements sit within orderly flow and are never struck by eddies, so they cost no energy. A rough pipe and a smooth pipe of the same diameter have **identical** laminar friction.

**The full picture across the regimes:**

| Regime | Re | f depends on | Relation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Laminar** | < 2000 | **Re only** | **f = 64/Re** |
| Transitional | 2000 – 4000 | Unpredictable | Avoid designing here |
| **Turbulent smooth** | > 4000 | Re only | Blasius: 0.316/Re^0.25 |
| **Turbulent transitional** | — | **Re AND k/D** | **Colebrook–White** |
| **Fully rough** | High | **k/D only** | Von Kármán |

**The Moody diagram** displays all of this, and its shape carries the story:

| Feature of the diagram | Meaning |
|---|---|
| A **single straight line** at low Re | The laminar f = 64/Re — **no roughness curves**, because roughness does not matter |
| A **gap** at 2000 – 4000 | The transitional region; behaviour is unpredictable |
| A **family of curves** in the turbulent zone | One per relative roughness k/D |
| The curves become **HORIZONTAL** at high Re | **Fully rough** — f no longer depends on Re |

**Why the curves flatten** is the physical heart of the diagram:

> As Re rises, the **VISCOUS SUBLAYER at the wall THINS**. Once the roughness elements **project through** it, they are exposed to the turbulent core and generate form drag directly. Further increases in Re do not change that geometry, so **f stops depending on Re**.

**Which means "smooth" and "rough" are properties of the pipe AND the flow, not of the pipe alone:**

| Condition | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Roughness **submerged** in the viscous sublayer | **Hydrodynamically SMOOTH** |
| Roughness **projecting through** | **Fully ROUGH** |

The same pipe is smooth at low Reynolds number and rough at high — which is why a pipe cannot be labelled once and for all.

**Practical consequence of the fully rough region**: for a large water main at high Reynolds number, **f is effectively constant** and independent of the flow rate. That is what justifies the simpler empirical formulae — **Hazen–Williams** and **Manning** — which contain no Reynolds number at all. They work precisely because water distribution operates in the fully rough zone.

**Where laminar flow actually occurs in civil engineering**: **groundwater seepage** (which is why **Darcy's law is linear**), **oil pipelines**, lubricating films, and flow in very fine tubes. For water in any normal pipe, turbulent flow is essentially universal — water at just 0.1 m/s in a 50 mm pipe already gives Re = 5000.

examTip.trap: 16/Re is the **Fanning** factor and 0.316/Re^0.25 is **Blasius** (turbulent smooth). Both are real formulae in the wrong place.
examTip.trick: It is **derived**, not measured — equate Hagen–Poiseuille to Darcy–Weisbach and f = 64/Re falls out.
examTip.mnemonic: **In laminar flow the ROUGHNESS IS IRRELEVANT** — the fluid moves in orderly layers and never feels the wall texture. Roughness only matters once turbulent eddies reach the projections.

questions.stem: When two pipes are connected in parallel between the same two points, the quantity that is the same in both is the:
questions.solution:
**The HEAD LOSS.**

**Series and parallel are exact duals**, and keeping them straight is the whole of simple pipe network analysis:

| | **SERIES** | **PARALLEL** |
|---|---|---|
| **Same in both pipes** | **DISCHARGE Q** | **HEAD LOSS h_f** |
| **Added together** | **HEAD LOSSES**: h_total = h₁ + h₂ + … | **DISCHARGES**: Q_total = Q₁ + Q₂ + … |
| Analogy | Resistors in series | Resistors in parallel |

**Why the head loss is common in parallel**: both pipes connect the **same two junction points**, and each junction has a single value of head. The difference between those two heads is the head loss — and it is the same difference for whichever route the water takes.

**Why the discharge is common in series**: whatever enters the first pipe must leave the second, by continuity.

**The electrical analogy is exact** and worth using deliberately:

| Hydraulic | Electrical |
|---|---|
| Head loss h_f | Voltage drop V |
| Discharge Q | Current I |
| Pipe resistance | Resistance R |
| **h_f = rQ²** | V = IR (but hydraulics is **non-linear**) |

> The one important difference: hydraulic resistance is **NON-LINEAR** — **h_f ∝ Q²**, not Q. That is why pipe networks cannot be solved by simple linear algebra and need an **iterative** method.

**Solving a parallel arrangement.** Writing **h_f = r Q²** with **r = 0.0826 f L/D⁵**:

> Same h_f in each: **r₁Q₁² = r₂Q₂²**, so **Q₁/Q₂ = √(r₂/r₁)**
> And **Q_total = Q₁ + Q₂**

**A worked case.** Two parallel pipes, both 500 m long, of 300 mm and 200 mm diameter, same f:

> **r ∝ 1/D⁵**, so **r₂/r₁ = (D₁/D₂)⁵ = (300/200)⁵ = 1.5⁵ = 7.59**
> **Q₁/Q₂ = √7.59 = 2.76**

So the 300 mm pipe carries **73%** of the flow and the 200 mm pipe only **27%**, despite being only 1.5 times the diameter. **Q ∝ D^2.5** for a given head loss — a steep relation, and the reason that adding a small parallel pipe to a large one buys much less capacity than intuition suggests.

**That is a genuinely useful practical result**: to increase a main's capacity, **duplicating it with an equal pipe gives 2× the flow**, whereas laying a pipe of half the diameter alongside adds only about **18%**.

**Why parallel pipes are used at all:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Increase capacity** without replacing the existing main | Duplication |
| **Redundancy** — one line can be taken out for maintenance | Often the decisive reason |
| **Staged construction** — lay a second line as demand grows | Defers capital cost |
| Reduce the head loss for a given flow | — |

**The EQUIVALENT PIPE concept** simplifies either arrangement into a single pipe giving the same h_f for the same Q — useful for reducing a complicated system before analysis:

> **Series (Dupuit's equation), equal f: L_e/D_e⁵ = L₁/D₁⁵ + L₂/D₂⁵ + …**
> **Parallel: 1/√(r_e) = 1/√(r₁) + 1/√(r₂) + …**

**For a full NETWORK of loops**, the **HARDY CROSS** method is the classical solution, and it is an iterative application of exactly these two rules:

| Condition | Statement |
|---|---|
| At every **junction** | **Σ Q = 0** — inflow equals outflow (continuity) |
| Around every **loop** | **Σ h_f = 0** — the head is single-valued (energy) |

> The correction applied to each loop's assumed flows is **ΔQ = −Σ(rQ²)/(2Σ|rQ|)**, iterated until the loop imbalances are acceptably small. Modern practice uses software, but the two conditions it enforces are exactly these, and understanding them is what lets an engineer judge whether an output is sensible.

examTip.trick: Both pipes join the **same two points**, and each point has one value of head — so the difference, which is the head loss, must be the same for either route.
examTip.mnemonic: **Series: same Q, add the losses. Parallel: same loss, add the Qs.** Exactly like resistors — except hydraulic resistance is **non-linear** (h ∝ Q²), which is why networks need iteration. Note **Q ∝ D^2.5**, so a half-diameter parallel pipe adds only about 18% capacity.

questions.stem: The Hazen–Williams formula for pipe flow uses a coefficient C whose value for new cast iron pipe is about:
questions.solution:
**About 130.**

> **V = 0.849 C R^0.63 S^0.54** (SI units), where R is the hydraulic radius and S the slope of the energy line
> Or: **h_f = 10.67 L Q^1.852 / (C^1.852 D^4.87)**

**Typical C values:**

| Pipe | C |
|---|---|
| **PVC, plastic, very smooth** | **150** |
| **Cement-lined ductile iron** | **140** |
| **New cast iron, new steel** | **130** |
| Concrete, well finished | 120 – 130 |
| 20-year-old cast iron | 100 |
| **40-year-old cast iron** | **80** |
| Old, badly tuberculated | **60 – 75** |

> **A HIGHER C means a SMOOTHER pipe** — the opposite convention to Manning's n and to the roughness height k, which is a frequent source of confusion.

**The ageing effect is the practical lesson**: cast iron's C falls from 130 to 80 over forty years through **tuberculation** — corrosion nodules growing on the bore. Since **Q ∝ C** in this formula, an old main carries only **60%** of its original flow at the same head. A distribution network designed on new-pipe values will fail to deliver in its later decades unless the design value of C is chosen for the **end of the design life**, not the beginning.

**Hazen–Williams versus Darcy–Weisbach:**

| | **Hazen–Williams** | **Darcy–Weisbach** |
|---|---|---|
| Basis | **EMPIRICAL** | **Theoretical / dimensionally rational** |
| Fluid | **WATER ONLY**, at ordinary temperatures | **ANY fluid** |
| Regime | **Turbulent water distribution** only | **All regimes**, laminar to fully rough |
| Reynolds number | **Does not appear** | Central |
| Solving | **EXPLICIT** — direct calculation | **Implicit** in f; needs Moody or iteration |
| Used for | **Water supply networks** | General hydraulics, penstocks, research |

**Why an empirical formula survives** alongside a rational one is worth understanding, and it is not laziness:

> Water distribution operates almost entirely in the **FULLY ROUGH turbulent zone**, where **f depends only on k/D and not on Re**. In that zone the Reynolds number carries no information, so a formula that omits it loses nothing — and gains a great deal in being **explicit** rather than requiring iteration.

Before computers that was decisive. It remains convenient, and Hazen–Williams is still what most water-supply codes and network software use.

**Its limitations must be respected:**

| Limitation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Water only** | Invalid for oil, air, sludge or any other fluid |
| **Turbulent flow only** | Fails in laminar flow |
| Best for **D > 50 mm and V < 3 m/s** | Outside that range the accuracy degrades |
| Assumes ordinary temperature | No viscosity term at all |

**The three formulae in common use**, and where each belongs:

| Formula | Belongs to | Roughness term |
|---|---|---|
| **Darcy–Weisbach** | **Pressure pipes**, any fluid | **f** (from k/D and Re) |
| **Hazen–Williams** | **Water distribution** networks | **C** — higher is smoother |
| **MANNING** | **OPEN CHANNELS**, and partly full sewers | **n** — higher is rougher |

**Manning is occasionally applied to pressure pipes** running full, especially large sewers and culverts, which is defensible since the pipe is then simply a closed conduit with R = D/4. But it belongs to open channel flow, and using it for a small pressurised main is poor practice.

**A note on the exponents.** Hazen–Williams gives **h_f ∝ Q^1.852**, against Darcy–Weisbach's **h_f ∝ Q²** in the fully rough zone. The slightly lower exponent reflects the transitional behaviour of real distribution mains, and it means the two formulae agree closely at the design flow but diverge at flows far from it — worth remembering when checking a network at fire-flow conditions far above the design point.

examTip.trap: The convention is **inverted** relative to Manning's n and to roughness height k: for Hazen–Williams, a **HIGHER C means a SMOOTHER pipe**.
examTip.trick: Anchor on two values: **150 for plastic, 130 for new cast iron**, falling to 80 after forty years of tuberculation.
examTip.mnemonic: **Since Q ∝ C, an old main carries only about 60% of its original flow.** Design with the **end-of-life** C, not the new-pipe value, or the network will fail to deliver in its later decades.

questions.stem: A surge tank is provided on a hydropower pressure conduit mainly to:
options: Store water for the dry season
Absorb water hammer pressure rise and supply water during load acceptance
questions.solution:
**To absorb the water hammer pressure rise and to supply water during load acceptance.**

**The problem it solves.** When a turbine's gates **close suddenly** on load rejection, the water column in the long tunnel or conduit **cannot stop instantly**. Its momentum generates a large pressure rise — **water hammer** — which can burst the conduit.

> **Joukowsky: Δp = ρ c ΔV.** Water at 3 m/s stopped instantly in a steel conduit (c ≈ 1200 m/s) generates **3.6 MPa ≈ 360 m** of additional head — frequently exceeding the static head itself.

**How the surge tank works:**

| Event | Surge tank action |
|---|---|
| **Load REJECTION** — gates close | The tunnel water **surges UP into the tank**, providing a **free surface** into which the momentum can discharge. The pressure rise is confined to the short penstock below the tank |
| **Load ACCEPTANCE** — gates open | The tank **SUPPLIES water immediately** while the long tunnel column accelerates, preventing a pressure **drop** and possible column separation |

**Its function stated compactly:**

> A surge tank **converts a PRESSURE problem into a LEVEL problem** — replacing a destructive pressure wave with a slow rise and fall of water level that the structure can accommodate.

**Where it is placed:**

> **As CLOSE to the turbine as topography allows** — because it protects only the conduit **UPSTREAM** of itself. The **penstock below the tank still experiences the full water hammer**, and is designed for it.

That division of duty is the essence of the arrangement: a **long, low-pressure tunnel** protected by the tank, and a **short, high-pressure penstock** built strong enough to take the surge.

**Types of surge tank:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Simple** | A plain vertical shaft; **large oscillations**, slow to damp |
| **RESTRICTED ORIFICE** | A throttle at the base — **damps the oscillation** by creating a head loss, but transmits a higher initial pressure |
| **DIFFERENTIAL (Johnson)** | An inner riser plus an outer tank — **fast response AND good damping**; the most effective |
| Gallery / expansion chamber | Extra storage at high and low levels, cut into rock |
| Air cushion chamber | A sealed rock cavern with compressed air; used where no surface site exists |

**The differential tank's advantage** is that it separates two conflicting requirements: the **narrow inner riser responds quickly** to supply water on load acceptance, while the **wide outer tank provides the storage volume** and its restricted connection damps the oscillation.

**Stability — the THOMA criterion.** A surge tank can be **too small**, in which case the oscillations **grow rather than decay** and the system becomes unstable:

> **A_min = L A_tunnel / (2 g c H₀)** — Thoma's minimum area

where L and A are the tunnel's length and area, H₀ the net head and c the head loss coefficient. Practice uses **1.5 to 1.8 times** the Thoma area for a margin.

**Why instability is possible at all** is a nice piece of control reasoning: a **governor holding constant POWER** demands **more discharge as the head falls**. So when the tank level drops, the turbine draws more water, dropping it further — a **positive feedback**. A large enough tank makes the level change slowly enough for the oscillation to damp; too small a tank lets the feedback dominate.

**Other methods of controlling water hammer:**

| Measure | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **SLOW valve closure** — longer than **2L/c** | The reflected wave returns before closure completes, greatly reducing the rise |
| **Surge tank** | A free surface near the machine |
| **Air vessel** | A compressible cushion — used on pumping mains |
| **Pressure relief valve** | Vents the surge |
| **Flywheel** on a pump | Slows the deceleration on power failure |
| Flexible (plastic) pipe | Lower wave speed c, hence lower Δp |

**The 2L/c criterion is the central rule**: L/c is the wave's travel time to the reservoir, 2L/c the round trip. A closure **slower** than 2L/c is a **"slow" closure** and the rise is reduced roughly in proportion; a closure **faster** gives the **full Joukowsky value**, however much faster it actually is.

examTip.trick: A surge tank **converts a pressure problem into a level problem** — it gives the decelerating water column a free surface to rise into instead of a closed pipe to compress.
examTip.mnemonic: **It protects only what is UPSTREAM of it**, so put it as close to the turbine as topography allows; the short penstock below still takes the full water hammer and is built strong enough. Thoma's criterion sets the minimum area — too small a tank and the oscillations **grow** instead of damping.

questions.stem: In a siphon, the section where cavitation is most likely is:
options: The summit, where the pressure is lowest
The middle of the descending limb
questions.solution:
**The SUMMIT, where the pressure is lowest.**

**How a siphon works.** It carries water **over an obstacle higher than the supply level**, driven by the **difference between the inlet and outlet water levels** — the summit height does not affect the discharge, only the pressure at the summit.

> **Discharge is set by the difference between the two RESERVOIR levels**, exactly as for any pipe.
> **Pressure at the summit is set by the summit's HEIGHT above the supply level.**

**Applying Bernoulli from the supply surface to the summit:**

> **p_summit/γ = −(z_summit − z_supply) − V²/2g − h_f(to summit)**

Every term on the right is negative, so the summit pressure is **below atmospheric** — the higher the summit, the more so.

**The limit:**

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| **Theoretical maximum summit height** | **10.33 m** at sea level — atmospheric pressure expressed as water |
| Less the **vapour pressure** (0.24 m at 20 °C) | — |
| Less the **velocity head** and **friction losses** to the summit | — |
| Less a safety margin | — |
| **PRACTICAL maximum** | **about 6 – 7 m** |

**What actually happens as the limit is approached** — and it happens well before cavitation:

| Stage | Effect |
|---|---|
| Pressure falls below atmospheric | **DISSOLVED AIR comes out of solution** |
| Air accumulates at the summit | Forms a **pocket** that **reduces the effective flow area** |
| The pocket grows | The discharge **falls progressively** |
| Eventually | The siphon **BREAKS** — the water column parts and flow stops entirely |
| If the pressure reaches vapour pressure | **CAVITATION** — vapour bubbles, noise, vibration and erosion |

> **Air release, not cavitation, is usually the practical limit** — and it is more insidious, because the siphon does not fail suddenly but simply delivers less and less until someone investigates.

**Which is why every siphon needs an AIR RELEASE VALVE at the summit** — the single most important detail in the design. Without it, a siphon that worked on commissioning will slowly stop working.

**And at ALTITUDE the limit is lower**, which matters directly in Nepal:

| Elevation | Atmospheric head | Practical siphon height |
|---|---|---|
| Sea level | 10.33 m | ~7 m |
| **Kathmandu (1400 m)** | **8.8 m** | **~5.5 m** |
| 3000 m | 7.1 m | ~4 m |

**Priming.** A siphon **cannot start itself** — the pipe must first be **filled with water**. Methods:

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Vacuum pump** at the summit | The standard method |
| Filling from an external supply | Simple where a supply exists |
| **Self-priming** designs | Use the flow itself to entrain air out |
| Foot valve plus manual filling | Small installations |

**Applications:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Reservoir outlet over a dam crest** | Avoids piercing the dam |
| **Emptying a tank** or excavation over a bund | — |
| **SIPHON SPILLWAY** | Automatic; runs **full-bore** at high discharge once primed, and **de-primes** as the level falls |
| Irrigation offtakes over a canal bank | Common and simple |
| Trapped drainage (the domestic U-bend) | The same principle |

**The siphon spillway** is the interesting case: it **primes automatically** when the reservoir rises above the hood, then discharges at **full bore** — a much higher rate per unit width than an open weir — and **de-primes** when the level falls. Its advantage is a large discharge from a compact structure with **no moving parts and no operator**; its drawbacks are the **sudden onset and cessation** of flow (which causes surging downstream) and vulnerability to **blockage by debris**, which is why trash screens are essential and why they have fallen out of favour for large dams.

examTip.trick: The **discharge** depends on the difference between the two reservoir levels; the **summit pressure** depends on the summit's height above the supply. Only the second causes trouble.
examTip.mnemonic: **AIR RELEASE, not cavitation, is usually the practical limit** — dissolved air comes out of solution, collects at the crown, and the siphon slowly strangles itself. Hence an **air valve at every summit**. Practical maximum about 6–7 m at sea level, **5.5 m at Kathmandu**.

questions.stem: Maximum power is transmitted through a pipeline when the friction head loss equals:
options: The whole of the supply head
One third of the supply head
One half of the supply head
One quarter of the supply head
questions.solution:
**One THIRD of the supply head: h_f = H/3.**

**Derivation.** The power delivered at the far end of the pipe is:

> **P = γ Q (H − h_f)**

with **h_f = k Q²** (from Darcy–Weisbach). Substituting:

> **P = γ Q H − γ k Q³**

Differentiating with respect to Q and setting **dP/dQ = 0**:

> **γH − 3γkQ² = 0**, so **kQ² = H/3**, that is **h_f = H/3** ✓

**And the efficiency at that condition:**

> **η = (H − h_f)/H = (H − H/3)/H = 2/3 = 66.7%**

**So maximum POWER transmission occurs at only 66.7% efficiency** — which is the point of the result and where it becomes interesting:

| Objective | Condition |
|---|---|
| **Maximum POWER** transmitted | **h_f = H/3**, **η = 66.7%** |
| **Maximum EFFICIENCY** | **h_f → 0**, but then **Q → 0** and the power is **negligible** |

> **The two objectives CONFLICT**, and one must be chosen deliberately.

**Which one governs in practice depends on what is scarce:**

| Situation | Design for |
|---|---|
| **HYDROPOWER**, where the water is a valuable resource | **EFFICIENCY** — h_f is typically kept to **5 – 10%** of the gross head, far from the maximum-power condition |
| A **fixed installation** where the pipe is already built and the flow can be varied | Maximum power, if power output is what is wanted |
| Water supply | Neither — the flow is set by demand |

**Hydropower designs for efficiency, not maximum power**, and the reason is economic: the water is a **limited resource** with a value, so wasting a third of the head in the penstock to maximise the power from a given pipe would be absurd. A **larger penstock** is bought instead, and the head loss kept small.

> The **economic penstock diameter** balances the **capital cost of a larger pipe** against the **value of the energy lost** in friction over the plant's life — and the optimum lands at a head loss of a few percent, not 33%.

**Where the maximum-power result does apply**: situations where the conduit is **fixed and the resource unlimited** — some pumping and hydraulic transmission problems, and, historically, the hydraulic power networks that once drove machinery in cities.

**The power relations:**

> **Power P = γ Q H_net** (watts, with γ in N/m³, Q in m³/s, H in m)
> **= 9.81 Q H_net** (kW)
> **With efficiency: P = 9.81 Q H_net η**

**A worked case for Nepal.** A micro-hydro scheme with **Q = 0.5 m³/s** and a **gross head of 60 m**, penstock loss 5%, overall efficiency 70%:

> **H_net = 60 × 0.95 = 57 m**
> **P = 9.81 × 0.5 × 57 × 0.70 = 196 kW**

**The 9.81QH shortcut in kW** is worth memorising, along with a rough overall efficiency of **0.7 to 0.85** for a small scheme — it gives a plant's output in one line from the two numbers a site survey provides.

**Note also the nozzle case**, which is the companion result: for **power transmitted by a JET** through a nozzle at the end of a pipe, maximum power again occurs at **h_f = H/3**, and the **optimum nozzle area** relative to the pipe area follows from it. That is the sizing rule for a **Pelton turbine's** jet — the nozzle is proportioned so the penstock's friction loss is a small fraction of the gross head at the design flow, and the jet takes the remainder as velocity head.

examTip.trick: Differentiate **P = γQ(H − kQ²)** and set dP/dQ = 0. You get **kQ² = H/3**, so h_f = H/3.
examTip.mnemonic: **Maximum POWER occurs at only 66.7% EFFICIENCY** — the two objectives conflict, and you must choose. **Hydropower designs for EFFICIENCY** (penstock loss kept to 5–10%), because the water is a valuable resource. Quick output estimate: **P ≈ 9.81 Q H η kW**.

questions.stem: Where the hydraulic grade line falls below the pipe centreline, the pressure in the pipe is:
questions.solution:
**Below atmospheric — a negative gauge pressure.**

**Because the HGL plots p/γ + z.** If the HGL lies **below** the pipe centreline (which is at elevation z), then **p/γ is negative**, so **p is negative** in gauge terms.

**The two lines and their properties:**

| Line | Plots | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **HGL** (hydraulic grade line) | **p/γ + z** | The level water would rise to in a **piezometer** at that point |
| **EGL** (energy grade line) | **p/γ + z + V²/2g** | The **total head** |

| Property | Statement |
|---|---|
| **EGL is always ABOVE the HGL** by **V²/2g** | The gap is the velocity head |
| **EGL always FALLS** in the direction of flow | Friction — unless a **pump** adds energy (a step **up**) |
| The EGL **steps DOWN** at a turbine or a local loss | — |
| **HGL may RISE** where the pipe **expands** | The velocity head converts back to pressure |
| The two **coincide** where V = 0 | At a reservoir surface |
| **HGL coincides with the water surface** in an open channel | Since p = 0 there |
| **HGL below the pipe** | **NEGATIVE pressure** — the case in question |

**Why negative pressure is a problem:**

| Problem | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **AIR is drawn IN** through joints, glands and any small defect | Forms pockets that **reduce the flow area** and the discharge |
| **DISSOLVED AIR comes out of solution** | Accumulates at high points |
| **CAVITATION** if the pressure reaches vapour pressure | Noise, vibration, erosion, loss of flow |
| **CONTAMINATION** — polluted groundwater can be **sucked into** the main | The most serious consequence for a water supply |
| **COLLAPSE** of a thin-walled or flexible pipe | External pressure exceeds internal |

**The contamination risk is the one that matters most in public health terms:**

> A water main at **negative pressure** passing through **contaminated ground** — near a leaking sewer, for instance — will **draw that contamination IN** through any joint or crack. A positive pressure leaks water out harmlessly; a negative pressure lets pathogens in.

That is why water supply codes require a **minimum positive pressure** to be maintained **throughout the network at all times**, including during peak demand and fire flow — typically **at least 7 m** of head, and often more.

**Where negative pressure arises:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| A **SIPHON** over a summit | Deliberate, and managed with an air valve |
| A pipeline crossing a **high point** | The classic case |
| The **suction side of a pump** | Inherent; managed by NPSH |
| During **water hammer** downsurge | Transient, but can cause **column separation** |
| Excessive demand drawing the HGL down | An operational failure |

**The design responses:**

| Response | Note |
|---|---|
| **Lay the pipe BELOW the HGL** throughout, wherever possible | The fundamental solution |
| **AIR VALVES at all high points** | Release accumulated air; admit air on draining |
| Break-pressure tanks | Reset the HGL |
| Increase the pipe diameter | Flattens the HGL, raising it above the pipe |
| Reroute to avoid the summit | — |

**Air valves deserve a word**, since they are the standard fitting and are frequently misunderstood. Three duties, often combined in one **double-orifice** valve:

| Duty | Orifice | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Release accumulated air** during operation | **Small** | Air collects at high points and must be bled continuously |
| **Admit air** when the main is drained or during downsurge | **Large** | Prevents **COLLAPSE** of the pipe under external pressure |
| **Exhaust air** during filling | Large | Lets the main fill without air locks |

**Sketching the HGL and EGL** is the quickest diagnostic in pipeline design: draw the reservoir levels, drop the EGL by each loss, subtract the velocity head to get the HGL, and see whether it ever falls below the pipe profile. If it does, the design has a problem that no amount of calculation will remove.

examTip.trick: The HGL plots **p/γ + z**. If it lies below the pipe's centreline elevation z, then p/γ must be negative.
examTip.mnemonic: **The serious risk is CONTAMINATION** — a main at negative pressure passing through polluted ground **draws it IN** through any joint. A positive pressure leaks harmlessly outward; a negative one imports pathogens. Hence codes require a **minimum positive residual head** everywhere, at all times.

questions.stem: Water flows at 0.05 m³/s through a 200 mm pipe 500 m long with f = 0.025. The friction head loss is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 8.1 m.**

> **A = π(0.2)²/4 = 0.03142 m²**
> **V = Q/A = 0.05/0.03142 = 1.592 m/s**
> **h_f = fLV²/(2gD) = 0.025 × 500 × 1.592²/(2 × 9.81 × 0.2)**
> **= 0.025 × 500 × 2.533/3.924 = 31.66/3.924 = 8.07 m ≈ 8.1 m** ✓

**Check by the discharge form**, which avoids computing the velocity at all:

> **h_f = 0.0826 f L Q²/D⁵ = 0.0826 × 0.025 × 500 × 0.0025/(0.2)⁵**
> **(0.2)⁵ = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴**
> **= 0.002581/3.2e−4 = 8.07 m** ✓

**Two forms worth carrying:**

> **h_f = f L V²/(2gD)** — when the **velocity** is known
> **h_f = 0.0826 f L Q²/D⁵** — when the **discharge** is known

**The second is the more useful in design**, because a specification gives discharge, not velocity. Committing the constant **0.0826** saves the conversion every time.

**The distractors and the errors that produce them:**

| Option | Comes from |
|---|---|
| **5.1 m** | **fLV/(2gD)** — forgetting to **square** V |
| **16.1 m** | Omitting the **2** in the denominator |
| **4.0 m** | Halving — a stray factor of 2 |

**The D⁵ dependence** is what the discharge form makes visible, and it is the dominant fact of pipeline economics:

| Diameter change | Head loss at the same Q |
|---|---|
| **× 1.25** (200 → 250 mm) | **× 0.33** — a third |
| **× 1.5** (200 → 300 mm) | **× 0.13** |
| **× 2** (200 → 400 mm) | **× 0.031** — a **thirty-second** |

> A modest increase in diameter produces a **dramatic** reduction in head loss — which is why the **economic diameter** so often turns out larger than intuition suggests, and why undersizing a rising main is such a costly and permanent error.

**Always check the flow regime:**

> **Re = VD/ν = 1.592 × 0.2/10⁻⁶ = 3.2 × 10⁵** — firmly **turbulent** ✓

so f = 0.025 is plausible; it corresponds to a relative roughness **k/D ≈ 0.0012**, or **k ≈ 0.24 mm** — about right for **cast iron**.

**And check the velocity against design practice:**

> **1.59 m/s** sits comfortably within the usual water-main range of **0.6 – 2.0 m/s** — fast enough to be self-cleansing, slow enough to avoid excessive friction, noise and water hammer.

**The engineering reading of the result**: 8.1 m of friction over 500 m is a **hydraulic gradient of 1.6%** — a reasonable figure for a distribution main. Had the same flow been forced through a **150 mm** pipe, the velocity would rise to 2.83 m/s and the loss to **27 m** over the same length: more than three times the head, for a pipe only 25% smaller.

examTip.trick: Two independent routes should agree: **fLV²/(2gD)** with V = 1.59 m/s, and **0.0826 fLQ²/D⁵**. Both give **8.07 m** ✓ — computing it twice is the fastest way to catch a slip.
examTip.mnemonic: **Memorise the constant 0.0826** and work straight from Q, since a specification gives discharge, not velocity. Then sanity-check: 1.59 m/s sits in the 0.6–2.0 m/s design band, and the gradient of 1.6% is reasonable for a main.

questions.stem: In the Hardy Cross method of pipe network analysis, the two conditions enforced are:
options: Constant velocity and constant diameter in every pipe
Continuity at each junction and zero net head loss around each loop
Equal discharge in every pipe and equal length
questions.solution:
**Continuity at each junction, and zero net head loss around each closed loop.**

| Condition | Statement | Analogy |
|---|---|---|
| **JUNCTION (node) condition** | **ΣQ = 0** — inflow equals outflow at every junction | Kirchhoff's **current** law |
| **LOOP condition** | **Σh_f = 0** around every closed loop, with sign convention | Kirchhoff's **voltage** law |

**Why the loop condition must hold**: the head at any point is a **single value**. Walking round a closed loop and returning to the starting point must bring you back to the same head — so the algebraic sum of the head changes is zero.

**The complication that makes it iterative:**

> **h_f = r Q²** — the resistance is **NON-LINEAR** in Q. So the two conditions cannot be solved as simultaneous **linear** equations, and an **iterative** method is required.

**The Hardy Cross procedure:**

1. **Assume** a set of flows satisfying **continuity at every junction** — this is essential; continuity is enforced by the assumption and never violated thereafter.
2. Compute **Σ(rQ²)** around each loop, with a **sign convention** (clockwise positive, say).
3. Compute the correction:

> **ΔQ = − Σ(r Q²) / (2 Σ |r Q|)**

4. **Apply ΔQ to every pipe in the loop**, in the loop's positive direction. Pipes common to two loops receive **both** corrections.
5. **Repeat** until the loop imbalances are acceptably small.

**Why the correction has that form**: it is a **Newton–Raphson** step. The numerator is the loop's head imbalance; the denominator is the derivative **d(Σh_f)/dQ = Σ2rQ**. The factor **2** comes from differentiating Q².

**Applying ΔQ to the whole loop preserves continuity** — adding the same increment to every pipe going round a closed circuit changes no junction's balance. That is the elegance of the method: **continuity is satisfied exactly at every iteration**, and only the loop condition is approached progressively.

**The exponent generalises**: if **h_f = rQⁿ** (n = 2 for Darcy–Weisbach, **1.852 for Hazen–Williams**), the correction becomes **ΔQ = −Σ(rQⁿ)/(n Σ|rQ^(n−1)|)**.

**Convergence:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| A **good initial guess** | Converges in **3 – 5** iterations |
| A poor guess | Slower, but the method is robust and usually still converges |
| **Many loops** | Slower; modern software uses the **linear theory** or **gradient (Todini)** method instead |

**Modern practice** uses software — **EPANET** is the standard free tool — which solves the whole system simultaneously by the gradient method rather than loop by loop. But the two conditions it enforces are **exactly these**, and understanding them is what lets an engineer judge whether an output is sensible.

**What network analysis is for:**

| Purpose | Output |
|---|---|
| **Sizing pipes** | Diameters that keep pressures and velocities within limits |
| **Checking PRESSURES** at every node | Against the **minimum residual head** requirement |
| **FIRE FLOW** analysis | Can the network deliver the fire demand while holding minimum pressure? |
| Locating **booster pumps and break-pressure tanks** | — |
| Water quality and age modelling | Where water stagnates |

**The fire-flow check is often the governing case**, and it is the one most likely to be omitted: normal peak demand may be comfortably met while the network collapses under a fire draw at an unfavourable node. Codes require the check at the **worst node**, with the rest of the system at peak hour demand simultaneously.

**A design note for hill towns**, relevant in Nepal: large elevation differences within a distribution zone produce **excessive pressures at low points** when the high points are adequately served. The remedy is to divide the network into **pressure zones** separated by **break-pressure tanks** or **pressure-reducing valves** — each zone served from its own hydraulic level, so that no part of the system sees more than about 60 m of head.

examTip.trick: The two conditions are Kirchhoff's laws for pipes: **ΣQ = 0 at every junction** and **Σh_f = 0 round every loop**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Apply the correction ΔQ to EVERY pipe in the loop** — that keeps continuity satisfied exactly at each iteration, so only the loop condition has to converge. That is the elegance of the method. The **fire-flow case** is the one most often omitted and is frequently what governs.

questions.stem: The pressure rise due to instantaneous closure of a valve in a pipeline is given by:
options: ρ c ΔV, where c is the pressure wave speed
questions.solution:
**Δp = ρ c ΔV** — the **JOUKOWSKY** equation, where **c** is the speed of the pressure wave.

**The wave speed:**

> **c = √(K/ρ)** for a **rigid** pipe — about **1440 m/s** for water
> **c = √(K/ρ) / √(1 + K D/(E t))** for an **elastic** pipe

where D is the diameter, t the wall thickness and E the pipe material's modulus.

**The magnitude is what makes it dangerous:**

> Water at **2 m/s** stopped instantly: **Δp = 1000 × 1440 × 2 = 2.88 MPa ≈ 288 m of head**

A modest velocity generates a pressure rise that would burst most distribution mains. And note that it depends on the **velocity change**, not on the pressure or the head — a low-pressure line at high velocity is as vulnerable as a high-pressure one.

**Note that Δp does NOT depend on the pipe length** — only on the velocity change and the wave speed. What the length **does** determine is the **timing**:

> **The wave travels to the reservoir and back in time 2L/c.**

**The critical distinction:**

| Closure time T | Classification | Pressure rise |
|---|---|---|
| **T < 2L/c** | **RAPID (instantaneous)** closure | **FULL Joukowsky value** |
| **T > 2L/c** | **SLOW** closure | **REDUCED**, roughly in the ratio **(2L/c)/T** |

**Why 2L/c is the threshold**: the reflected **negative** wave returning from the reservoir arrives back at the valve after 2L/c. If the valve is **still closing** when it arrives, the reflection **cancels part of the rise**. If closure is already complete, the full rise has developed and the reflection comes too late.

> So closing a valve in 0.1 s instead of 0.5 s makes **no difference at all** if 2L/c is 0.05 s — both are "instantaneous". The relevant comparison is always against **2L/c**, not against some absolute idea of fast.

**A worked case.** A 2 km pipeline, c = 1200 m/s:

> **2L/c = 4000/1200 = 3.3 seconds**

So any closure **faster than 3.3 s** produces the full Joukowsky rise. A valve closed by hand in 10 s is a **slow** closure and the rise is roughly a third of the maximum; the same valve slammed shut, or a power-operated valve closing in 2 s, gives the full value.

**Wave speeds in different pipe materials** — the elasticity matters greatly:

| Pipe | c (m/s) |
|---|---|
| **Rigid (theoretical)** | **1440** |
| Steel | 1000 – 1300 |
| Cast iron / ductile iron | 1000 – 1200 |
| Concrete | 1000 – 1200 |
| **PVC** | **300 – 500** |
| **Polyethylene (PE)** | **200 – 300** |

> **Plastic pipes have a much lower wave speed**, so **Δp = ρcΔV is much smaller** — often by a factor of four or five. That is a genuine and useful advantage of plastic pipe against water hammer, and it is why PE rising mains are more tolerant of pump trips than steel ones.
