**Note also that entrained AIR drastically reduces c** — even 1% of free air can halve the wave speed, because air's compressibility dominates. That is protective against surge but harmful in every other respect (loss of capacity, measurement errors, corrosion), so it is never relied on.

**Control measures**, in rough order of preference:

| Measure | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **SLOW closure** — longer than 2L/c | The cheapest and most effective where operationally acceptable |
| **Surge tank** | A free surface near the machine — hydropower |
| **Air vessel** | A compressible cushion — the standard for **pumping mains** |
| **Pressure relief / surge anticipation valve** | Vents the surge |
| **FLYWHEEL** on the pump | Extends the run-down time on **power failure** |
| Flexible pipe material | Lower c |
| Bypass and non-return valve arrangements | — |

**The pump power failure case** is the one most often overlooked in water supply, and it is worse than valve closure: the pump stops in a fraction of a second, the column decelerates, and a **DOWNSURGE** occurs first — potentially causing **column separation** at high points, followed by a violent **rejoining** shock that can exceed the upsurge. A **flywheel** or an **air vessel** is the standard protection, and the analysis must cover the downsurge as carefully as the upsurge.

examTip.trick: **Δp = ρcΔV** contains **no length term** — the pipe's length does not affect the magnitude, only the **timing**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Compare the closure time against 2L/c**, the wave's round trip. Faster than that gives the FULL rise however fast you actually go; slower reduces it roughly in proportion. **Plastic pipe has c of 200–500 m/s against steel's 1200**, so it is far more tolerant of surge.

questions.stem: In the three-reservoir (branching pipe) problem, the direction of flow in the branch to the middle reservoir is determined by:
options: The relative diameters of the three pipes
The reservoir with the largest volume
Whether the piezometric head at the junction is above or below the middle reservoir's level
The lengths of the pipes only
questions.solution:
**By whether the piezometric head at the junction is above or below the middle reservoir's water level.**

**The problem.** Three reservoirs at different levels are connected by pipes meeting at a common junction J. The **highest** reservoir always supplies flow; the **lowest** always receives it. The **middle** one may do either, and which it does is not known in advance.

**The governing quantity is the piezometric head H_J at the junction:**

| Condition | Middle reservoir |
|---|---|
| **H_J > z_middle** | **RECEIVES** flow — the junction is at higher head, so water flows toward it |
| **H_J < z_middle** | **SUPPLIES** flow — the reservoir is at higher head |
| **H_J = z_middle** | **NO FLOW** in the middle branch — the boundary case |

**The solution method is trial and error on H_J:**

1. **Assume H_J = z_middle** (no flow in the middle branch) as a first trial.
2. Compute **Q₁** (from the highest reservoir) and **Q₃** (to the lowest) using **h_f = rQ²** with the head differences that assumption implies.
3. **Compare:**

| Result | Interpretation | Next step |
|---|---|---|
| **Q₁ > Q₃** | Too much coming in — the junction head must be **higher** | **Raise H_J**; the middle reservoir **receives** |
| **Q₁ < Q₃** | Too much going out — the head must be **lower** | **Lower H_J**; the middle reservoir **supplies** |
| Q₁ = Q₃ | The trial was exactly right | Done |

4. Iterate until **continuity at the junction is satisfied**:

> **ΣQ into J = ΣQ out of J**

**The first trial is chosen deliberately** — setting H_J = z_middle is not a guess but a **test**, because it immediately reveals the flow direction in the middle branch from the sign of (Q₁ − Q₃). Once the direction is known, the iteration is straightforward.

**The equations:**

> **Pipe 1 (high reservoir to J): z₁ − H_J = r₁Q₁²**
> **Pipe 2 (middle to/from J): |z₂ − H_J| = r₂Q₂²**
> **Pipe 3 (J to low reservoir): H_J − z₃ = r₃Q₃²**
> **Continuity: Q₁ ± Q₂ = Q₃** — sign depending on the middle branch's direction

with **r = 0.0826 f L/D⁵**, and velocity heads and minor losses usually neglected as small against the reservoir level differences.

**Why this problem matters** — it is not an academic exercise:

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Multiple sources feeding one distribution network** | A common water supply arrangement |
| **Service reservoirs** that fill at night and supply at peak | The flow **reverses** daily — exactly this problem, twice a day |
| **Interconnected schemes** in hill towns | Springs at various elevations feeding a common main |
| Any pipe **junction of three or more branches** | The general case |

**The service reservoir case is the everyday one**: a balancing reservoir on a network **receives** water when demand is low (the junction head is high) and **supplies** it when demand peaks (the junction head falls below the reservoir level). The reversal happens automatically, and designing for it means checking **both** conditions.

**Extension to more branches**: with four or more pipes at a junction the same logic applies — assume H_J, compute every branch's flow from its own head difference, and adjust H_J until the junction balances. That is precisely a **single-node** version of what the **Hardy Cross** and gradient methods do for a whole network, and it is a good way to build intuition for how network solvers behave.

**A practical caution**: the analysis assumes all pipes remain **full and pressurised**. If the junction head falls below a pipe's summit, that branch may **de-prime** and the analysis breaks down — so the pipe profiles must be checked against the computed HGL, not just the reservoir levels.

examTip.trick: Start by **assuming H_J equals the middle reservoir's level** — that is not a guess but a **test**. If Q_in exceeds Q_out, H_J must be higher and the middle reservoir receives; if less, it supplies.
examTip.mnemonic: **A service reservoir does BOTH, twice a day** — filling at night when the junction head is high, supplying at peak when it falls. So both conditions must be checked, not just one.

questions.stem: The economic diameter of a pumping main is the diameter at which:
options: The sum of annual capital cost and annual pumping cost is minimum
questions.solution:
**The diameter at which the SUM of the annualised capital cost and the annual pumping cost is a minimum.**

**The two costs pull in opposite directions:**

| Cost | Varies with diameter |
|---|---|
| **CAPITAL** — pipe, laying, fittings | **INCREASES** with D, roughly as **D^1.0 to D^1.5** |
| **PUMPING energy** over the life | **DECREASES steeply** with D — as **1/D⁵** through the head loss |

> **Total annual cost = (capital × capital recovery factor) + (annual energy cost)**

and the minimum of that sum is the economic diameter.

**The energy side falls very steeply**, which is the key insight:

> **h_f ∝ 1/D⁵**, and **pumping power ∝ Q h_f**, so the running cost falls as **1/D⁵** while the capital cost rises only as about **D^1.2**.

> The optimum therefore lies at a **LARGER diameter — and a LOWER velocity — than intuition suggests.**

**That is the practical lesson**: engineers under capital pressure habitually **undersize** rising mains, and the penalty is paid every day for the life of the scheme in electricity that need not have been consumed. The mistake is permanent, because replacing a buried main costs far more than laying the right one initially.

**Typical resulting velocities:**

| System | Economic velocity |
|---|---|
| **Pumping mains** | **0.9 – 1.5 m/s** |
| Gravity mains | 0.6 – 2.0 m/s (set by other limits) |
| **Long transmission mains, expensive power** | Lower — **0.8 – 1.2 m/s** |
| Short mains, cheap power | Higher |

**Lea's formula** and similar empirical rules give a quick first estimate:

> **D = k √Q**, with k around **0.97 – 1.22** in SI units for continuous pumping

but a proper optimisation is preferred for any significant scheme, since the answer depends on local pipe prices, the **energy tariff**, the **discount rate** and the **hours of pumping per day**.

**The factors that shift the optimum:**

| Factor | Effect on the economic diameter |
|---|---|
| **Higher energy cost** | **LARGER** — energy dominates |
| **Higher pipe cost** | Smaller |
| **More pumping hours per day** | **LARGER** — more energy consumed |
| **Longer design life** | Larger |
| **Higher discount rate** | Smaller — future savings are worth less today |
| Expected **demand growth** | Larger — allow for it now |

**Two considerations beyond pure economics** often override the calculation:

| Consideration | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Future demand growth** | A main is a **50-year asset** in a growing town. Sizing for today's demand alone guarantees an early and expensive duplication |
| **Minimum self-cleansing velocity** | The pipe must not be so large that sediment settles — a real issue for sewage rising mains, where **0.75 m/s** must be achieved at least daily |

**The sewage rising main is the case where the two conflict directly**: economics pushes toward a large pipe and low velocity; self-cleansing demands a minimum velocity. The usual resolution is a **smaller pipe accepting higher pumping costs**, or **intermittent pumping at a higher rate** so the self-cleansing velocity is reached during each pumping cycle even though the average flow is low.

**A note on staging.** Where demand will grow substantially, the choice is between **one large pipe now** and **duplicating later**. Duplication is often the better answer financially — the capital is deferred and the second pipe provides **redundancy** — but it requires that the route and the wayleaves be preserved, which is a planning decision that must be made at the outset rather than discovered to be impossible twenty years on.

examTip.trick: Capital cost rises roughly as **D^1.2**; pumping cost falls as **1/D⁵**. The steep second term pushes the optimum to a **larger diameter and lower velocity** than intuition suggests.
examTip.mnemonic: **Engineers under capital pressure habitually UNDERSIZE rising mains**, and the penalty is paid in electricity every day for fifty years. Typical economic velocity **0.9–1.5 m/s** — but a **sewage** rising main must still reach 0.75 m/s to stay self-cleansing, which pulls the other way.

questions.stem: Two pipes are laid in series. Compared with a single pipe of the same total length and the larger diameter, the combination will:
options: Carry more flow for the same head
Carry less flow for the same head
questions.solution:
**It will carry LESS flow for the same head.**

**Because in series the head losses ADD**, and the smaller pipe contributes a disproportionately large share:

> **h_total = h₁ + h₂ = r₁Q² + r₂Q²**, with **r = 0.0826 f L/D⁵**

Since **r ∝ 1/D⁵**, the **smaller pipe's resistance dominates** the total. Replacing part of a large pipe with a smaller one therefore **increases the total resistance** substantially, and for a fixed available head the flow must fall.

**A worked comparison.** 1000 m available at a head of 20 m, f = 0.02:

| Arrangement | Resistance r | Q |
|---|---|---|
| **All 300 mm** | 0.0826 × 0.02 × 1000/(0.3)⁵ = **680** | √(20/680) = **0.172 m³/s** |
| **500 m of 300 mm + 500 m of 200 mm** | 340 + 0.0826 × 0.02 × 500/(0.2)⁵ = 340 + **2581** = **2921** | √(20/2921) = **0.083 m³/s** |

> Replacing **half** the length with a pipe of **two thirds** the diameter **more than halves** the discharge — and note that the 200 mm section alone accounts for **88%** of the total resistance despite being half the length.

**The general lesson:**

> **In a series system, the SMALLEST pipe controls.** It is the bottleneck, and enlarging any other section achieves little until the constriction is removed.

That is a genuinely useful diagnostic in practice: when an existing main underperforms, look for the **smallest section, the partly closed valve, or the tuberculated length** before considering wholesale replacement.

**Series and parallel compared:**

| | **SERIES** | **PARALLEL** |
|---|---|---|
| Same in each pipe | **DISCHARGE** | **HEAD LOSS** |
| Added | **HEAD LOSSES** | **DISCHARGES** |
| Effect of adding a pipe | **Increases** total resistance | **Decreases** total resistance |
| Controlled by | The **SMALLEST** pipe | The **LARGEST** pipe |

**The equivalent pipe for a series arrangement — Dupuit's equation**, for equal f:

> **L_e/D_e⁵ = L₁/D₁⁵ + L₂/D₂⁵ + …**

Usually the equivalent length is found for a chosen convenient diameter, reducing a stepped main to a single uniform pipe for further analysis.

**Where series arrangements arise legitimately:**

| Situation | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Tapering a main** as demand is drawn off along its length | Each successive section carries less flow, so a smaller diameter is appropriate and economical |
| **Extending an existing main** with a different available size | Practical constraint |
| Passing through a **constrained crossing** — under a road, through a culvert | A shorter, smaller section may be unavoidable |
| Different **pressure classes** along a profile | Thicker walls, hence smaller bore, at high-pressure sections |

**Tapering is the good case** and worth distinguishing from the bad: a distribution main that sheds flow along its route **should** reduce in diameter, because each section is sized for the flow it actually carries. That is not a bottleneck — the discharge falls as the diameter does, so the velocity and hydraulic gradient stay reasonable.

**The bad case** is a **constriction on a full-flow main** — a short small-diameter section, an undersized valve, or a partly closed gate — where the full discharge must pass through a reduced bore. The head loss there can exceed that of kilometres of correctly sized pipe.

**A practical illustration**: a **half-closed gate valve** on a main can have a K of 5 or more, equivalent to **hundreds of metres** of straight pipe. Operators who throttle a valve to control flow are, in effect, inserting an expensive constriction — which is why flow control on a pumped system is better achieved by **variable speed drives** than by throttling.

examTip.trick: Resistance goes as **1/D⁵**, so in series the **smallest pipe dominates the total** — half the length at two-thirds the diameter can contribute nearly 90% of the resistance.
examTip.mnemonic: **In series, the smallest pipe controls.** Useful diagnostic: when an existing main underperforms, look for the short small section or the **half-closed valve** (K ≈ 5, worth hundreds of metres of pipe) before considering replacement.

questions.stem: In the Colebrook–White equation, the friction factor depends on:
options: Both the Reynolds number and the relative roughness
questions.solution:
**Both the Reynolds number and the relative roughness.**

> **1/√f = −2 log₁₀[ k/(3.7D) + 2.51/(Re √f) ]**

**The equation is IMPLICIT in f** — f appears on both sides — which is why it must be solved iteratively, and why the **Moody diagram** (a graphical solution) has remained in use for a century.

**Its great merit is that it spans the whole turbulent range**, reducing correctly to the two limiting cases:

| Limit | The equation becomes | Regime |
|---|---|---|
| **k → 0** (smooth pipe) | **1/√f = −2log₁₀[2.51/(Re√f)]** — the **Prandtl smooth-pipe** law | f depends on **Re only** |
| **Re → ∞** (fully rough) | **1/√f = −2log₁₀[k/(3.7D)]** — the **von Kármán rough-pipe** law | f depends on **k/D only** |
| In between | Both terms matter | The **transitional** zone |

**The physical picture** behind the two limits is the **viscous sublayer**:

| Condition | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Roughness **buried within** the viscous sublayer | The flow never feels it — **hydrodynamically SMOOTH** |
| Roughness **projecting through** the sublayer | Full form drag on the projections — **fully ROUGH** |
| Comparable | **Transitional** |

> As Re increases the **sublayer THINS**, so the same pipe moves from smooth behaviour toward rough. **"Smooth" and "rough" describe the FLOW as much as the PIPE.**

**That is why the Moody curves flatten** at high Reynolds number: once the roughness is fully exposed, further increases in Re change nothing about the geometry of the drag, so f becomes constant.

**Explicit approximations** were developed for computer use, and are accurate to within a percent or so:

| Approximation | Form |
|---|---|
| **Swamee–Jain** | **f = 0.25/[log₁₀(k/(3.7D) + 5.74/Re^0.9)]²** |
| **Haaland** | **1/√f = −1.8 log₁₀[(k/(3.7D))^1.11 + 6.9/Re]** |

Both avoid iteration entirely and are what modern software uses.

**Solving Colebrook–White by hand** is straightforward if approached sensibly: start from the **fully rough** value (dropping the Re term), then substitute back and iterate. Two passes are almost always enough, because the logarithm makes the function very insensitive to the starting guess.

**Relative roughness k/D is what matters, not k alone** — which has a consequence worth noting:

> **A LARGE pipe is hydraulically SMOOTHER than a small one of the same material.** A roughness of 0.26 mm gives k/D = 0.0052 in a 50 mm pipe but only 0.00026 in a 1 m pipe — a twentyfold difference in relative terms.

So large transmission mains have low friction factors (f ≈ 0.012–0.015) while small service pipes of the same material run at f ≈ 0.03 or more.

**The three types of pipe problem**, and how the implicitness affects each:

| Problem | Given | Find | Difficulty |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Type 1** | Q, D, L, k | **h_f** | **Direct** — compute Re, get f, apply Darcy–Weisbach |
| **Type 2** | h_f, D, L, k | **Q** | **Iterative** — f depends on Q through Re |
| **Type 3** | h_f, Q, L, k | **D** | **Most iterative** — D appears in Re, k/D and D⁵ |

**Type 3 is the design problem** and the hardest: assume a diameter, check the head loss, adjust. Swamee–Jain published an explicit formula for it too, which is what design software uses:

> **D = 0.66[ k^1.25 (LQ²/(g h_f))^4.75 + ν Q^9.4 (L/(g h_f))^5.2 ]^0.04**

**A practical caution on k.** The roughness of a real pipe is **not known precisely** — published values are ranges, and an installed pipe's roughness depends on joints, alignment, and age. A calculation carried to four significant figures on a k taken from a table is false precision; the sensible practice is to **bracket the answer** with the range of plausible k and design for the unfavourable end.

examTip.trick: The equation is **implicit in f**, which is why the Moody diagram survives. It reduces correctly to the two limits: smooth (Re only) and fully rough (k/D only).
examTip.mnemonic: **"Smooth" and "rough" describe the FLOW as much as the PIPE** — as Re rises the viscous sublayer thins until the roughness projects through it. That is why the Moody curves go **horizontal** at high Re. Also: a **large pipe is hydraulically smoother** than a small one of the same material, since k/D is smaller.

questions.stem: Minor losses in a pipeline may reasonably be neglected when the pipe length exceeds about:
questions.solution:
**About 1000 diameters.**

**The reasoning.** Friction loss is **h_f = fLV²/(2gD)**, and a single fitting is **h_L = KV²/(2gD) × D**, that is **KV²/2g**. Comparing:

> Friction loss over length L: **f(L/D) × V²/2g**
> One fitting: **K × V²/2g**

So the fitting matters when **K is comparable to f(L/D)**. With f ≈ 0.02 and L/D = 1000, the friction term is **20** — against a total K of perhaps 2 to 5 for a normal run of fittings. The fittings then contribute **10–25%**, and beyond that length their share falls further.

**But the rule must be applied with judgement:**

| Situation | Are minor losses minor? |
|---|---|
| A **long transmission main** — kilometres of pipe, a few valves | **YES** — negligible |
| **Pump house or treatment plant internal pipework** | **NO** — the fittings dominate completely |
| **Domestic plumbing** | **NO** |
| A short suction line | **NO** — and here they are critical, because they eat into the **NPSH** |
| A penstock with a bend and a valve over 500 m | Marginal — include them |

> **"Minor" is a name, not a promise.** In short pipework with many fittings the local losses can be **most of the total**, and calling them minor has misled generations of students.

**The equivalent length method** is the convenient way to include them:

> **L_e = K D/f** — each fitting is replaced by an equivalent length of straight pipe
> Then **h_total = f(L + ΣL_e)V²/(2gD)**

**Typical equivalent lengths** (for f = 0.02, so L_e = 50 K D):

| Fitting | K | L_e |
|---|---|---|
| **Gate valve, fully open** | 0.2 | **10 D** |
| **90° long-radius bend** | 0.3 | 15 D |
| **90° sharp elbow** | 0.9 | **45 D** |
| **Sharp entrance** | 0.5 | 25 D |
| **Exit into a tank** | 1.0 | 50 D |
| **Swing check valve** | 2.5 | 125 D |
| **Globe valve, fully open** | **10** | **500 D** |

**The globe valve at 500 diameters** is the striking entry: a single fully open globe valve on a 100 mm line is equivalent to **50 metres of straight pipe**. That is why globe valves are used for **throttling** (where the loss is the point) and gate or butterfly valves for **isolation** (where it is not.)

**And the check valve at 125 D** matters on pumping mains, where a swing check valve is fitted at every pump — a loss that is unavoidable but should at least be counted.

**The suction-side case deserves separate emphasis:**

> On a **pump SUCTION line**, every minor loss **subtracts directly from the NPSH available**. A foot valve, a strainer, a bend and an eccentric reducer can easily total 1.5 m — which may be the entire margin against cavitation.

That is why good practice keeps the suction line **short, straight, and one size larger than the pump inlet**, with the **minimum possible number of fittings**, and never fits a throttling valve on it.

**How to reduce minor losses** where they matter:

| Measure | Saving |
|---|---|
| **Round the entrance** (bell-mouth) | K from **0.5 to 0.05** — a tenfold reduction |
| **Long-radius bends** instead of sharp elbows | K from 0.9 to 0.3 |
| **Gate or butterfly valves** for isolation duty | K from 10 to 0.2 |
| **Gradual** rather than sudden transitions | Avoids separation |
| Fewer fittings; straighter routes | — |

**The bell-mouth entrance is the outstanding value**: a tenfold reduction in K for nothing more than a rounded edge on the intake. It is why every well-designed intake, culvert entry and pump suction bell is flared, and why a square-cut pipe end projecting into a tank is the mark of a job done without thought.

examTip.trick: Compare **f(L/D)** with **ΣK**. At L/D = 1000 and f = 0.02 the friction term is 20, against a typical total K of 2–5 — so the fittings are then under a quarter of the loss and falling.
examTip.mnemonic: **"Minor" is a name, not a promise.** In a pump house or a domestic installation the fittings are MOST of the loss. And on a **pump SUCTION line** they subtract directly from the NPSH, where 1.5 m may be the entire margin against cavitation.

questions.stem: An air valve at a high point on a rising main is required primarily to:
options: Increase the pressure in the main
Release accumulated air and admit air when the main is drained
questions.solution:
**To release accumulated air during operation and to admit air when the main is drained or during a downsurge.**

**Three distinct duties**, usually combined in one **double-orifice** valve:

| Duty | Orifice | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Release accumulated air** during normal running | **SMALL** | Air comes out of solution and collects at high points; must be bled continuously against full main pressure |
| **Admit air** when the main is **emptied**, or during a **DOWNSURGE** | **LARGE** | Prevents the pipe **COLLAPSING** under external atmospheric pressure |
| **Exhaust air** rapidly during **filling** | **LARGE** | Lets the main fill without air locks or damaging surge |

**Why the two orifices differ in size** is the design point:

> The **small orifice must open against the full working pressure**, so it must be small — a large orifice could not be sealed against, say, 60 m of head by a float. The **large orifice** operates only at or near atmospheric pressure, so it can be large.

A single-orifice valve can therefore do only one job properly, which is why the combined double-orifice type is standard.

**Why trapped air is damaging:**

| Problem | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Reduces the effective flow area** | An air pocket at a summit acts as a **partial blockage**; the discharge falls, sometimes drastically |
| **Increases the head loss** | The flow must pass beneath the pocket at higher velocity |
| **Corrosion** | Oxygen accelerates internal corrosion of steel and iron |
| **Measurement errors** | Meters read wrongly with entrained air |
| **Surge amplification** | A moving air pocket can generate severe transients when it is finally expelled |
| Air locks | Can stop the flow entirely |

**Why admitting air matters even more:**

> When a main is **drained** — for repair, or by a burst — the water leaving creates a **vacuum**. Atmospheric pressure then acts on the outside with nothing balancing it inside, and a **thin-walled or plastic pipe will COLLAPSE**.

> The same happens transiently during the **DOWNSURGE** following a **pump trip**, and it is why the large orifice is sized for the maximum rate at which the main can empty.

**Collapse is a real and expensive failure mode**, and it happens on commissioning and maintenance far more often than in normal operation — typically when a main is drained faster than the air valves can admit air, or when the valves are isolated or seized.

**Where air valves are placed:**

| Location | Reason |
|---|---|
| **All HIGH points** on the profile | Where air collects |
| **Long ascending runs** — at intervals of 400–800 m | Air migrates uphill |
| **Long descending runs** | To admit air on draining |
| **Upstream of a reducing section** | Air tends to be trapped there |
| Downstream of the pump discharge valve | — |

**Related fittings on a rising main**, which complete the picture:

| Fitting | Location | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **AIR valve** | **High** points | As above |
| **WASHOUT (scour) valve** | **LOW** points | **Drain** the main and **flush out sediment** |
| **Isolating valves** | At intervals, and at branches | Sectionalise for repair |
| **Non-return valve** | At the pump | Prevents reverse flow |
| **Pressure relief / surge vessel** | As surge analysis dictates | — |

> The pairing is worth remembering: **air valves at the HIGH points, washouts at the LOW points** — air rises, sediment settles.

**A maintenance note** that matters in practice: air valves are **the most neglected fitting on any main**. They sit in chambers, fill with silt, seize shut, and are then blamed for nothing in particular. A seized air valve gives no immediate symptom — the main simply loses capacity slowly as air accumulates, or it collapses the next time someone drains it. Regular inspection and exercising is part of a competent operation and maintenance schedule, and its absence is one of the commonest reasons a rising main underdelivers years after commissioning.

examTip.trick: Two duties needing two orifice sizes: a **small** one to bleed air against full working pressure, and a **large** one to admit air fast when the main drains.
examTip.mnemonic: **Air valves at the HIGH points, washouts at the LOW points** — air rises, sediment settles. The large orifice prevents the pipe **COLLAPSING** under external pressure while draining, which is a real failure mode during maintenance. Air valves are also the most neglected fitting on any main.

questions.stem: Manning's equation for mean velocity in an open channel is:
questions.solution:
**V = (1/n) R^(2/3) S^(1/2).**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **n** | **Manning's roughness coefficient** — higher means **rougher** |
| **R** | **Hydraulic radius = A/P** — area divided by **wetted perimeter** |
| **S** | Slope of the **energy line** (= bed slope in uniform flow) |

> **Q = AV = (1/n) A R^(2/3) S^(1/2)**

**Note the exponents: R to the two-thirds, S to the one-half.** Option (c) has n in the numerator, which would make a rougher channel flow faster — dimensionally possible but physically backwards, and worth rejecting on that ground alone.

**Manning's n is the reverse convention to Hazen–Williams C**, which catches people out:

| Coefficient | Higher value means |
|---|---|
| **Manning's n** | **ROUGHER** |
| **Hazen–Williams C** | **SMOOTHER** |
| Roughness height k | Rougher |

**Typical values of n:**

| Surface | n |
|---|---|
| **Glass, smooth plastic** | **0.010** |
| **Smooth concrete, well finished** | **0.012** |
| Concrete, ordinary | 0.014 |
| Brick, cement mortar | 0.015 |
| **Earth channel, clean and straight** | **0.022** |
| Earth, weedy and winding | 0.030 |
| **Natural stream, clean and regular** | **0.030** |
| Natural stream, stony and weedy | 0.040 – 0.050 |
| **Flood plain, heavy brush and trees** | **0.10 and above** |

**The variation matters enormously**: n from 0.012 to 0.030 is a **factor of 2.5 in velocity** at the same slope and section — and since flood levels depend on it, the choice of n is often the largest single uncertainty in a river study.

**Uniform flow is the condition Manning describes:**

> The **gravity component driving the flow exactly balances the boundary friction resisting it**, so the depth stays constant along the channel — the **NORMAL DEPTH**, and the water surface is **parallel to the bed**.

**It requires** a prismatic channel of constant slope, roughness and discharge, long enough for the depth to settle. Real channels rarely satisfy all of that, which is why gradually varied flow analysis exists.

**Hydraulic radius R = A/P** is the parameter that makes one equation serve every channel shape, and its values are worth knowing:

| Section | R |
|---|---|
| **Wide shallow channel** | **≈ y** (the depth) — since P ≈ b |
| **Full circular pipe** | **D/4** |
| **Half-full circular pipe** | **D/4** — the same |
| Rectangular b × y | by/(b + 2y) |

**That a pipe running half full has the same R as one running full** is a genuinely useful result, and it has a striking consequence: since Q = (1/n)AR^(2/3)S^(1/2) and the half-full pipe has **half the area** with the **same R**, it carries **exactly half** the discharge — at the **same velocity**.

**And the related surprise**: a circular pipe carries its **maximum discharge at about 94% depth**, not when full — because beyond that the wetted perimeter grows faster than the area, so R falls. The **maximum velocity** occurs at about **81%** depth. Both facts matter for sewer design, where pipes are deliberately sized to run part full.

**Manning versus Chezy:**

> **Chezy: V = C√(RS)**, with **C = R^(1/6)/n** — so the two are the same relation with C expressed through n.

Chezy came first (1769) and is more general; Manning (1889) fixed the exponent empirically and is far more convenient, because **n is a property of the surface alone** while **C depends on R as well** — meaning C changes as the depth changes, and n does not.

examTip.trap: Option (c) puts **n in the numerator**, which would make a rougher channel flow faster — reject it on physical grounds without checking the exponents.
examTip.trick: Remember the exponents as **two-thirds and one-half**: R^(2/3) S^(1/2).
examTip.mnemonic: **Manning's n rises as the channel gets rougher** — the OPPOSITE of Hazen–Williams C. Values: smooth concrete 0.012, earth channel 0.022, natural stream 0.030, **flood plain with trees 0.10+**. That spread is the largest single uncertainty in a river study.

questions.stem: The hydraulic radius of a circular pipe flowing full of diameter D is:
questions.solution:
**D/4.**

> **R = A/P = (πD²/4)/(πD) = D/4** ✓

**Hydraulic radius R = A/P** — cross-sectional **area** divided by **wetted perimeter**. It is the parameter that lets one equation (Manning or Chezy) serve every channel shape, by expressing how efficiently a section conveys flow relative to the boundary it must drag against.

**A high R means an efficient section**: much area per unit of friction-generating perimeter.

**Standard values:**

| Section | R |
|---|---|
| **Circular, running FULL** | **D/4** |
| **Circular, running HALF full** | **D/4 — the SAME** |
| Circular at maximum discharge (94% depth) | Slightly more than D/4 |
| **Rectangular b × y** | **by/(b + 2y)** |
| **WIDE shallow channel** | **≈ y** — since P ≈ b when b ≫ y |
| **Most economical rectangle (b = 2y)** | **y/2** |
| **Most economical trapezoid** | **y/2** |
| **Semicircle** (flowing full) | **y/2** |

**Note that three of the last four are y/2** — that is not a coincidence, and it is the central result of economical section design:

> **Every most-economical section has R = y/2** — half the depth. The semicircle is the **theoretical optimum** among all shapes, and the best rectangle and best trapezoid achieve the same hydraulic radius by approaching it as closely as their geometry allows.

**Why the semicircle is optimal**: for a given area, the **circle has the least perimeter** of any shape. A **semicircle** is therefore the best open channel section, since the free surface contributes no friction.

**Why semicircles are nevertheless rarely built:**

| Objection | Note |
|---|---|
| **Difficult to construct** in earth or masonry | Curved formwork; unstable side slopes in soil |
| **Unstable** in erodible material | The steep upper sides collapse |
| Difficult to maintain and clean | — |
| Impractical for large channels | — |

**So practical channels approximate it**: the **trapezoid with side slopes at 60°** (i.e. 1:√3) is the best trapezoidal section, and it is exactly the shape that **circumscribes a semicircle** — the closest a straight-sided section can come to the ideal.

**The half-full circular pipe deserves comment**, because its equal hydraulic radius has a neat consequence:

> Half full, the pipe has **half the area** and the **same R** — so by Manning it carries **exactly half the discharge at exactly the same velocity** as when running full.

That is the design basis for **sewers**, which are sized to run part full at the design flow, leaving capacity in hand and a ventilated air space above.

**And the counter-intuitive maxima in a circular section:**

| Quantity | Maximum at depth |
|---|---|
| **DISCHARGE** | **≈ 0.94 D** — **not** when full |
| **VELOCITY** | **≈ 0.81 D** |

> Beyond 94% depth the **wetted perimeter grows faster than the area** as the section closes over, so **R falls** and the discharge with it. A pipe running just below full carries **more** than the same pipe running full.

**In pressure pipe formulae**, R = D/4 is what connects Manning to Darcy–Weisbach: substituting it into Manning and comparing gives

> **f = 124.5 n²/D^(1/3)**

which is occasionally useful for converting a roughness given in one convention to the other — for a concrete pipe of n = 0.013 and D = 1 m, f = 0.021, a sensible value.

examTip.mnemonic: **A pipe running HALF FULL has the SAME R as one running full** — so it carries exactly **half the discharge at the same velocity**. And the discharge maximum is at **94% depth**, not 100%, because beyond that the perimeter grows faster than the area.

questions.stem: The most economical rectangular channel section is one in which the bed width equals:
options: Four times the depth of flow
questions.solution:
**Twice the depth of flow: b = 2y.**

**What "most economical" means:**

> The section that carries the **MAXIMUM discharge for a given area** — equivalently, the section of **MINIMUM AREA (and minimum excavation) for a given discharge**.

**Since Q = (1/n)AR^(2/3)S^(1/2)**, maximising Q for fixed A means **maximising R = A/P**, which means **MINIMISING the wetted perimeter P**.

**Derivation.** For a rectangle: **A = by** and **P = b + 2y**. Substituting b = A/y:

> **P = A/y + 2y**
> **dP/dy = −A/y² + 2 = 0**
> **A = 2y²**, and since A = by, **b = 2y** ✓

**And then:**

> **R = A/P = 2y²/(2y + 2y) = 2y²/4y = y/2**

**The universal signature of an economical section:**

| Section | Condition | R |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle** | **b = 2y** | **y/2** |
| **Trapezoid** | Side slope **60°** (1:√3); **top width = 2 × sloping side** | **y/2** |
| **Triangle** | Side slopes at **45°** | y/(2√2) |
| **Semicircle** | Radius = depth | **y/2** |

> **R = y/2 is the mark of an economical section**, and it is a useful check on any such calculation.

**The unifying geometric statement:**

> For **every** most-economical section, a **SEMICIRCLE centred on the water surface and of radius equal to the depth is TANGENTIAL to the wetted boundary**.

That single property generates all the specific conditions above, and it explains why they share R = y/2: each is the closest its family of shapes can come to the semicircle, which is the true optimum.

**For the TRAPEZOID**, the most useful case in practice, the conditions are:

| Condition | Statement |
|---|---|
| Best **side slope** | **60° to the horizontal**, i.e. **1 vertical : 1/√3 horizontal** |
| **Top width** | **= 2 × the length of a sloping side** |
| **Hydraulic radius** | **y/2** |
| The section is | **Half a regular HEXAGON** |

**But the theoretical best side slope is usually NOT what is built**, and this is where design judgement enters:

> The side slope of an **earth** channel is dictated by the **STABILITY of the soil**, not by hydraulic efficiency. A 60° slope stands only in rock or very stiff clay.

| Material | Practical side slope (H:V) |
|---|---|
| **Rock** | **Near vertical to 0.25:1** |
| Stiff clay, earth with lining | 0.5:1 to 1:1 |
| **Firm clay, ordinary earth** | **1:1 to 1.5:1** |
| **Loose sandy soil** | **2:1** |
| Sandy loam, porous clay | 2:1 to 3:1 |

So the usual design procedure is: **fix the side slope from soil stability**, then find the **most economical proportions for THAT slope** — a constrained optimisation rather than the free one.

**Other practical departures from the theoretical optimum:**

| Consideration | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Freeboard** | Add 0.3 – 1.0 m above the design water level; not part of the hydraulic section |
| **Maximum permissible velocity** | To prevent **erosion** — may force a wider, shallower section |
| **Minimum velocity** | To prevent **siltation** — typically 0.6 m/s |
| **Depth limits** | Excavation cost, water table, land width available |
| Lining cost | May favour a different shape than excavation cost alone |

**The economical section minimises EXCAVATION and LINING area**, which is why it matters: for a long irrigation canal those are the dominant costs, and a few percent saved on perimeter over tens of kilometres is a real sum.

examTip.trick: Most economical means **minimum wetted perimeter** for a given area. Minimising P = A/y + 2y gives **b = 2y**, and then **R = y/2**.
examTip.mnemonic: **R = y/2 is the signature of EVERY economical section** — rectangle, trapezoid and semicircle alike. The unifying geometry: a semicircle centred on the water surface is tangential to the wetted boundary. Use it as a check on any such answer.

questions.stem: Flow in an open channel is supercritical when the Froude number is:
questions.solution:
**Greater than 1.**

> **Fr = V/√(g y)** for a rectangular channel (more generally, **V/√(g A/T)** with T the top width)

| Froude number | Regime | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Fr < 1** | **SUBCRITICAL** (tranquil, streaming) | **Deep and slow**; disturbances travel **BOTH** ways |
| **Fr = 1** | **CRITICAL** | Minimum specific energy |
| **Fr > 1** | **SUPERCRITICAL** (rapid, shooting) | **Shallow and fast**; disturbances travel **DOWNSTREAM only** |

**What the Froude number physically is:**

> **Fr = flow velocity / speed of a small surface wave**

and the wave speed in shallow water is **c = √(gy)**. So Fr compares how fast the water moves with how fast a disturbance can propagate through it.

**The consequence is the most important idea in open channel flow:**

| Regime | Can a disturbance travel upstream? | Control is |
|---|---|---|
| **SUBCRITICAL (Fr < 1)** | **YES** — the wave outruns the flow | **DOWNSTREAM** |
| **SUPERCRITICAL (Fr > 1)** | **NO** — the flow outruns the wave | **UPSTREAM** |

> **A subcritical flow "knows" what lies downstream and adjusts to it; a supercritical flow does not.**

**That is why backwater curves behave as they do**: a weir or a bridge constriction raises the level **upstream** in subcritical flow, because the information travels up. In supercritical flow it cannot, and the effect propagates only downstream.

**And it dictates where computation starts:**

| Flow | Compute the water surface profile |
|---|---|
| **Subcritical** | **From DOWNSTREAM, working UPSTREAM** |
| **Supercritical** | **From UPSTREAM, working DOWNSTREAM** |

Getting this backwards produces a profile that diverges instead of converging, and it is the commonest error in gradually varied flow computation.

**Typical occurrences:**

| Regime | Where |
|---|---|
| **Subcritical** | **Most natural rivers**; canals on mild slopes; reservoirs |
| **Supercritical** | **Steep chutes and spillways**; downstream of a **sluice gate**; steep mountain streams; flow over a weir crest |
| Critical | **AT a control** — the crest of a broad-crested weir, a free overfall, the entry to a steep slope |

**Critical flow at a control is what makes flow measurement possible:**

> At a **critical section**, the depth and discharge are **uniquely related** — **y_c = (q²/g)^(1/3)** for a rectangular channel. So measuring one gives the other, independently of the roughness or the downstream conditions.

That is the operating principle of the **broad-crested weir**, the **Parshall flume**, the **venturi flume** and the **free overfall** — each forces critical flow at a known section, so a single depth measurement yields the discharge.

**The transition between regimes:**

| Transition | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Supercritical → subcritical** | **HYDRAULIC JUMP** — abrupt, turbulent, with large energy loss |
| **Subcritical → supercritical** | **Smooth and gradual** — through a critical section; no jump |

> The asymmetry is thermodynamic: a jump **dissipates** energy, which is permissible. The reverse would have to **create** energy, which is not — so the transition down to supercritical happens smoothly, and the transition back up must be a jump.

**Froude number similarity** governs **hydraulic model studies** of spillways, stilling basins, harbours and river works, because those flows are dominated by **gravity and inertia** rather than viscosity. A model is built to the same Fr as the prototype, giving the scaling laws **V_r = √L_r**, **Q_r = L_r^(5/2)** and **T_r = √L_r** — so a 1:25 model runs at one fifth the velocity and one twenty-five-hundredth of the discharge.

examTip.trick: **Fr = V/√(gy)** compares the flow speed with the speed of a surface wave. Above 1, the flow outruns its own disturbances.
examTip.mnemonic: **Subcritical is controlled from DOWNSTREAM; supercritical from UPSTREAM.** That decides where a backwater computation must START — get it backwards and the profile diverges instead of converging. Also: **supercritical → subcritical needs a JUMP** (energy is lost); the reverse happens smoothly.

questions.stem: For a rectangular channel carrying a discharge of q per unit width, the critical depth is:
questions.solution:
**y_c = (q²/g)^(1/3)**, where **q = Q/b** is the discharge per unit width.

**Derivation.** Critical flow is the condition of **minimum specific energy** for a given discharge:

> **E = y + V²/2g = y + q²/(2gy²)**
> **dE/dy = 1 − q²/(gy³) = 0**
> **y_c³ = q²/g**, so **y_c = (q²/g)^(1/3)** ✓

**Equivalent statements of the critical condition**, all worth recognising:

| Statement | Form |
|---|---|
| **Froude number is unity** | **Fr = 1** |
| **Specific energy is minimum** for the given Q | **dE/dy = 0** |
| **Discharge is maximum** for the given E | **dQ/dy = 0** |
| Velocity equals the **wave speed** | **V_c = √(g y_c)** |
| **Minimum specific FORCE** | The momentum equivalent |

**And the two useful consequences:**

> **E_c = 1.5 y_c** — at critical flow the specific energy is exactly **1.5 times** the depth, since the velocity head is **y_c/2**.
> **V_c = √(g y_c)**

**The SPECIFIC ENERGY CURVE** is the organising picture, and it is worth carrying:

> Plotting **E against y** for a fixed q gives a **C-shaped curve** with its **nose at the minimum, E_min = 1.5y_c**. For any **E greater than E_min** there are **TWO possible depths** — the **ALTERNATE depths** — one subcritical (upper limb) and one supercritical (lower limb).

| Limb | Depth | Regime |
|---|---|---|
| **Upper** | **y > y_c** | **Subcritical** — deep and slow |
| **Nose** | **y = y_c** | Critical |
| **Lower** | **y < y_c** | **Supercritical** — shallow and fast |

**For E less than E_min the flow is IMPOSSIBLE** at that discharge — which is the physical meaning of the minimum and the reason a channel constriction can "choke".

**CHOKING** is the practical consequence and a real design issue:

> Narrowing a channel raises **q = Q/b**, which raises **y_c** and therefore **E_min**. If the available specific energy falls below the new **E_min**, the flow **cannot pass** — so the upstream level **RISES** until it can.

That is what happens at an undersized **bridge opening** or **culvert**: the constriction chokes, and the afflux — the upstream rise — can be metres. It is why bridge waterway openings are checked for choking, not merely for velocity.

**Alternate depths versus conjugate depths** — a distinction that is routinely confused:

| Pair | Same quantity conserved | Occurs at |
|---|---|---|
| **ALTERNATE depths** | **Same SPECIFIC ENERGY** | Two possible states for the same E and q |
| **CONJUGATE (sequent) depths** | **Same SPECIFIC FORCE (momentum)** | Either side of a **HYDRAULIC JUMP** |

> A hydraulic jump connects **CONJUGATE** depths, not alternate ones — because energy is **lost** in the jump, so the two depths cannot share a specific energy. They share **momentum**, since the external forces are small.

**Note that y_c depends only on q, not on the SLOPE or the ROUGHNESS.** That is what makes critical flow so valuable for measurement: force the flow through critical at a known section, measure the depth, and the discharge follows — independent of the channel's condition, which may change with weed growth and siltation.

**A worked value.** For q = 2 m³/s per metre:

> **y_c = (4/9.81)^(1/3) = (0.4077)^(1/3) = 0.742 m**
> **V_c = √(9.81 × 0.742) = 2.70 m/s**
> **E_c = 1.5 × 0.742 = 1.11 m**

**For non-rectangular sections** the general condition is **Q²T/(gA³) = 1**, with T the top width — solved by trial, since A and T both vary with depth.

examTip.trick: Set **dE/dy = 0** for E = y + q²/(2gy²) and you get y_c³ = q²/g directly.
examTip.mnemonic: **y_c depends ONLY on q — not on slope, not on roughness.** That independence is exactly what makes critical flow useful for measurement: a broad-crested weir or flume gives a discharge that does not drift as the channel silts or grows weed. Also **E_c = 1.5 y_c**.

questions.stem: A hydraulic jump can occur only when the flow approaching it is:
questions.solution:
**Supercritical (Fr₁ > 1).**

**A hydraulic jump is the abrupt transition from SUPERCRITICAL to SUBCRITICAL flow**, accompanied by violent turbulence and a substantial **loss of energy**.

**Why it can only go that way** is a thermodynamic argument worth understanding:

> A jump **DISSIPATES** energy, which is always permissible. The reverse — an abrupt rise from subcritical to supercritical — would have to **CREATE** energy, which is impossible.

So the transition **downward** into supercritical flow happens **smoothly**, through a critical section; the transition **back up** must be a **jump**.

**The conjugate (sequent) depth relation**, derived from the **MOMENTUM** equation:

> **y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1]**

**Momentum, not energy**, because the energy loss in the jump is large and unknown in advance — whereas the external forces are small and the momentum balance is exact. This is the standard illustration of the rule:

> Use **ENERGY** where the losses are **small or known**. Use **MOMENTUM** where the losses are **large or unknown** but the forces are what you need.

**Energy loss in the jump:**

> **E_L = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4 y₁ y₂)**

which can be a very large fraction of the incoming energy — up to 85% for a strong jump.

**Classification by the approach Froude number (USBR):**

| Fr₁ | Type | Character | Energy loss |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1.0 – 1.7** | **Undular** | A train of small waves | < 5% |
| 1.7 – 2.5 | **Weak** | Smooth surface rollers | 5 – 15% |
| **2.5 – 4.5** | **OSCILLATING** | An **unstable jet** oscillating between bed and surface — **generates WAVES that travel far downstream** | 15 – 45% |
| **4.5 – 9.0** | **STEADY** | **Well balanced and stable — the BEST for a stilling basin** | **45 – 70%** |
| **> 9.0** | **Strong** | Very rough, effective but the surface is choppy | 70 – 85% |

**The oscillating jump (2.5 – 4.5) is the one to AVOID in design**, and the reason is practical rather than hydraulic:

> Its **unstable oscillation generates surface waves that propagate a long way downstream**, eroding banks and damaging structures. A stilling basin designed to operate in this range performs badly however well it is built.

So basins are proportioned to fall in the **steady range (4.5 – 9)** wherever possible — and where the Froude number cannot be raised, **baffle blocks** are used to force stability.

**Uses of the hydraulic jump:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **ENERGY DISSIPATION** below a spillway, sluice or chute | The principal use — a **STILLING BASIN** |
| **Mixing** chemicals in water treatment | The turbulence is intense and rapid |
| **AERATION** of the flow | Raises dissolved oxygen — used deliberately in effluent discharge |
| Raising the water level for offtakes | — |
| Removing air pockets from culverts | — |

**Stilling basin design** is the main application, and it is where the theory becomes a structure:

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| The **TAILWATER depth must match y₂** | Too little tailwater and the jump **sweeps out** downstream, eroding the riverbed |
| **Length** of basin | Typically **5 to 6 times y₂** |
| **Baffle blocks and end sill** | **Shorten** the basin and **stabilise** the jump |
| Chute blocks at the entrance | Break up the incoming jet |

**The tailwater problem is the critical one**: the jump forms where the momentum balances, and if the downstream river level is lower than y₂ the jump is **swept downstream** out of the paved basin and onto erodible bed — which is how spillway aprons are undermined. The remedy is a **depressed basin** (lowering the floor so the required tailwater is available), an **end sill**, or a **stilling pool**.

**The USBR standard basins** (Types I–IV) codify these arrangements for different Froude ranges, and IS 4997 gives the Indian equivalent — worth knowing by name, since spillway design in the region follows them.

examTip.trick: The direction is fixed by thermodynamics: a jump **dissipates** energy, which is allowed. The reverse would have to **create** it, which is not — so the downward transition happens smoothly and only the upward one is a jump.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use MOMENTUM, not energy, across a jump** — the loss is large and unknown in advance, but the external forces are small. Avoid designing a stilling basin in the **oscillating range Fr 2.5–4.5**: it throws waves far downstream. Aim for the **steady range 4.5–9**.

questions.stem: In a channel where the normal depth exceeds the critical depth, the slope is described as:
questions.solution:
**Mild.**

**Slope classification compares the NORMAL depth y_n with the CRITICAL depth y_c:**

| Slope | Condition | Uniform flow is |
|---|---|---|
| **MILD (M)** | **y_n > y_c** | **Subcritical** |
| **STEEP (S)** | **y_n < y_c** | **Supercritical** |
| **CRITICAL (C)** | y_n = y_c | Critical |
| **HORIZONTAL (H)** | S₀ = 0 — **no normal depth exists** | — |
| **ADVERSE (A)** | S₀ < 0, rising downstream — **no normal depth** | — |

**"Mild" and "steep" are hydraulic terms, not geometric ones**, and that is the point most often missed:

> A slope is mild or steep **relative to the critical slope for THAT discharge and roughness** — not by any absolute gradient. **The SAME channel can be mild at one discharge and steep at another**, because y_c depends on q.

So a phrase like "a steep channel" means nothing without stating the discharge.

**Gradually varied flow profiles** are named by the slope letter and a zone number:

| Zone | Position | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Above BOTH** y_n and y_c | Depth greater than both |
| **2** | **Between** them | Depth between the two |
| **3** | **Below BOTH** | Depth less than both |

**The thirteen profiles**, of which a handful matter in practice:

| Profile | Where it occurs | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| **M1** | **Upstream of a DAM, weir or obstruction** on a mild slope | **BACKWATER curve** — depth rises, asymptotic to horizontal far upstream |
| **M2** | Upstream of a **free overfall** or a change to a steeper slope | **Drawdown** — depth falls toward y_c |
| **M3** | Downstream of a **SLUICE GATE** on a mild slope | Depth rises toward a **HYDRAULIC JUMP** |
| **S1** | Behind an obstruction on a steep slope | — |
| **S2** | Below a change from mild to steep | Drawdown |
| **S3** | Below a sluice gate on a steep slope | — |
| H2, H3, A2, A3, C1, C3 | Horizontal and adverse reaches | Less common |

**M1 is by far the most important in practice** — it is the **backwater curve** behind every dam, weir and bridge constriction, and computing it establishes the **extent of upstream flooding and the land to be acquired**. A large barrage can raise levels for tens of kilometres upstream, and the M1 curve is what defines the submergence zone.

**Three rules that govern every profile**, worth committing:

| Rule | Statement |
|---|---|
| **1** | The profile approaches **y_n ASYMPTOTICALLY** — it never crosses it |
| **2** | The profile crosses **y_c VERTICALLY** — the GVF equation is singular there, so the theory breaks down at a control section |
| **3** | In **zone 1 and zone 3 the depth INCREASES** downstream; in **zone 2 it DECREASES** |

**The governing GVF equation:**

> **dy/dx = (S₀ − S_f)/(1 − Fr²)**

**Reading the signs of the numerator and denominator** tells you the shape without any computation — which is how the thirteen profiles are derived, and a far better approach than memorising them.

**Direction of computation** follows from the control principle:

| Flow | Start from | Work |
|---|---|---|
| **SUBCRITICAL** | **Downstream** control | **Upstream** |
| **SUPERCRITICAL** | **Upstream** control | **Downstream** |

> Because subcritical flow is controlled from downstream, and supercritical from upstream. Computing in the wrong direction gives a profile that **diverges** instead of converging on the normal depth, and it is the classic error in backwater computation.

**Methods of computation:**

| Method | Suits |
|---|---|
| **Direct step** | **Prismatic** channels — step in depth, solve for distance |
| **Standard step** | **Natural** channels — step in distance, solve for depth by trial |
| HEC-RAS and similar software | The professional standard for river studies |

**The standard step method is what river modelling uses**, because natural cross-sections are irregular and given at surveyed chainages — so the distance is fixed and the depth must be found iteratively at each section.

examTip.trap: "Mild" and "steep" sound geometric but are **hydraulic** terms — the SAME channel can be mild at one discharge and steep at another, because y_c depends on q.
examTip.trick: Compare y_n (from Manning — slope and roughness) with y_c (from discharge alone). y_n > y_c means uniform flow would be subcritical, hence mild.
examTip.mnemonic: **M1 is the backwater curve behind every dam and bridge** — and computing it is what defines the upstream submergence zone and the land to be acquired.

questions.stem: The discharge over a rectangular sharp-crested weir is proportional to the head H raised to the power:
questions.solution:
**H^1.5.**

> **Q = (2/3) C_d √(2g) L H^(3/2)**, or approximately **Q = 1.84 L H^(3/2)** with C_d ≈ 0.62

**Where the 3/2 comes from.** Integrating the velocity **√(2gh)** over the depth of the nappe from 0 to H, across width L:

> **Q = ∫₀^H L √(2gh) dh = (2/3) L √(2g) H^(3/2)** ✓

The **velocity varies as √h** and the **area of flow varies as h**, so their product integrates to h^(3/2).

**The exponents for different weirs**, which is the family worth knowing:

| Weir | Discharge | Exponent |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangular** | **Q = 1.84 L H^(3/2)** | **1.5** |
| **V-notch (triangular)**, angle θ | **Q = (8/15)C_d√(2g) tan(θ/2) H^(5/2)** | **2.5** |
| **90° V-notch** | **Q = 1.4 H^(5/2)** | 2.5 |
| **Trapezoidal (Cipolletti)** | **Q = 1.86 L H^(3/2)** | 1.5 |
| Broad-crested | Q = 1.7 L H^(3/2) | 1.5 |

**Why the V-notch has the higher exponent**: its width **increases with depth**, so both the velocity and the width grow with h — giving h^(1/2) × h × ... which integrates to h^(5/2).

**And that higher exponent is exactly why the V-notch is used for SMALL flows:**

> Because **Q ∝ H^2.5**, a **small discharge produces a relatively LARGE head** — which can be measured accurately. A rectangular weir at the same small flow would give a head of a few millimetres, unmeasurable in practice.

| Weir | Best for |
|---|---|
| **V-notch** | **SMALL** discharges — laboratory work, small streams, leak measurement |
| **Rectangular** | **LARGE** discharges — canals, spillways |
| **Cipolletti (trapezoidal, 1:4 side slopes)** | Medium; the side slope **compensates for end contractions**, so no correction is needed |

**End contractions** on a rectangular weir reduce the effective length:

> **Francis formula: L_effective = L − 0.1 n H**, where **n** is the number of end contractions (2 for a fully contracted weir, 0 for a suppressed one)

**The Cipolletti weir's 1 in 4 side slopes are designed so the added triangular area exactly offsets the end contraction loss** — a neat piece of engineering that removes the correction entirely, which is why it is favoured for irrigation measurement where field staff must read the flow without calculation.

**Conditions for accurate weir measurement:**

| Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|
| The nappe must be **fully AERATED** underneath | An unventilated nappe **clings** to the weir plate, the pressure beneath falls, and the **discharge INCREASES unpredictably** |
| **Sharp, square upstream edge** | The coefficient depends on it; a rounded or worn edge reads high |
| Head measured **upstream at 3–4 H** from the weir | Beyond the surface **drawdown** |
| **Minimum head about 30 mm** | Below that, **surface tension** distorts the nappe |
| **Free (unsubmerged)** discharge | Submergence changes the relation entirely |
| Approach channel straight, still and wide | So the velocity of approach is negligible |

**Aeration is the requirement most often neglected in practice**, and its effect is large: a clinging nappe can read **10% or more** high, and it fluctuates as the nappe alternately clings and springs clear. A simple **vent pipe** through the wall beneath the nappe fixes it permanently.

**Velocity of approach**, where the channel is not wide enough for it to be negligible, is included by replacing H with **(H + h_a)** where **h_a = V_a²/2g**:

> **Q = 1.84 L [(H + h_a)^(3/2) − h_a^(3/2)]**

which requires iteration, since V_a depends on Q.

**Broad-crested weirs** work on a different principle — they force **CRITICAL flow** over the crest, so **Q depends only on the head and the crest width**, independent of the downstream conditions. That makes them robust for permanent gauging structures, and they are less sensitive to edge wear and debris than a sharp-crested plate.

examTip.trick: Integrating √(2gh) over the depth gives h^(3/2) — the velocity varies as √h and the area as h.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rectangular 3/2, V-notch 5/2.** The V-notch's higher exponent is exactly why it suits **SMALL flows**: a small discharge still produces a readable head. Two practical requirements: the nappe must be **AERATED** (a clinging nappe reads 10% high) and the head at least **30 mm** (below that, surface tension distorts it).

questions.stem: A channel carries 6 m³/s in a rectangular section 3 m wide. The critical depth is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 0.74 m.**

> **q = Q/b = 6/3 = 2 m³/s per metre**
> **y_c = (q²/g)^(1/3) = (4/9.81)^(1/3) = (0.4077)^(1/3) = 0.742 m** ✓

**The cube root** is the step most likely to go wrong by hand. A quick check: **0.74³ = 0.405** ✓, close to 0.4077.

**And the associated quantities**, which are usually wanted too:

> **V_c = q/y_c = 2/0.742 = 2.70 m/s**
> Check: **V_c = √(g y_c) = √(9.81 × 0.742) = 2.70 m/s** ✓ — the two routes agree, confirming Fr = 1
> **E_c = 1.5 y_c = 1.11 m**

**The internal consistency check is worth doing routinely**: at critical depth **V_c = √(gy_c)** must hold, and computing V two ways confirms the arithmetic in one line.

**What critical depth tells you about the channel:**

| If the actual depth is | Regime | Fr |
|---|---|---|
| **Greater than 0.742 m** | **Subcritical** — deep and slow | < 1 |
| **Equal to 0.742 m** | Critical | = 1 |
| **Less than 0.742 m** | **Supercritical** — shallow and fast | > 1 |

**The CRITICAL SLOPE** — the bed slope at which uniform flow would be critical — follows from Manning:

> **S_c = n²V_c²/R_c^(4/3)**

For this channel with n = 0.015: **A_c = 3 × 0.742 = 2.23 m²**, **P = 3 + 2(0.742) = 4.48 m**, **R = 0.497 m**

> **S_c = (0.015)² × (2.70)²/(0.497)^(4/3) = 0.000225 × 7.29/0.394 = 0.00416 ≈ 1 in 240**

| Actual bed slope | Classification | Uniform flow |
|---|---|---|
| **Flatter than 1 in 240** | **MILD** | Subcritical |
| **1 in 240** | Critical | Critical |
| **Steeper than 1 in 240** | **STEEP** | Supercritical |

**That calculation is how "mild" and "steep" acquire numerical meaning** for a particular channel and discharge — and it makes concrete the earlier point that the classification is **not absolute**: at a different discharge, y_c and hence S_c both change, and the same channel may switch classification.

**A caution about critical flow in design:**

> **Flow AT or very near critical depth is UNSTABLE.** Small changes in energy produce large changes in depth, because the specific energy curve is **flat at its nose** — dE/dy = 0 there by definition.

The consequence is a **wavy, surging water surface** that is hard to predict and unpleasant to live with. So channels are deliberately designed **away from critical** — comfortably subcritical (Fr < 0.8) or clearly supercritical (Fr > 1.3) — and never at Fr ≈ 1 except at a deliberate control section where the instability is confined to a short length and is in fact the point.

**Where critical flow IS wanted:**

| Structure | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Broad-crested weir** | Forces critical flow so **Q depends on head alone** |
| **Parshall / venturi flume** | The same, with minimal head loss and self-cleansing |
| **Free overfall** | Critical occurs about **3 to 4 y_c upstream** of the brink |
| Entry to a steep chute | The transition point |

**The free overfall is a useful field measurement**: at a sharp drop the depth at the brink is about **0.715 y_c**, so measuring the brink depth gives y_c and hence the discharge — a rough but serviceable method requiring no structure at all.

examTip.mnemonic: **Cross-check every critical-depth answer with V_c = √(gy_c).** If the two routes disagree, the cube root went wrong. Flow **near** critical is unstable and wavy, which is why channels are designed away from Fr = 1.

questions.stem: The Chezy coefficient C is related to Manning's n by:
questions.solution:
**C = R^(1/6)/n.**

**Derived by equating the two formulae:**

> **Chezy: V = C√(RS)**
> **Manning: V = (1/n) R^(2/3) S^(1/2)**
> Equating: **C√(RS) = (1/n)R^(2/3)S^(1/2)**
> **C R^(1/2) = (1/n)R^(2/3)**, so **C = R^(1/6)/n** ✓

**Note that n is in the DENOMINATOR** — a rougher channel (higher n) gives a lower C, and both formulae then give a lower velocity, as they must.

**The key difference between the two coefficients:**

| | **Chezy C** | **Manning n** |
|---|---|---|
| Depends on | **Roughness AND the hydraulic radius R** | **Roughness ALONE** |
| Changes as the depth changes? | **YES** — because R changes | **NO** |
| Dimensions | **Not dimensionless** — m^(1/2)/s | Also not dimensionless (s/m^(1/3)) |
| Convenience | Must be recomputed at each depth | **Fixed for a given surface** |

> **That is why Manning superseded Chezy in practice**: n can be tabulated once per surface type and used at any depth, while C must be recalculated whenever the depth changes. For a channel whose depth varies through the year, that is a decisive convenience.

**Historically Chezy came first (1769)** and is the more fundamental form — it follows directly from balancing the gravity component against the boundary shear:

> Gravity force on a slice: **γ A L S**
> Boundary shear: **τ₀ P L**
> Balancing: **τ₀ = γ R S** — the fundamental **uniform flow** relation
> With **τ₀ = k ρV²**, this rearranges to **V = C√(RS)** ✓

**Manning (1889) fixed the exponent empirically**, and it happens that R^(1/6) fits observation well over the range of interest — which is why Manning is called semi-empirical while Chezy is rational.

**Other formulae for C** exist, and appear in older references:

| Formula | Form |
|---|---|
| **Bazin** | **C = 157.6/(1 + m/√R)** |
| **Kutter (Ganguillet–Kutter)** | A complicated expression in n, R and S |
| **Manning-derived** | **C = R^(1/6)/n** — the one in use |

**Kutter's formula includes the SLOPE**, which Manning's does not — a refinement that matters at very flat slopes but is generally ignored today.

**The fundamental relation τ₀ = γRS** deserves emphasis in its own right, because it is used well beyond velocity calculation:

| Application | Use of τ₀ = γRS |
|---|---|
| **Tractive force method** of stable channel design | The bed shear must not exceed the **critical tractive stress** of the bed material |
| **Sediment transport** — incipient motion | Shields' criterion is written in terms of τ₀ |
| **Scour** prediction | — |
| **Riprap sizing** | The stone must resist the shear |

**The tractive force method** is the modern approach to designing an unlined channel, and it is more rational than the older **maximum permissible velocity** method:

> **Permissible velocity** asks whether the water is moving too fast. **Tractive force** asks whether the **force on the bed grains** exceeds what holds them — which is the actual mechanism of erosion.

For a wide channel R ≈ y, so **τ₀ ≈ γ y S** — and the design proceeds by choosing y and S so that τ₀ stays below the critical value for the bed material, typically **2 – 4 N/m²** for fine sand and **30 N/m²** or more for stiff clay and gravel.

**A note on side slopes**: the tractive stress on the **sloping sides** is lower than on the bed (about 0.75 τ₀), but the grains there are also **less stable**, being partly supported against gravity. The two effects are combined through the **angle of repose** of the material, and for cohesionless soils the sides usually govern the design rather than the bed.

examTip.trick: Equate Chezy and Manning and R^(1/2) cancels down to **C = R^(1/6)/n**. Note n is in the **denominator** — rougher means lower C.
examTip.mnemonic: **Manning replaced Chezy because n depends on the SURFACE ALONE, while C also depends on R** — so C must be recomputed every time the depth changes. Behind both lies **τ₀ = γRS**, which is the basis of tractive-force channel design and riprap sizing.

questions.stem: The specific energy of flow in an open channel is a minimum at:
questions.solution:
**Critical depth.**

> **E = y + V²/2g = y + Q²/(2gA²)**

Specific energy is measured **from the CHANNEL BED**, not from a fixed datum — which is what distinguishes it from total energy and makes it useful for analysing transitions.

**The specific energy curve** for a fixed discharge:

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| Shape | A **C-shaped curve**, asymptotic to the line **E = y** above and to the E axis below |
| **Nose (minimum)** | At **y = y_c**, where **E_min = 1.5 y_c** for a rectangular channel |
| **Upper limb** | **y > y_c** — **subcritical**; E increases with y |
| **Lower limb** | **y < y_c** — **supercritical**; E increases as y decreases |
| For any **E > E_min** | **TWO depths** are possible — the **ALTERNATE depths** |
| For **E < E_min** | **NO flow possible** at that discharge |

**Distinguishing normal from critical depth**, since option (a) is the natural trap:

| | **NORMAL depth y_n** | **CRITICAL depth y_c** |
|---|---|---|
| Determined by | **Manning** — the **SLOPE and ROUGHNESS** | **y_c = (q²/g)^(1/3)** — the **DISCHARGE only** |
| Physical meaning | The depth at which **gravity balances friction** | The depth of **minimum specific energy** |
| Depends on roughness? | **YES** | **NO** |
| Depends on slope? | **YES** | **NO** |

> **Critical depth is independent of slope and roughness** — which is precisely what makes it useful for measurement. A control structure that forces critical flow gives a discharge reading that does not drift as the channel silts up or grows weed.

**The two dual statements of criticality:**

| Fixed quantity | At critical depth |
|---|---|
| **Discharge Q** | **Specific energy is MINIMUM** |
| **Specific energy E** | **Discharge is MAXIMUM** |

Both are true, and the second is the one that explains **choking**.

**CHOKING** — the practical consequence:

> A channel **constriction** raises **q = Q/b**, which raises **y_c** and therefore **E_min**. If the **available specific energy is less than the new E_min**, the flow **cannot pass** — so the **upstream water level RISES** until enough energy is available.

That upstream rise is the **afflux**, and it is why an undersized **bridge opening** or **culvert** floods the land behind it. Checking a waterway opening for choking is a required part of bridge hydraulic design, and it is a different check from simply keeping the velocity acceptable.

**Flow over a HUMP** is the classic illustration of the curve in action:

| Approach flow | As the flow passes over a small hump |
|---|---|
| **Subcritical** | The **water surface DROPS** — the depth falls toward y_c |
| **Supercritical** | The **water surface RISES** — the depth rises toward y_c |

> **Both move TOWARD critical** — because raising the bed reduces the specific energy available, and reduced E means moving along the curve toward its nose from whichever limb you started on.

The subcritical case is genuinely counter-intuitive: **raise the bed, and the water surface goes DOWN**. It happens because the flow must speed up to pass over the hump, and the extra velocity head comes out of the depth.

**If the hump is too high**, E falls below E_min and the flow **chokes** — the upstream level rises, and critical flow establishes **on the crest**. That is exactly the operating principle of the **broad-crested weir**, which is a hump built deliberately high enough to choke the flow and force a critical section.

**Practical design note**: flow **at or near critical** is **unstable** — the curve is flat at its nose, so small energy changes produce large depth changes, giving a **wavy, surging surface**. Channels are therefore designed comfortably away from Fr = 1, except at deliberate control sections.

examTip.trap: **Normal depth** is the natural wrong answer — but that comes from Manning (slope and roughness), while critical depth comes from the discharge alone. Different quantities entirely.
examTip.trick: The specific energy curve is C-shaped with its nose at y_c; for any E above the minimum there are **two alternate depths**, one subcritical and one supercritical.
examTip.mnemonic: **Below E_min the flow is IMPOSSIBLE — so the upstream level RISES. That is CHOKING**, and it is what floods land behind an undersized bridge or culvert.

questions.stem: A circular sewer carries its maximum discharge when flowing at a depth of about:
questions.solution:
**About 94% of the diameter — not when running full.**

**Why not full.** By Manning, **Q = (1/n) A R^(2/3) S^(1/2)**, so the discharge depends on **A R^(2/3)**. As the depth rises above about 94%:

| Effect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| The **AREA** still increases | Slightly |
| But the **WETTED PERIMETER increases FASTER** | The section is closing over, adding perimeter for very little area |
| So **R = A/P FALLS** | And R^(2/3) with it |
| Net effect | **A R^(2/3) reaches a maximum and then DECREASES** |

> So a pipe running **just below full carries MORE than the same pipe running full** — about **7% more** at the 94% depth.

**The two maxima in a circular section:**

| Quantity | Maximum at depth | Value relative to full |
|---|---|---|
| **VELOCITY** | **≈ 0.81 D** | **1.14 × V_full** |
| **DISCHARGE** | **≈ 0.94 D** | **1.07 × Q_full** |

**Both exceed the full-bore values**, which surprises people, and both are explained by the same hydraulic radius argument.

**The proportional-depth relationships** used constantly in sewer design:

| d/D | a/A | r/R | v/V | q/Q |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.2 | 0.14 | 0.48 | 0.61 | 0.09 |
| **0.5** | **0.50** | **1.00** | **1.00** | **0.50** |
| 0.8 | 0.86 | 1.22 | 1.14 | 0.98 |
| **0.94** | 0.97 | 1.19 | 1.12 | **1.07** |
| 1.0 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |

**The half-full row is the memorable one:**

> At **half full**, a circular pipe has **half the area**, the **SAME hydraulic radius (D/4)**, the **SAME velocity**, and therefore **exactly half the discharge**.

**Why sewers are designed to run PART FULL:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **VENTILATION** | Sewer gases — hydrogen sulphide, methane — must escape. A full sewer cannot ventilate |
| **Surcharge capacity** in reserve | For peak and storm flows beyond the design |
| **Free-surface (gravity) flow** is maintained | Pressurising a gravity sewer causes surcharging at manholes |
| **Access and inspection** | — |
| Corrosion control | H₂S accumulating in a sealed sewer produces sulphuric acid — the **crown corrosion** that destroys concrete sewers |

**Design practice (CPHEEO):**

| Sewer | Design depth at peak flow |
|---|---|
| **Small (< 400 mm)** | **1/2 full** |
| Medium (400 – 900 mm) | 2/3 full |
| **Large (> 900 mm)** | **3/4 full** |

**The two velocity limits** that govern the slope:

| Limit | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Minimum (SELF-CLEANSING)** | **0.6 – 0.75 m/s** at the **minimum** daily flow | Keeps solids in suspension; below it, **silt deposits and the sewer blocks** |
| **Maximum** | **3.0 m/s** | Prevents **erosion** of the invert |

**The self-cleansing requirement at MINIMUM flow is the binding one**, and it is the reason sewer design is harder than water main design:

> A sewer must be **large enough for the peak flow** and **steep enough to be self-cleansing at the minimum flow** — and in a newly developed area, where initial flows are a small fraction of the ultimate design flow, those requirements conflict directly.

The usual resolutions are **steeper gradients than hydraulics alone would require**, **flushing arrangements** at the head of runs, or **staged construction**. In flat terrain the gradient requirement often forces deep excavation and pumping stations, which is why sewerage in the Terai is so much more expensive per household than in the hills.

**Crown corrosion** deserves a closing note because it destroys sewers within decades: **H₂S** released from septic sewage is oxidised by bacteria on the moist crown to **sulphuric acid**, which attacks the cement. The defences are maintaining **self-cleansing velocity** (so sewage does not go septic), **ventilation**, and **acid-resistant linings** on large sewers.

examTip.trap: "100% — completely full" is the intuitive answer and is wrong: a pipe running just below full carries about **7% MORE** than one running full.
examTip.trick: Beyond 94% the section is closing over, so the **wetted perimeter grows faster than the area**, R falls, and with it the discharge.
examTip.mnemonic: **Maximum Q at 0.94D, maximum V at 0.81D, and half-full carries exactly half at the same velocity.** Sewers are designed part-full for **ventilation** — a sealed sewer accumulates H₂S, which oxidises to sulphuric acid and destroys the crown.

questions.stem: Downstream of a sluice gate discharging under a mild slope, the water surface profile is:
options: M3, rising toward a hydraulic jump
questions.solution:
**M3, rising toward a hydraulic jump.**

**The sequence of events below a sluice gate on a mild slope:**

1. Water issues from beneath the gate at a **small depth and high velocity** — **supercritical**, with **y < y_c**.
2. Since the slope is **mild**, the channel's **normal depth is subcritical (y_n > y_c)**, so the flow cannot remain supercritical indefinitely.
3. The depth **increases downstream** along an **M3** profile — zone 3, below both y_n and y_c.
4. When the depth reaches the **conjugate** of the local depth, a **HYDRAULIC JUMP** occurs.
5. Beyond the jump the flow is **subcritical**, approaching **y_n** along an **M2 or M1** profile.

**Why M3.** The naming rule:

| Letter | Slope | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| **M** | **Mild** | **y_n > y_c** |
| **3** | **Zone 3** | **y < BOTH y_n and y_c** |

**The zone rule and profile behaviour:**

| Zone | Depth | Behaviour downstream |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | Above **both** | **INCREASES** |
| **2** | **Between** the two | **DECREASES** |
| **3** | Below **both** | **INCREASES** |

**The three rules that govern every GVF profile:**

| Rule | Statement |
|---|---|
| **1** | The profile approaches **y_n ASYMPTOTICALLY** — it never crosses it |
| **2** | The profile crosses **y_c VERTICALLY** — the theory is **singular** there, which is why a jump (a discontinuity) is needed rather than a smooth curve |
| **3** | Zones 1 and 3: depth **increases** downstream. Zone 2: depth **decreases** |

**Rule 2 is why the hydraulic jump exists at all**: gradually varied flow theory **cannot pass through critical depth smoothly** — the equation **dy/dx = (S₀ − S_f)/(1 − Fr²)** has **Fr = 1 in the denominator**, so dy/dx becomes infinite. Nature resolves the impossibility with an abrupt, energy-dissipating **jump**.

**The common profiles and where to expect them:**

| Profile | Situation |
|---|---|
| **M1** | **Backwater upstream of a DAM, weir or bridge** — the flood-extent curve |
| **M2** | **Drawdown** upstream of a **free overfall** or a change to a steeper slope |
| **M3** | **Below a SLUICE GATE** on a mild slope — this question |
| **S2** | Below a change from mild to steep slope |
| **S3** | Below a sluice gate on a **steep** slope |
| **S1** | Behind an obstruction on a steep slope, downstream of a jump |

**Where the jump forms** is a genuine design question, not a detail:

> The jump locates itself where the **M3 profile's depth reaches the CONJUGATE of the downstream (tailwater) depth**. Raise the tailwater and the jump **moves upstream**, toward the gate; lower it and the jump **moves downstream**.

**That mobility is the central problem in stilling basin design:**

| Tailwater | Jump behaviour | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
