| **Too LOW** | The jump **SWEEPS OUT** downstream | High-velocity flow escapes the paved apron onto **erodible bed** — the apron is undermined |
| **Correct** | The jump forms **within the basin** | Energy dissipated where intended |
| **Too HIGH** | The jump is **DROWNED (submerged)** | Poor dissipation; the fast jet dives along the bed |

**The remedies:**

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **DEPRESS the basin floor** | Creates the required tailwater depth locally |
| **End sill** | Raises the level in the basin and deflects the residual jet upward |
| **Baffle blocks** | Force the jump to form and shorten the basin |
| Chute blocks | Break up the incoming jet |
| Sloping apron | Accommodates a range of tailwater levels |

**Sweep-out is the failure mode that destroys spillways**, and it typically occurs not at the design flood but at **intermediate discharges**, where the tailwater rating curve and the required conjugate depth diverge most. The basin must therefore be checked across the **full range** of operating discharges, not only at the design flood — a check that is sometimes omitted, with expensive results.

examTip.trick: Name it from the two comparisons: slope **M**ild (y_n > y_c), and zone **3** (y below both). Zone 3 profiles **increase** downstream, so the depth rises until it reaches the conjugate of the tailwater and jumps.
examTip.mnemonic: **GVF theory is SINGULAR at y_c** (the denominator 1 − Fr² vanishes), which is precisely why nature needs a discontinuity — the hydraulic jump. The design risk is the jump **SWEEPING OUT** of the paved basin when the tailwater is too low, which undermines the apron.

questions.stem: A Parshall flume is preferred to a weir for flow measurement in an irrigation channel mainly because it:
options: Measures flow more precisely at all heads
Has a low head loss and passes sediment without silting up
questions.solution:
**Because it has a LOW head loss and passes sediment without silting up.**

**The comparison:**

| | **WEIR** | **FLUME (Parshall, venturi)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Head loss** | **HIGH** — the full drop over the crest | **LOW** — typically a quarter of a weir's |
| **SEDIMENT** | **Silts up behind the weir**; the pool traps deposits | **SELF-CLEANSING** — flow accelerates through the throat and flushes sediment on |
| Floating debris | Can lodge on the crest | Passes through |
| Construction | Simple, cheap | More complex, dearer |
| Accuracy | Good, if the crest stays sharp | Good and **more durable** — no sharp edge to wear |
| Maintenance | Crest wear and desilting | Little |
| Submergence tolerance | Poor | **Tolerates up to 70% submergence** |

**The two decisive advantages in an irrigation setting:**

**1. Low head loss.** In flat irrigation country, **head is the scarcest commodity**. A weir consumes perhaps 0.3 m of fall at every measuring point, and on a long distributary with several offtakes that adds up to command area lost. A flume takes a fraction of it.

**2. Sediment passage.** Nepali and north Indian rivers carry very heavy silt loads. A weir creates a **stilling pool that traps it**, so the structure silts up, the approach conditions change, and the calibration drifts — requiring constant desilting. A flume's **throat accelerates the flow**, keeping sediment moving.

**How a Parshall flume works:**

| Section | Function |
|---|---|
| **Converging** section | Accelerates the flow |
| **THROAT** — with a **downward-sloping floor** | Forces **CRITICAL flow** |
| **Diverging** section — floor rising | Recovers head |

> Because **CRITICAL flow** is forced at the throat, **Q depends on the upstream head H_a alone** — independent of the downstream conditions, the roughness, or the channel's state:

> **Q = C H_a^n**, with n between **1.52 and 1.60** depending on the throat width

**Free versus submerged flow:**

| Condition | Submergence ratio H_b/H_a | Measurement |
|---|---|---|
| **FREE flow** | Below the limit (0.6 – 0.8 depending on size) | **ONE reading, H_a** — the normal case |
| **Submerged** | Above the limit | **TWO readings**, H_a and H_b, with a correction |

**The tolerance of submergence is itself an advantage**: a weir's calibration is destroyed by any submergence, while a Parshall flume continues to measure — with a correction — up to 70% or more. In a channel where downstream levels vary with gate settings, that robustness matters.

**Other measuring structures**, for completeness:

| Structure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sharp-crested weir** | Accurate; high head loss; silts; edge wears |
| **Broad-crested weir** | Robust; forces critical flow; moderate head loss |
| **Parshall flume** | Low loss; self-cleansing; the irrigation standard |
| **Cut-throat flume** | Simpler — a flat floor, no throat section; cheaper to build |
| **Venturi flume** | A width contraction only |
| **Current meter gauging** | For natural rivers; the velocity–area method |
| **Stage–discharge (rating) curve** | For a gauged river section, calibrated by current meter |

**The rating curve** is how most river discharge data is actually produced: the **stage (water level) is recorded continuously** by an automatic gauge, and the **discharge is measured occasionally** by current meter to establish and check the **stage–discharge relation**. Continuous flow records then come from continuous level records, which are far cheaper to collect.

**Its weakness** is that the relation **shifts** when the channel scours, deposits, or grows vegetation — so the curve must be **re-checked regularly**, and extrapolating it beyond the range of measured flows (which is exactly what one must do for a flood) is a recognised source of error in flood estimation.

examTip.trick: Two advantages that both matter in irrigation: **low head loss** (head is the scarcest commodity on flat land) and **self-cleansing** (the throat accelerates the flow and flushes silt through).
examTip.mnemonic: **A weir creates a stilling pool that SILTS UP; a flume does not.** In Nepal's silt-laden rivers that is decisive. A flume also tolerates up to **70% submergence**, where a weir's calibration is destroyed by any submergence at all.

questions.stem: For a hydraulic jump with an approach Froude number of 4.0, the ratio of the sequent depth to the initial depth is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 5.2.**

> **y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1]**
> **= ½[√(1 + 8 × 16) − 1] = ½[√129 − 1] = ½[11.36 − 1] = ½ × 10.36 = 5.18 ≈ 5.2** ✓

**Option (b), 4.0**, is the trap — assuming the depth ratio equals the Froude number. It does not, and a useful sanity check is that the ratio is always **somewhat greater than Fr₁** for Fr₁ above about 2.

**A useful approximation for large Fr₁:**

> For **Fr₁ ≫ 1**: **y₂/y₁ ≈ √2 × Fr₁ − 0.5 ≈ 1.41 Fr₁**

Check: 1.41 × 4 = 5.66, less 0.5 = 5.16 ✓ — close enough for a rapid estimate.

**Values worth having a feel for:**

| Fr₁ | y₂/y₁ | Jump type | Energy loss |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.5 | 1.7 | Undular | ~2% |
| 2.0 | 2.4 | Weak | 6% |
| 3.0 | 3.8 | **Oscillating — AVOID** | 27% |
| **4.0** | **5.2** | Oscillating/steady boundary | 39% |
| 6.0 | 8.0 | **Steady — best** | 56% |
| 9.0 | 12.2 | Steady/strong boundary | 70% |

**And the energy loss** for this case:

> **E_L = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4 y₁ y₂)**

With y₁ = 1 (unit) and y₂ = 5.18:

> **E_L = (4.18)³/(4 × 1 × 5.18) = 73.0/20.7 = 3.53** units
> **E₁ = y₁ + V₁²/2g = y₁(1 + Fr₁²/2) = 1 + 8 = 9** units
> **Loss = 3.53/9 = 39%** of the incoming energy

**The derivation uses MOMENTUM, not energy**, and it is worth being clear why:

> The energy loss in a jump is **large and not known in advance**, so an energy balance has an unknown on both sides. But the **external forces are small** (the jump is short, so bed friction over its length is negligible), which makes the **momentum balance exact**.

> **Specific force M = A ȳ + Q²/(gA)** is **the same on both sides** of the jump — and equating it gives the conjugate depth relation directly.

**Conjugate versus alternate depths**, restated because it is routinely confused:

| Pair | Conserved | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **CONJUGATE (sequent)** | **Specific FORCE (momentum)** | **Across a hydraulic jump** |
| **ALTERNATE** | **Specific ENERGY** | Two possible states at the same E |

**Length of the jump** is empirical, since no theory predicts it:

> **L ≈ 5 to 7 × y₂**, commonly taken as **6 y₂**

which, with y₂ = 5.2 y₁, means the basin must be about **31 times the initial depth** long — a substantial structure, and why baffle blocks (which shorten the jump by 30–50%) are worth their cost.

**Design application.** For a spillway discharging q = 10 m³/s per metre at y₁ = 0.5 m:

> **V₁ = 20 m/s**, **Fr₁ = 20/√(9.81 × 0.5) = 9.03**
> **y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1 + 8 × 81.5) − 1] = ½[25.6 − 1] = 12.3**
> **y₂ = 6.15 m** — the **required tailwater depth**
> **Basin length ≈ 6 × 6.15 = 37 m**

**The required tailwater is the governing output**: if the river downstream cannot supply 6.15 m at that discharge, the jump will **sweep out** of the basin and undermine it. The design response is to **depress the basin floor** so that the local depth reaches 6.15 m even though the river level is lower — which is why stilling basin floors are set well below the downstream bed.

**And the check must be made across the full discharge range**, because the tailwater rating curve and the required conjugate depth vary differently with Q. Sweep-out often occurs not at the design flood but at some intermediate discharge, where the two curves are furthest apart.

examTip.trap: "4.0" is offered on the assumption that the depth ratio equals the Froude number. It does not — for Fr₁ above about 2 the ratio is always noticeably **larger**.
examTip.trick: **y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1] = ½[√129 − 1] = 5.18.** Quick approximation for large Fr₁: **≈ 1.41 Fr₁ − 0.5**.
examTip.mnemonic: **The tailwater must actually SUPPLY y₂**, or the jump sweeps downstream out of the basin. Check across the **full discharge range** — sweep-out often occurs at an intermediate flow, not at the design flood.

questions.stem: A trapezoidal channel is most economical when its side slopes make an angle with the horizontal of:
questions.solution:
**60° — a side slope of 1 vertical to 1/√3 horizontal.**

**The conditions for the most economical trapezoidal section:**

| Condition | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Side slope** | **60° to the horizontal** (1 : 0.577) |
| **Top width** | **= 2 × the length of a sloping side** |
| **Hydraulic radius** | **R = y/2** |
| The shape | **HALF A REGULAR HEXAGON** |
| Geometric property | A **semicircle of radius y centred on the water surface is TANGENTIAL** to the bed and both sides |

**Why 60°.** Minimising the wetted perimeter for a given area, with **both** the bed width and the side slope free to vary, yields the half-hexagon. Among all trapezoids it is the closest approach to the true optimum — the **semicircle**, which has the least perimeter of any shape enclosing a given area.

**The universal signature R = y/2** connects it to the other economical sections:

| Section | Condition | R |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle** | b = 2y | **y/2** |
| **Trapezoid** | 60° sides | **y/2** |
| **Semicircle** | — | **y/2** |

**But 60° is usually NOT what gets built**, and understanding why is the practical half of the question:

> The side slope of an **EARTH** channel is set by the **STABILITY OF THE SOIL**, not by hydraulic efficiency. A 60° slope (about 1:0.58) stands only in **rock or very stiff clay**; in ordinary soil it slumps.

| Material | Practical side slope (H:V) | Angle |
|---|---|---|
| **Rock** | Near vertical to 0.25:1 | 76 – 90° |
| Stiff clay, lined | 0.5:1 to 1:1 | 45 – 63° |
| **Firm earth** | **1:1 to 1.5:1** | **34 – 45°** |
| **Loose sandy soil** | **2:1** | **27°** |
| Sandy loam, porous clay | 2:1 to 3:1 | 18 – 27° |

**So the real design procedure is a CONSTRAINED optimisation:**

1. **Fix the side slope** from soil stability (or lining type).
2. Find the **most economical proportions for that fixed slope** — which still gives **R = y/2**, remarkably, since that condition holds for the best trapezoid of *any* fixed side slope.
3. Check the **velocity** against erosion and siltation limits.
4. Add **freeboard**.

**That step 2 result is worth stating clearly:**

> For a trapezoid with **any given side slope**, the most economical proportions still yield **R = y/2**. The 60° condition is what you get when the side slope is *also* free to be optimised.

**The other practical constraints:**

| Constraint | Typical requirement |
|---|---|
| **Freeboard** | **0.3 m** for small channels to **1.0 m** for large; not part of the hydraulic section |
| **Maximum velocity** | To prevent erosion — 0.6 m/s in fine sand, 1.5 m/s in stiff clay, 2.5 m/s in lined channels |
| **Minimum velocity** | **0.6 m/s** typically, to prevent **siltation** and weed growth |
| **Bed width to depth ratio** | Often constrained by construction plant and land width |
| **Depth limits** | Water table, excavation cost |

**The velocity window is often what actually governs an irrigation canal**, not the economical section at all: the channel must be **slow enough not to erode** and **fast enough not to silt**, and in a silt-laden river system that window can be narrow. **Kennedy's** and **Lacey's** regime theories were developed precisely for this problem — designing a channel that neither scours nor silts in alluvial soil.

**Lacey's regime equations**, still used for canal design in the subcontinent:

> **V = 0.4382(f R)^(1/2)**, **P = 4.75√Q**, **R = 0.473(Q/f)^(1/3)**, **S = f^(5/3)/(3340 Q^(1/6))**

where **f is Lacey's silt factor** (**f = 1.76√d_mm**, with d the mean grain size). These give a channel **in regime** — one that has adjusted to carry both its water and its sediment load without net scour or deposition, which is a different and more demanding criterion than hydraulic efficiency alone.

examTip.trick: The best trapezoid is **half a regular hexagon**, which is the closest a straight-sided section can come to the true optimum, a semicircle. And it too gives **R = y/2**.
examTip.mnemonic: **60° is the theoretical answer but almost never what is built** — an earth channel's side slope is set by **SOIL STABILITY** (1:1 in firm earth, 2:1 in loose sand). The real procedure is: fix the slope from the soil, then optimise within that constraint — which still yields R = y/2.

questions.stem: In gradually varied flow, the governing equation dy/dx = (S₀ − S_f)/(1 − Fr²) becomes singular when:
options: The friction slope equals the bed slope
questions.solution:
**When the Froude number equals 1** — that is, at **critical depth**, where the denominator (1 − Fr²) vanishes.

**What the singularity means physically:**

> **dy/dx → ∞** — the theory predicts a **VERTICAL water surface**, which is impossible. Gradually varied flow theory has broken down.

**It has broken down because its central assumption has failed:**

> GVF assumes the depth changes **SLOWLY**, so that the pressure distribution stays **hydrostatic** and the friction slope can be computed from a uniform-flow formula (Manning). Near critical depth the depth changes **rapidly**, the streamlines curve sharply, the pressure is no longer hydrostatic, and Manning no longer applies.

**Nature's resolution** depends on the direction of the transition:

| Transition | Resolution |
|---|---|
| **Supercritical → subcritical** | A **HYDRAULIC JUMP** — an abrupt discontinuity with energy loss |
| **Subcritical → supercritical** | A **smooth passage** through critical at a control section |

**Reading the equation** is the best way to derive the profile shapes rather than memorise them:

> **dy/dx = (S₀ − S_f)/(1 − Fr²)**

| Numerator (S₀ − S_f) | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Positive** | Bed slope exceeds friction slope → depth **tends to increase** |
| **Zero** | **Uniform flow** — y = y_n, the profile is horizontal in depth terms |
| **Negative** | Friction exceeds available slope → depth **tends to decrease** |

| Denominator (1 − Fr²) | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Positive** (Fr < 1) | **Subcritical** |
| **Zero** (Fr = 1) | **Critical — singular** |
| **Negative** (Fr > 1) | **Supercritical** |

**Combining the signs gives every profile**, which is why the thirteen curves need not be memorised:

| Zone | Numerator | Denominator | dy/dx | Depth downstream |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **M1** (y > y_n > y_c) | **+** | **+** | **+** | **Increases** |
| **M2** (y_n > y > y_c) | **−** | **+** | **−** | **Decreases** |
| **M3** (y_n > y_c > y) | **−** | **−** | **+** | **Increases** |

**The two asymptotic behaviours** also fall out of the signs:

| As y → | Behaviour | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **y_n** | **dy/dx → 0** — approaches **ASYMPTOTICALLY** | S_f → S₀, so the numerator vanishes |
| **y_c** | **dy/dx → ∞** — crosses **VERTICALLY** | 1 − Fr² → 0, so the denominator vanishes |

**Practical consequences of the critical-depth singularity:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| A **CONTROL SECTION** exists at critical depth | The depth is fixed there by the discharge alone — the starting point for a GVF computation |
| Computation **must start at a control** | And proceed **away** from it, in the direction the flow can carry information |
| **Numerical methods fail near Fr = 1** | Step sizes must shrink, and the solution becomes unstable |
| Flow near critical is **physically unstable** | A wavy, surging surface — which is why channels are designed away from Fr = 1 |

**The control section is the key practical idea:**

> A **control** is any section where the **depth–discharge relation is known independently** of the rest of the channel. Critical sections are controls; so are weirs, sluice gates, free overfalls and reservoir surfaces.

**And the direction of computation follows from the control principle:**

| Flow | Control is | Compute |
|---|---|---|
| **Subcritical** | **Downstream** | **Upstream** from it |
| **Supercritical** | **Upstream** | **Downstream** from it |

> Computing in the wrong direction makes the solution **diverge** rather than converge on the normal depth — the classic error in backwater computation, and one that a plausible-looking output can conceal.

**Methods:**

| Method | Suits |
|---|---|
| **Direct step** | **Prismatic** channels — choose a depth increment, solve for the distance |
| **Standard step** | **Natural** channels — the distance is fixed by surveyed sections, so the depth is found by **trial** at each one |
| **HEC-RAS** and similar | The professional standard; implements the standard step method with allowance for bridges, culverts and floodplains |

examTip.trick: The denominator **1 − Fr²** vanishes at Fr = 1, so dy/dx → ∞ — a vertical water surface, which is impossible. The theory has broken down because the depth is no longer changing *gradually*.
examTip.mnemonic: **Reading the SIGNS of numerator and denominator generates all thirteen profiles** — no memorisation needed. Two rules follow: the profile approaches **y_n asymptotically** but crosses **y_c vertically**. Start every computation at a **control** and work in the direction the flow carries information.

questions.stem: In the hydrologic cycle, the process by which water vapour is returned to the atmosphere from plant surfaces is:
questions.solution:
**Transpiration.**

**The processes of the hydrologic cycle:**

| Process | Description |
|---|---|
| **PRECIPITATION** | Water falling from the atmosphere — rain, snow, hail |
| **EVAPORATION** | Liquid water → vapour from **free water surfaces and soil** |
| **TRANSPIRATION** | Water vapour released from **PLANT** surfaces, drawn up through the roots |
| **EVAPOTRANSPIRATION (ET)** | **Evaporation + transpiration combined** — they cannot be separated in the field |
| **INFILTRATION** | Water entering the **soil surface** |
| **PERCOLATION** | Downward movement **through** the soil to groundwater |
| **RUNOFF** | Flow over the surface to streams |
| Interception | Rain caught by vegetation and evaporated before reaching the ground |
| Depression storage | Water held in surface hollows |
| Condensation | Vapour → liquid, forming clouds |

**Evapotranspiration is treated as a single quantity** because separating the two components in the field is impractical — and for water balance purposes it is the total that matters.

**The catchment water balance**, which is the organising equation of hydrology:

> **P = R + ET + ΔS + G**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **P** | Precipitation |
| **R** | **Runoff** |
| **ET** | **Evapotranspiration** |
| **ΔS** | Change in **storage** (soil moisture, snow, surface) |
| **G** | Deep **groundwater** outflow |

> Over a **long period** (a year or more) **ΔS ≈ 0**, so the balance simplifies to **P ≈ R + ET + G** — which is how catchment yields are estimated from rainfall records.

**Two definitions of ET that must be kept apart:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **POTENTIAL evapotranspiration (PET)** | What **WOULD** occur if water were **freely available** — a climatic demand |
| **ACTUAL evapotranspiration (AET)** | What **DOES** occur, limited by the available soil moisture |

> **AET ≤ PET always.** They are equal only when the soil is wet; as it dries, AET falls below PET, and the difference is the **soil moisture deficit** that irrigation must supply.

**Estimating PET:**

| Method | Basis | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **PENMAN (and Penman–Monteith)** | **Energy balance + aerodynamic** | The most rigorous; the **FAO standard** |
| **Blaney–Criddle** | Temperature and daylight hours | Simple; used where data are scarce |
| Thornthwaite | Temperature only | Crude |
| **Pan evaporation** | Measured, × a **pan coefficient (0.7 – 0.8)** | Direct and widely used |

**Crop water requirement** follows from PET:

> **ET_crop = K_c × PET**

where **K_c** is the **crop coefficient**, varying with the crop and its growth stage — from about 0.3 at emergence to 1.15 at mid-season for many crops. That relation is the basis of **irrigation scheduling**, and it is why FAO's crop coefficient tables are among the most consulted documents in agricultural engineering.

**Why the water balance matters practically:**

| Application | Use |
|---|---|
| **Reservoir yield** studies | How much water a catchment can reliably deliver |
| **Irrigation** demand | The deficit ET must supply |
| **Groundwater recharge** estimation | The residual after runoff and ET |
| **Low-flow** estimation | Dry-season availability |
| Climate change impact assessment | Shifts in P and PET |

**A note for Nepal**: the **monsoon concentration of rainfall** — typically **80% of the annual total falling between June and September** — means the water balance is strongly seasonal. Annual figures conceal a wet season of surplus and a dry season of deficit, and it is the **dry-season** balance that governs whether a scheme is viable. Storage, not annual yield, is usually the constraint.

examTip.trick: Evaporation is from **water and soil surfaces**; transpiration is through **plants**. They are lumped as **evapotranspiration** because they cannot be separated in the field.
examTip.mnemonic: **P = R + ET + ΔS + G**, and over a year ΔS ≈ 0. Keep **PET** (the climatic demand, if water were freely available) apart from **AET** (what actually happens, limited by soil moisture) — **AET ≤ PET always**, and the gap is what irrigation must supply.

questions.stem: The Thiessen polygon method of computing mean areal rainfall over a catchment:
options: Weights each gauge by the area nearer to it than to any other gauge
Takes the simple arithmetic mean of all gauges
Uses only the gauge nearest the catchment centroid
questions.solution:
**It weights each gauge by the area that is nearer to it than to any other gauge.**

> **P_mean = Σ(A_i P_i)/ΣA_i**, where **A_i** is the Thiessen polygon area for gauge i

**Construction**: join adjacent gauges with straight lines, draw the **perpendicular bisector** of each line, and the bisectors enclose a polygon around each gauge containing all points closer to it than to any other. The polygons are clipped at the catchment boundary.

**The three methods compared:**

| Method | Basis | Suits | Accounts for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ARITHMETIC MEAN** | Simple average | **Uniformly distributed** gauges, **flat** terrain, small variation | Nothing |
| **THIESSEN POLYGON** | **Area-weighted** by proximity | **Non-uniform gauge spacing** | **Gauge distribution** |
| **ISOHYETAL** | Areas between **lines of equal rainfall** | **Mountainous** terrain; the **most accurate** | **Gauge distribution AND terrain/orographic effects** |

**The isohyetal method is the best** because the person drawing the isohyets can incorporate **knowledge of the terrain** — pulling the contours to follow ridges and valleys where orographic effects are known to concentrate rainfall. Thiessen polygons are purely geometric and know nothing about topography.

> **Thiessen's weakness**: the polygons are **fixed by geometry alone**, so a gauge in a valley is given the same weight over its polygon as a ridge-top gauge over its own — even where the rainfall differs by a factor of two across a few kilometres.

**That matters greatly in Nepal**, where **orographic rainfall** varies enormously over short distances:

| Location | Annual rainfall |
|---|---|
| **Pokhara** (windward, southern slope) | **~4000 mm** |
| Kathmandu Valley | ~1400 mm |
| **Jomsom** (in the rain shadow, trans-Himalaya) | **~250 mm** |

Gauges tens of kilometres apart can differ **sixteenfold** — so a purely geometric weighting is a poor guide, and the isohyetal method, drawn by someone who knows the terrain, is far preferable.

**Advantages of Thiessen nevertheless:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Objective and reproducible** | No judgement, so no dispute |
| **Weights computed ONCE** for a fixed gauge network | Then applied to every storm — a great saving |
| Better than the arithmetic mean whenever gauges are unevenly spaced | — |
| Easily automated | GIS does it directly |

**The fixed-weights property is the practical advantage**: once the polygons are drawn for a network, the weights are constants, and computing the areal rainfall for any storm is a single weighted sum. Isohyets must be redrawn for **every** storm.

**Rain gauge network density (WMO / IS 4987):**

| Region | One gauge per |
|---|---|
| **Flat regions, temperate** | 600 – 900 km² |
| **Mountainous regions** | **100 – 250 km²** |
| **Arid and polar** | 1500 – 10 000 km² |

**Mountainous regions need the densest network** precisely because of the orographic variability — and it is exactly where gauges are hardest to install and maintain, which is the standing difficulty of Himalayan hydrology.

**Types of gauge:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **Non-recording (Symons)** | A simple collector, read **daily at 0830** — the standard IS 5225 gauge |
| **Recording — TIPPING BUCKET** | Each 0.25 mm tips a bucket and closes a switch — gives **intensity** and is easily telemetered |
| Recording — weighing type | Records the accumulated weight; works with snow |
| Recording — float (siphon) type | A chart record |

**Only recording gauges give INTENSITY**, which is what storm drainage and flood design require — a daily total tells you nothing about whether it fell in an hour or over a day.

**Checking record consistency** — the **DOUBLE MASS CURVE**: plot the cumulative rainfall at the suspect gauge against the cumulative mean of surrounding gauges. A **change of slope** indicates the record has become inconsistent (the gauge was moved, or trees grew around it), and the earlier record is corrected by the ratio of the slopes.

examTip.trick: Perpendicular bisectors between gauges enclose the area nearer to each. It is purely **geometric** — the polygons know nothing about terrain.
examTip.mnemonic: **Arithmetic mean (crude) → Thiessen (weights gauge SPACING) → Isohyetal (weights spacing AND TERRAIN, most accurate).** In Nepal, orographic effects are enormous — Pokhara 4000 mm against Jomsom 250 mm — so a purely geometric weighting is weak and isohyets drawn by someone who knows the hills are far better. Thiessen's compensating advantage: the weights are computed **once** and reused for every storm.

questions.stem: In the rational formula Q = CIA, the intensity I must correspond to a storm duration equal to the:
options: Time of concentration of the catchment
questions.solution:
**The TIME OF CONCENTRATION of the catchment.**

> **Q = C I A**, or in consistent SI units **Q = 0.278 C I A** with I in mm/h, A in km² and Q in m³/s

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **C** | **Runoff coefficient** — the fraction of rainfall becoming runoff |
| **I** | Rainfall **intensity** for a duration equal to **t_c** |
| **A** | Catchment **area** |

**Why the duration must equal t_c** — the reasoning is the heart of the method:

> **Time of concentration t_c** is the time for runoff to travel from the **most remote point** of the catchment to the outlet. Only after t_c is the **WHOLE catchment contributing simultaneously**, giving the peak discharge.

| Storm duration | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Shorter than t_c** | The **whole catchment never contributes at once** — a higher intensity, but over a smaller effective area |
| **Equal to t_c** | **The whole area contributes at the highest intensity that can be sustained for that long — the PEAK** |
| **Longer than t_c** | The whole area contributes, but at a **lower intensity** (intensity falls with duration) |

> The peak therefore occurs at **duration = t_c**, which is why the intensity must be read from the **IDF curve at that duration**.

**Intensity–Duration–Frequency (IDF) curves** supply I: for a chosen **return period**, intensity **falls as duration increases** — a short cloudburst is intense, a day-long rain is not.

**Estimating t_c** — Kirpich's formula is the common one:

> **t_c = 0.01947 L^0.77 S^(−0.385)** (minutes, L in m, S the slope)

For urban drainage, t_c is split into **inlet (overland) time** plus **travel time in the drain**.

**Runoff coefficient C:**

| Surface | C |
|---|---|
| **Asphalt, concrete pavement, roofs** | **0.70 – 0.95** |
| Gravel | 0.35 – 0.70 |
| Urban residential | 0.30 – 0.50 |
| **Lawns, sandy soil** | **0.05 – 0.20** |
| **Cultivated land** | 0.20 – 0.40 |
| Forest | 0.10 – 0.30 |
| **Steep barren rock** | **0.80 – 0.90** |

**For a mixed catchment**, a **weighted C** is used: **C = Σ(C_i A_i)/ΣA_i**.

**The limitations of the rational method are severe and must be respected:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **SMALL catchments only** — under about **50 km²**, preferably **< 25 km²** | The assumption of uniform rainfall over the whole area fails at larger scales |
| Gives **only the PEAK**, not a hydrograph | No volume, no shape, no timing |
| Assumes **uniform** rainfall in space and time | Rarely true |
| Assumes **C is constant** | In fact C rises during a storm as the ground saturates |
| Assumes the **return period of the rainfall equals that of the runoff** | An approximation |
| No allowance for **antecedent moisture** or storage | — |

**Despite all that it remains the standard method for urban storm drainage**, because for a small paved catchment the assumptions are least wrong: the area is small, the surface is uniform, C is high and stable, and only the peak is needed to size a pipe.

**For larger catchments**, the alternatives:

| Method | Suits |
|---|---|
| **UNIT HYDROGRAPH** | Medium catchments; gives the **full hydrograph** |
| **SCS Curve Number** | Estimates runoff volume from soil type and land use |
| **Flood frequency analysis** | Where a **long gauged record** exists — the most reliable |
| Regional flood formulae (Dickens, Ryves, Inglis) | Ungauged catchments, preliminary estimates |
| Rainfall–runoff models (HEC-HMS) | Complex catchments |

**Where a long gauged record exists, frequency analysis is always preferable** to any rainfall-based method, because it uses the catchment's **actual observed behaviour** rather than a chain of assumptions about how rainfall becomes runoff.

examTip.trick: Only after **t_c** is the **whole catchment contributing at once**. A shorter storm is more intense but drains a smaller effective area; a longer one covers the area at a lower intensity. The peak is at duration = t_c exactly.
examTip.mnemonic: **Read I off the IDF curve AT t_c** — using a one-hour or 24-hour intensity instead is the commonest misuse of the formula. Also respect the limit: the rational method is for catchments **under about 25–50 km²** only.

questions.stem: A 6-hour unit hydrograph is the direct runoff hydrograph resulting from:
options: 6 hours of rainfall of any depth
6 cm of effective rainfall in 6 hours
1 cm of effective rainfall occurring uniformly over the catchment in 6 hours
questions.solution:
**1 cm (or 1 unit) of EFFECTIVE rainfall occurring UNIFORMLY over the catchment in 6 hours.**

**Every element of that definition matters:**

| Element | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **1 cm** — a **unit** depth | The hydrograph is scaled linearly for other depths |
| **EFFECTIVE (excess) rainfall** | The rainfall **remaining after losses** — infiltration, interception, depression storage. **Not** the total rainfall |
| **UNIFORMLY over the catchment** | Both in space and at a constant rate through the 6 hours |
| **6 hours** — the **duration** | The UH is specific to its duration; a 6-h UH differs from a 3-h UH |
| **DIRECT runoff** | **Base flow is EXCLUDED** and must be separated out |

**The two commonest misunderstandings** are that the duration refers to the hydrograph's length (it refers to the **rainfall** duration), and that the 1 cm is total rainfall (it is **effective** rainfall).

**The two principles the method rests on:**

| Principle | Statement |
|---|---|
| **PROPORTIONALITY (linearity)** | **2 cm** of effective rainfall in 6 h produces a hydrograph with **all ordinates DOUBLED** — same shape, same time base |
| **SUPERPOSITION** | Hydrographs from **successive** rainfall blocks are **added with appropriate time lags** |

**Note that the TIME BASE is unchanged by the depth** — doubling the rainfall doubles the ordinates but does not lengthen the hydrograph. That is a direct consequence of linearity, and it is one of the assumptions the method makes about a system that is not really linear.

**The assumptions, and where they fail:**

| Assumption | Reality |
|---|---|
| The catchment responds **LINEARLY** | It does not — larger storms run off proportionally **more**, as the ground saturates |
| Rainfall is **uniform** in space | Rarely true beyond small catchments |
| Rainfall is uniform **in time** | Rarely true |
| The UH is **time-invariant** | Land use changes; the UH must be revised |
| Base flow separation is unambiguous | It is a matter of convention |

**Despite these, the UH remains the workhorse of flood hydrology** for medium catchments, because it captures the **shape and timing** of the response — which the rational method cannot.

**Deriving a UH** from an observed event:

1. Plot the observed **flood hydrograph**.
2. **Separate the BASE FLOW** to leave the direct runoff hydrograph (DRH).
3. Compute the **volume** of direct runoff and divide by the catchment area to get the **depth of effective rainfall**.
4. **Divide every DRH ordinate** by that depth in cm — giving the UH.
5. Note the **duration** of the effective rainfall; that is the UH's duration.

**Base flow separation** methods, all conventional rather than physical:

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| **Straight line** | From the start of the rise to where the recession rejoins the pre-storm level |
| **Fixed base length** | The recession is extrapolated forward; **N = 0.83 A^0.2** days after the peak |
| Variable slope | The pre-storm recession extended forward and the post-storm recession backward |

**Changing the duration of a UH:**

| Case | Method |
|---|---|
| To a **multiple** of the original (6-h → 12-h) | **Superposition** — lag and add, then divide by the number of blocks |
| To **any** duration | The **S-CURVE** method |

**The S-CURVE** is the general tool: it is the hydrograph from a **continuous** effective rainfall of 1 cm per original duration, formed by summing UHs lagged by that duration. Offsetting two S-curves by the desired new duration and dividing the difference gives the new UH.

**SYNTHETIC unit hydrographs** — for **UNGAUGED** catchments, where no observed event is available:

| Method | Basis |
|---|---|
| **Snyder's** | Catchment length and centroid distance |
| **SCS dimensionless UH** | A standard shape scaled by the time to peak |
| **CWC regional formulae** | Regionalised for Indian and Nepali subzones |

**In Nepal**, most catchments are **ungauged**, so synthetic methods and regional formulae dominate practice — with all the additional uncertainty that implies. Where a gauged record does exist, using it is always preferable.

examTip.trap: Two errors hide here: the depth is **EFFECTIVE** rainfall (after losses), not total; and the duration refers to the **RAINFALL**, not to the length of the hydrograph.
examTip.trick: Unit means **1 cm**; the duration names the UH (a 6-h UH differs from a 3-h UH); and **base flow is excluded** — it is a DIRECT runoff hydrograph.
examTip.mnemonic: **Proportionality and superposition.** Doubling the rainfall doubles every ordinate but leaves the **time base unchanged** — a direct consequence of assuming linearity, which real catchments only approximate.

questions.stem: The probability that a flood of 100-year return period will be equalled or exceeded at least once in the next 50 years is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 40%.**

> **Risk R = 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ**, where **T** is the return period and **n** the design life
> **R = 1 − (1 − 0.01)⁵⁰ = 1 − (0.99)⁵⁰ = 1 − 0.605 = 0.395 ≈ 40%** ✓

**Derivation.** The probability of **non-exceedance in any one year** is **(1 − 1/T)**. For **n independent years** it is **(1 − 1/T)ⁿ**. The probability of **at least one** exceedance is the complement.

**This result is genuinely alarming and is the point of the question:**

> A structure designed for the **100-year flood** and expected to last **50 years** has a **40% chance of being overtopped at least once** in its life. That is not a remote possibility — it is closer to a coin toss than to a rarity.

**Risk for various combinations:**

| Design life ↓ / Return period → | T = 50 | T = 100 | T = 500 | T = 1000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **n = 10 years** | 18% | **10%** | 2% | 1% |
| **n = 25 years** | 40% | **22%** | 5% | 2.5% |
| **n = 50 years** | 64% | **40%** | 10% | 5% |
| **n = 100 years** | 87% | **63%** | 18% | 10% |

**Two rules of thumb worth carrying:**

> When **n = T**, the risk is always about **63%** — a structure designed for its own lifetime's return period is **more likely than not** to see that event.
> To keep the risk at **10%** over n years, choose **T ≈ 10n**.

**"Return period" is the most misunderstood term in hydrology:**

| Misconception | Correction |
|---|---|
| "It happens once every 100 years" | It has a **1% chance in ANY year** |
| "It just happened, so we are safe for 100 years" | **Completely wrong** — the probability next year is unchanged at 1% |
| "Two in a decade means the estimate is wrong" | Not necessarily; the probability of two 100-year floods in a decade is about 0.4%, which is small but not negligible across many catchments |

> **The events are treated as INDEPENDENT.** A 100-year flood this year does nothing to reduce next year's probability — the dice have no memory.

**Because of this, design return periods are chosen by CONSEQUENCE, not convention:**

| Structure | Design return period |
|---|---|
| Urban storm drain, minor | **2 – 10 years** |
| Urban drainage, major system | 25 – 50 years |
| **Highway culvert** | **25 – 50 years** |
| **Bridge** | **50 – 100 years** |
| **Levee protecting a town** | **100 – 200 years** |
| **Small dam spillway** | 100 – 1000 years |
| **LARGE DAM spillway** | **PMF — Probable Maximum Flood** |

**The PMF for a large dam** is the recognition that risk analysis has limits: the consequences of a large dam failing are so catastrophic — potentially thousands of lives — that no acceptable annual probability can be assigned. So the design flood is the **largest flood physically possible** for the catchment, derived from the **Probable Maximum Precipitation**, rather than any statistical return period.

**Flood frequency analysis** produces the T-year flood:

| Distribution | Note |
|---|---|
| **GUMBEL (EV1)** | The classic; **X_T = X̄ + K σ**, with K from the reduced variate |
| **Log-Pearson Type III** | The **US federal standard** |
| Log-normal | Common |
| GEV | Increasingly preferred |

**The fundamental limitation** applies to all of them:

> Extrapolating a **30-year record** to estimate the **100-year flood** is a considerable extrapolation, and to the **1000-year flood** it is little better than speculation. The confidence intervals widen dramatically beyond about **twice the record length** — and they are rarely quoted, which gives a false impression of precision.

**In Nepal** the difficulty is compounded by short records, sparse gauging, and **GLOFs** — glacial lake outburst floods — which are not part of the same statistical population as rainfall floods at all, and must be assessed separately as a distinct hazard.

examTip.trap: "2%" comes from misreading the question as the annual probability. Over 50 years the risk compounds enormously.
examTip.mnemonic: **When n = T the risk is always about 63%.** A 100-year design with a 50-year life is closer to a coin toss than to a rarity. And "100-year flood" means **1% chance in ANY year** — one happening this year does nothing to reduce next year's probability.

questions.stem: Horton's equation describes the variation of infiltration capacity with time as:
options: An exponential decay from an initial to a final constant rate
questions.solution:
**An exponential decay from an initial rate to a final constant rate.**

> **f = f_c + (f₀ − f_c) e^(−kt)**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **f₀** | **Initial** infiltration capacity — high, on dry soil |
| **f_c** | **Final (ultimate) constant** rate — approximately the **saturated permeability** |
| **k** | Decay constant |

**Why infiltration capacity decreases with time:**

| Cause | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Soil pores FILL with water** | Reducing the available storage and the capillary suction gradient |
| **Swelling of clay** particles | Closes the pores |
| **Surface sealing** by raindrop impact | Fine particles are washed into the surface pores, forming a crust |
| Air trapped below the wetting front | Impedes further entry |
| Reduced **suction gradient** | As the wetting front advances, the driving gradient falls |

**Infiltration CAPACITY versus actual infiltration** — an important distinction:

> **Capacity f** is the **maximum rate** the soil **can** absorb.
> **Actual infiltration** is the **lesser** of the capacity and the **rainfall intensity**.

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| **Rainfall intensity < f** | **All** the rain infiltrates; **no surface runoff** |
| **Rainfall intensity > f** | Infiltration proceeds **at capacity**; the **excess becomes RUNOFF** |

**That is the Hortonian mechanism of runoff generation**, and it explains a familiar observation:

> A **short intense cloudburst** on dry ground produces **more runoff** than a longer, gentler rain of the same total depth — because the intensity exceeds the infiltration capacity for much of its duration.

**Typical infiltration rates:**

| Soil | f_c (mm/h) |
|---|---|
| **Sand** | **> 20** |
| Sandy loam | 10 – 20 |
| **Loam** | **5 – 10** |
| Clay loam | 1 – 5 |
| **Clay** | **< 1** |

**Measurement:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **DOUBLE RING infiltrometer** | Two concentric rings; the **outer ring prevents LATERAL spreading**, so the inner ring measures true vertical infiltration |
| Single ring | Overestimates, because of lateral flow |
| **Rainfall simulator** | More realistic — includes the raindrop-impact sealing effect |
| Hydrograph analysis (φ-index) | Inferred from a real storm |

**The double ring's outer ring is the essential detail**: without it, water spreads sideways as well as down, and the measured rate is too high — often by a factor of two.

**The φ-INDEX** is the simple practical alternative used in flood hydrology:

> **φ-index** = the **CONSTANT loss rate** which, subtracted from the rainfall hyetograph, leaves a volume of **effective rainfall equal to the observed direct runoff**.

It is crude — real losses are not constant — but it is exactly what unit hydrograph derivation needs, and it is determined directly from an observed storm and its hydrograph without any soil testing.

**Other infiltration models:**

| Model | Basis |
|---|---|
| **Horton** | Empirical exponential decay |
| **Green–Ampt** | **Physically based** — a sharp wetting front, Darcy's law |
| **Philip** | Two-term series solution |
| **SCS Curve Number** | Empirical; combines soil type and land use into a single **CN** |

**The SCS Curve Number method** is the most used in practice for ungauged catchments:

> **Q = (P − 0.2S)²/(P + 0.8S)**, with **S = 25400/CN − 254** (mm)

CN ranges from about **30** (deep sand, forest) to **98** (paved). It folds soil, land use and antecedent moisture into one number, and its convenience has made it ubiquitous despite well-known theoretical weaknesses.

**Factors affecting infiltration**, worth listing since they explain the range of CN:

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Soil texture** | Sand high, clay low |
| **Antecedent moisture** | Wet soil infiltrates **less** |
| **VEGETATION** | **Increases** it greatly — roots open channels, litter protects the surface from sealing |
| **COMPACTION** | **Reduces** it sharply — hence the runoff from tracks, paths and construction sites |
| Surface sealing and crusting | Reduces |
| Slope | Steeper gives less time to infiltrate |

**The vegetation and compaction entries together explain most land-use hydrology**: clearing forest and compacting the soil can turn a catchment that absorbed most of its rainfall into one that sheds it, raising flood peaks and reducing dry-season base flow at the same time — a pattern seen across the Nepali middle hills.

examTip.trick: **f = f_c + (f₀ − f_c)e^(−kt)** — high at first on dry soil, decaying to the saturated permeability as the pores fill, the clay swells and raindrop impact seals the surface.
examTip.mnemonic: **Actual infiltration is the LESSER of the capacity and the rainfall intensity** — runoff is the excess. Which is why a short intense burst on dry ground produces **more** runoff than a gentle rain of the same total depth.

questions.stem: An aquifer bounded above and below by impermeable strata, in which the water is under pressure greater than atmospheric, is called:
questions.solution:
**A confined (artesian) aquifer.**

**The terminology of groundwater formations:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **AQUIFER** | A formation that **stores AND transmits** water in usable quantities — sand, gravel, fractured rock |
| **AQUITARD** | **Transmits SLOWLY** — leaky; silt, sandy clay |
| **AQUICLUDE** | **Stores but does NOT transmit** usefully — **clay** |
| **AQUIFUGE** | Neither stores nor transmits — solid **unfractured rock** |

**Clay is an aquiclude, not an aquifer**, which surprises people: clay has a **high porosity** (40–60%) but a **minute permeability**, so it holds a great deal of water and yields almost none. **Porosity and permeability are different properties**, and confusing them is the commonest error in groundwater.

**Types of aquifer:**

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| **UNCONFINED (water table, phreatic)** | The **upper surface is the WATER TABLE**, at atmospheric pressure. Recharged directly from above |
| **CONFINED (artesian)** | **Bounded above and below by impermeable layers**; water is **under pressure** exceeding atmospheric |
| **PERCHED** | A **local** saturated zone above an impermeable lens, **separated from the main water table** by unsaturated soil |
| **Leaky (semi-confined)** | Bounded by an **aquitard** that permits slow vertical leakage |

**In a confined aquifer:**

> Water in a well rises **ABOVE the top of the aquifer**, to the **PIEZOMETRIC (potentiometric) surface**. Where that surface lies **above ground level**, the well **FLOWS without pumping** — a **flowing artesian well**.

**Storage behaves quite differently in the two types**, and this is the substantive distinction:

| | **UNCONFINED** | **CONFINED** |
|---|---|---|
| Storage parameter | **SPECIFIC YIELD S_y** | **STORAGE COEFFICIENT S** |
| Typical value | **0.1 – 0.3** | **0.00005 – 0.005** |
| Water released by | **DRAINING the pores** | **Compression of the aquifer and expansion of the water** |
| Ratio between them | — | **Roughly 100 to 1000 times smaller** |

**Why confined storage is so small**: the aquifer stays **fully saturated** — no pores drain. The water released comes only from the **elastic compression** of the skeleton and **expansion** of the water as the pressure falls. So a small volume pumped produces a **large and widespread** drop in the piezometric surface.

> That is why pumping a confined aquifer **lowers the piezometric level over a very wide area**, while pumping an unconfined aquifer produces a **localised** cone of depression. It is also why over-abstraction from confined aquifers causes **LAND SUBSIDENCE** — the compression is partly irreversible.

**Well hydraulics — steady state (Dupuit–Thiem):**

| Aquifer | Discharge |
|---|---|
| **Confined** | **Q = 2πkb(h₂ − h₁)/ln(r₂/r₁)** — **linear** in the head difference |
| **Unconfined** | **Q = πk(h₂² − h₁²)/ln(r₂/r₁)** — depends on the **difference of SQUARES** |

**The unconfined case involves h² because the SATURATED THICKNESS ITSELF decreases** as the water table is drawn down — the aquifer thins as it is pumped, which the confined case does not.

**Key definitions:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Transmissivity T** | **T = k b** — permeability × saturated thickness (m²/day) |
| **Drawdown** | The **lowering** of the water level at a point |
| **Cone of depression** | The drawdown surface around a pumping well |
| **Radius of influence** | Distance to where the drawdown becomes negligible |
| **Specific capacity** | Q per unit drawdown — a practical measure of well performance |

**Unsteady analysis** uses the **Theis** solution, or the **Jacob (Cooper–Jacob) straight-line approximation** — plotting drawdown against log time gives a straight line whose slope yields **T** and whose intercept yields **S**. That **pumping test** is the standard field method for characterising an aquifer.

**Problems of over-abstraction:**

| Problem | Note |
|---|---|
| **Falling water table** | Wells must be deepened; pumping costs rise |
| **LAND SUBSIDENCE** | Irreversible compression of clay layers — Kathmandu Valley, Bangkok, Mexico City |
| **Saline intrusion** | In coastal aquifers |
| Drying of springs and base flow | Reduces dry-season river flow |
| Deterioration in water quality | Drawing in poorer-quality water from depth |

**The Kathmandu Valley** is a documented case: abstraction from its deep confined aquifer has for decades exceeded recharge, the piezometric surface has fallen tens of metres, and measurable **land subsidence** has occurred — a consequence that cannot be reversed by later reducing the pumping.

examTip.trap: Clay has high **porosity** but negligible **permeability**, so it is an **aquiclude**, not an aquifer. Confusing porosity with permeability is the standard error in groundwater.
examTip.trick: Confined means bounded above and below, so the water is under pressure and rises **above** the aquifer's top in a well — to the **piezometric surface**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Specific yield 0.1–0.3 (unconfined, pores DRAIN) against storage coefficient 0.00005–0.005 (confined, only elastic compression).** A factor of a hundred or more — which is why pumping a confined aquifer drops the piezometric surface over a huge area, and why over-abstraction causes **irreversible land subsidence**, as in the Kathmandu Valley.

questions.stem: The Muskingum method is used for:
options: Routing a flood wave through a river reach
questions.solution:
**Routing a flood wave through a river reach.**

**Flood routing** computes how a flood hydrograph is **modified** as it travels through a reach or a reservoir — its **peak attenuated** and its **timing delayed**.

> **The governing principle is CONTINUITY: I − O = dS/dt** — inflow minus outflow equals the rate of change of storage.

**Two families of routing:**

| Type | Storage depends on | Method |
|---|---|---|
| **RESERVOIR (level pool) routing** | **Outflow ALONE** — a level pool has a unique stage–storage–discharge relation | Modified Puls, Goodrich |
| **CHANNEL (river) routing** | **BOTH inflow and outflow** | **MUSKINGUM**, Muskingum–Cunge |

**The Muskingum storage equation:**

> **S = K[x I + (1 − x) O]**

| Parameter | Meaning | Typical range |
|---|---|---|
| **K** | **Travel time** through the reach | Hours to days |
| **x** | **Weighting factor** — how much the inflow influences storage | **0 to 0.5** |

**The meaning of x:**

| x | Storage type | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | **PURE PRISM** — storage depends on outflow only | Behaves like a **reservoir**; maximum attenuation |
| **0.2 – 0.3** | **Typical natural river** | Moderate attenuation |
| **0.5** | **PURE WEDGE** | **NO attenuation** — the wave translates unchanged |

**Prism and wedge storage** is the physical picture behind the equation:

> **PRISM storage** is the volume under a water surface **parallel to the bed** — it depends on the outflow depth.
> **WEDGE storage** is the **additional** volume under the **sloping** surface of the advancing flood wave — **positive on the rising limb** (inflow exceeds outflow) and **negative on the falling limb**.

That wedge is precisely why a **river** reach differs from a **reservoir**: a level pool has no wedge, so its storage depends on outflow alone.

**The routing equation:**

> **O₂ = C₀I₂ + C₁I₁ + C₂O₁**

with

> **C₀ = (−Kx + 0.5Δt)/D**, **C₁ = (Kx + 0.5Δt)/D**, **C₂ = (K − Kx − 0.5Δt)/D**
> where **D = K − Kx + 0.5Δt**, and **C₀ + C₁ + C₂ = 1** — a useful arithmetic check.

**Determining K and x** from observed inflow and outflow hydrographs: plot the **accumulated storage against [xI + (1−x)O]** for trial values of x, and choose the x that makes the plot collapse to a **single straight line** (rather than a loop). **K is then the slope**.

**The choice of time step matters:**

> **2Kx ≤ Δt ≤ K** — outside this range the computation can produce **negative outflows** or oscillations, which are numerical artefacts rather than physics.

**Why routing matters:**

| Application | Use |
|---|---|
| **Flood forecasting** | Predicting downstream levels and timing from upstream gauges — the basis of **early warning** |
| **Reservoir operation** | How much a reservoir will attenuate an incoming flood |
| **Spillway design** | The **outflow** hydrograph, which sizes the spillway — always **less** than the inflow peak |
| Levee and floodplain design | Levels along the reach |
| Assessing the effect of channel works | Straightening a river **reduces** attenuation and **raises** downstream peaks |

**The spillway design point is economically significant:**

> A reservoir **attenuates** the inflow flood, so the **spillway need only pass the routed OUTFLOW peak**, not the inflow peak. For a reservoir with substantial flood storage that can mean a **much smaller and cheaper spillway** — and routing is what quantifies the saving.

**The channel-works point is a caution**: straightening, dredging or embanking a river **reduces its storage**, so it attenuates less. The flood arrives downstream **sooner and higher**. Local flood protection works therefore routinely **transfer** the problem downstream, which is why catchment-scale assessment is required before approving them.

**Muskingum–Cunge** is the modern refinement: it derives K and x from **channel hydraulic properties** (width, slope, celerity) rather than requiring observed hydrographs — so it can be applied to **ungauged** reaches, which is the usual situation.

examTip.trick: All routing is continuity: **I − O = dS/dt**. What differs is what storage depends on — **outflow alone** for a level-pool reservoir, but **both inflow and outflow** for a river reach, because of the **wedge** under the advancing flood wave.
examTip.mnemonic: **x = 0 behaves like a reservoir (maximum attenuation); x = 0.5 gives NO attenuation. Natural rivers are 0.2–0.3.** Practical consequence: **straightening or embanking a river removes storage**, so the flood arrives downstream sooner and higher — local works transfer the problem.

questions.stem: The stage–discharge (rating) curve of a river must be reviewed periodically because:
options: The channel section scours, deposits or grows vegetation, shifting the relation
The gauge datum is unstable by design
questions.solution:
**Because the channel section scours, deposits or grows vegetation, shifting the stage–discharge relation.**

**How river discharge data is actually produced:**

| Step | Frequency |
|---|---|
| **STAGE (water level)** recorded | **CONTINUOUSLY**, by an automatic gauge — cheap |
| **DISCHARGE** measured by **current meter** | **OCCASIONALLY** — expensive and labour-intensive |
| A **RATING CURVE** established from the paired measurements | Periodically reviewed |
| Continuous discharge derived from continuous stage | — |

> The rating curve is what converts a cheap continuous measurement into the expensive quantity actually wanted. Nearly all published river flow data is produced this way.

**The rating curve form:**

> **Q = C(G − a)ⁿ**

where **G** is the gauge reading, **a** the stage at zero flow, and **n** typically between **2 and 3**.

**Why the relation SHIFTS:**

| Cause | Effect |
|---|---|
| **SCOUR** of the bed | Lowers the bed — **more** discharge at the same stage |
| **DEPOSITION** | Raises the bed — **less** discharge at the same stage |
| **VEGETATION** growth in summer | Increases roughness — **less** discharge at the same stage |
| **Ice** effects | Where relevant |
| Downstream backwater | From a confluence or a structure |
| Channel works, dredging, gravel extraction | Direct alteration |

**In Nepal's rivers the shifting is severe**, because they carry **very heavy sediment loads** and their beds are mobile — a single monsoon can rework the section entirely. Rating curves therefore need frequent re-measurement, and a curve more than a season or two old should be treated with suspicion.

**The LOOP rating** is a second complication:

> During a flood, the **RISING limb carries MORE discharge at a given stage than the falling limb** — because the energy slope is steeper as the wave front passes. Plotting stage against discharge through a flood traces a **LOOP**, not a line.

A single-valued rating curve therefore **understates** the rising-limb discharge and **overstates** the falling-limb discharge. The correction uses the rate of change of stage, and it matters most for large, fast-rising floods on flat rivers.

**The velocity–area method** used to make each measurement:

> **Q = Σ(a_i v_i)** — the section is divided into segments, each with a measured mean velocity.

**Depths at which to measure**, standardised:

| Depth | Method |
|---|---|
| **Shallow water** | **One point at 0.6 × depth** from the surface |
| **Deeper water** | **Two points, at 0.2 and 0.8 depth**, averaged |
| Very deep or irregular | Three points: 0.2, 0.6, 0.8, weighted |

**The 0.6-depth rule** works because a logarithmic velocity profile has its **mean at about 0.6 of the depth** — a convenient property that halves the fieldwork.

**Methods of measurement:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **CURRENT METER**, wading or from a bridge/cableway | The standard |
| **ADCP** (acoustic Doppler) | Modern; a boat traverse gives the whole section rapidly |
| **Float** method | Crude — surface floats × 0.85 for mean velocity |
| **Dilution gauging** | For **turbulent mountain streams** where a current meter cannot be used |
| **Slope–area** method | For **flood peaks measured after the event** from high-water marks and Manning's equation |

**Dilution gauging suits Nepali mountain streams** particularly well: a boulder-strewn torrent has no measurable cross-section and no place to stand, but a tracer injected upstream and sampled downstream gives the discharge from the **dilution ratio** alone, independent of the geometry.

**The slope–area method** is how the biggest floods get measured — nobody is gauging a river at the peak of a destructive flood, so the discharge is reconstructed **afterwards** from **high-water marks** on the banks, the surveyed cross-section, and Manning's equation. It is the least accurate method and produces the most important numbers, which is an uncomfortable but unavoidable feature of flood hydrology.

**Extrapolation** is the standing weakness: the largest measured discharge is usually far below the design flood, so the rating curve must be **extrapolated** well beyond its data — precisely into the range where accuracy matters most, and where the channel may behave quite differently as the flow spills onto the floodplain.

examTip.trick: Stage is recorded **continuously and cheaply**; discharge is measured **occasionally and expensively**. The rating curve is what converts one into the other — so its validity is the validity of all the published flow data.
examTip.mnemonic: **Nepali rivers carry heavy sediment and rework their beds every monsoon**, so a curve more than a season old deserves suspicion. Watch also for the **LOOP rating**: the rising limb carries more discharge at a given stage than the falling limb.

questions.stem: Darcy's law for flow through a porous medium, v = ki, is valid only when the flow is:
questions.solution:
**Laminar.**

> **v = k i**, where **i = h/L** is the hydraulic gradient and **k** the coefficient of permeability

**The relation is LINEAR in the gradient**, and that linearity is the signature of laminar flow — where resistance is proportional to velocity, not to velocity squared.

**The validity limit** is expressed as a Reynolds number based on the grain size:

> **Re = v d/ν < 1** (some references allow up to 10), with **d** typically **d₁₀**

**Where Darcy's law FAILS:**

| Situation | Why |
|---|---|
| **Coarse GRAVEL and ROCKFILL** at high gradients | The flow becomes **TURBULENT** |
| **Flow toward a well very close to the screen** | Velocities are high near the well |
| Flow through **rockfill dams and gabions** | Turbulent throughout |
| **Very fine clays at very low gradients** | A **threshold gradient** must be exceeded before flow begins at all |

**In those cases a non-linear law is needed**, such as **v = k i^m** with m about 0.5 for fully turbulent flow — which is why rockfill drains are analysed quite differently from sand filters.

**Note that v is the DISCHARGE VELOCITY, not the actual velocity of the water:**

| Velocity | Definition | Relation |
|---|---|---|
| **Discharge (superficial) velocity v** | **Q/A**, over the **TOTAL** cross-sectional area | What Darcy's law gives |
| **SEEPAGE (actual) velocity v_s** | Through the **VOIDS only** | **v_s = v/n**, with n the porosity |

> Since **n is typically 0.3 to 0.5**, the **actual water moves 2 to 3 times faster** than Darcy's velocity suggests. For **contaminant travel time** that distinction is critical — using v instead of v_s overestimates the time by that factor, with obvious consequences for a pollution assessment.

**Typical permeabilities**, spanning an extraordinary range:

| Soil | k (m/s) |
|---|---|
| **Clean GRAVEL** | **10⁻¹ – 10⁻²** |
| **Clean SAND** | **10⁻³ – 10⁻⁵** |
| Silty sand | 10⁻⁵ – 10⁻⁷ |
| **SILT** | **10⁻⁷ – 10⁻⁹** |
| **CLAY** | **< 10⁻⁹** |

> **Ten orders of magnitude** from gravel to clay — a wider range than almost any other engineering property, and the reason permeability dominates so many geotechnical decisions.

**Measuring k:**

| Method | Suits |
|---|---|
| **CONSTANT HEAD** permeameter | **Coarse** soils — sands and gravels (IS 2720 Part 17) |
| **FALLING (variable) HEAD** permeameter | **Fine** soils — silts and clays |
| Indirectly from the **consolidation test** | Very fine soils: **k = c_v m_v γ_w** |
| **PUMPING TEST** in the field | The most reliable — tests a **large volume** of ground in situ |
| Hazen's formula | **k ≈ C d₁₀²** — a rough estimate for clean sand |

**Field pumping tests are far more reliable than laboratory tests**, and the reason is fundamental:

> A laboratory specimen is **small, remoulded and unrepresentative**. It cannot capture the **fissures, laminations, sand lenses and root channels** that dominate the mass permeability of a natural deposit — and which may make the field value **orders of magnitude higher** than the laboratory result.

**ANISOTROPY** is the systematic version of the same problem:

> Natural soils are usually **more permeable HORIZONTALLY than vertically**, because deposition builds up in layers. **k_h/k_v of 2 to 10 is common**, and in varved clays it can reach 100.

Seepage analysis handles it by drawing the flow net on a **transformed section** — horizontal dimensions scaled by **√(k_v/k_h)** — and computing the discharge with **k_eq = √(k_h k_v)**.

**Temperature correction**: since **k = K γ_w/μ**, and μ varies by nearly a factor of two between 10 °C and 30 °C, laboratory results are **corrected to 27 °C** under IS 2720 before use. It is a real correction, not a formality.

**Why permeability matters:**

| Application | Use |
|---|---|
| **Seepage** through and under dams | Quantity and exit gradient |
| **Dewatering** design | Pumping rates |
| **Consolidation** rate | **c_v = k/(m_v γ_w)** — how fast settlement occurs |
| **Drainage** and filter design | — |
| **Contaminant transport** | Travel times, using the **seepage** velocity |
| Well and tubewell yield | — |

examTip.trick: **v = ki is LINEAR**, and linear resistance is the signature of laminar flow. Validity is roughly **Re = vd/ν < 1**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Darcy FAILS in coarse gravel and rockfill**, where the flow turns turbulent — those need a non-linear law. Also remember **v is not the real velocity**: **v_s = v/n**, so water actually travels **2–3× faster**. Use the seepage velocity for contaminant travel times or you will overestimate the time by that factor.

questions.stem: The design flood adopted for the spillway of a large dam whose failure would cause major loss of life is normally the:
questions.solution:
**The Probable Maximum Flood (PMF).**

**Design flood standards scale with the CONSEQUENCE of failure:**

| Structure | Design flood |
|---|---|
| Minor urban storm drain | **2 – 10 year** |
| Highway culvert | 25 – 50 year |
| Bridge | 50 – 100 year |
| Levee protecting a town | 100 – 200 year |
| **Small dam** (low hazard) | **100 – 1000 year** |
| **LARGE DAM, high hazard** | **PMF** |

**Why the PMF and not a return period.** For a large dam:

> The consequences of failure are **so catastrophic** — potentially thousands of lives and the destruction of everything downstream — that **NO annual probability of failure is acceptable**.

So the design abandons statistics and asks a different question: **what is the largest flood physically possible** for this catchment? The PMF is derived from the **Probable Maximum Precipitation (PMP)** — the greatest depth of rainfall meteorologically possible over the catchment for a given duration — routed through the catchment's unit hydrograph.

**The PMP is estimated by:**

| Method | Basis |
|---|---|
| **Storm maximisation** | Take the largest observed storm and **maximise its moisture content** to the theoretical limit |
| **Storm transposition** | Move a severe storm observed **elsewhere in a meteorologically similar region** onto this catchment |
| Statistical (Hershfield) | An envelope approach on observed maxima |
| Combination | Usual in practice |

**Classification of design floods (IS 11223):**

| Class | Storage / height | Design flood |
|---|---|---|
| **Small** | < 10 Mm³ or < 12 m | **100-year** |
| **Intermediate** | 10 – 60 Mm³ or 12 – 30 m | **Standard Project Flood (SPF)** |
| **Large** | > 60 Mm³ or > 30 m | **PMF** |

**The Standard Project Flood** sits between: it is derived from the **most severe storm actually observed** in the region (not maximised to the theoretical limit), and is typically **40 to 60% of the PMF**.

**Why spillway adequacy is the dominant dam safety issue:**

> **Overtopping is the leading cause of failure of EMBANKMENT dams.** An earth dam overtopped by even a modest depth **erodes rapidly** and can breach within hours. A concrete dam tolerates overtopping far better.

That asymmetry is why embankment dams are given the more generous spillway provision, and why **freeboard** is treated as a critical design quantity rather than a detail.

**Freeboard** must allow for:

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **Wind-generated WAVE height** | From fetch and design wind speed |
| **Wave RUN-UP** on the slope | Depends on the slope and surface roughness |
| **Settlement** of the embankment | Post-construction |
| **Seismic** effects — seiche and slumping | — |
| A safety margin | — |

**Types of spillway:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **Ogee (overflow)** | The standard for concrete dams; the profile follows the **lower nappe** of a free jet |
| **Chute (trough)** | Common for embankment dams; carries flow away from the toe |
| **Side channel** | Where the crest length must exceed the available width |
| **Shaft (morning glory)** | A vertical shaft to a tunnel; compact but **cannot be enlarged** once the shaft chokes |
| **Siphon** | Automatic; sudden onset; debris-prone |
| **Emergency / fuse plug** | A deliberately erodible section that washes out in an extreme flood |

**The ogee profile** is designed so the water **just maintains contact** with the crest at the design head — following the shape of the underside of a free-falling nappe. At **lower** heads the flow presses on the crest (safe); at **higher** heads it tends to **separate**, creating **sub-atmospheric pressure** and the risk of **cavitation** damage. That is why the design head is chosen carefully and why crest profiles are built to tight tolerances.

**A note on GLOFs.** In Nepal, **glacial lake outburst floods** are a hazard that conventional flood frequency analysis cannot address — they arise from moraine dam failure, not from rainfall, and belong to a different statistical population entirely. Dams downstream of glacial lakes require a **separate GLOF assessment**, and the design flood may be governed by that rather than by the PMF from precipitation.

examTip.trick: For a large dam the consequences of failure are so severe that **no annual probability is acceptable** — so the design abandons statistics and asks what is **physically possible** instead.
examTip.mnemonic: **Small dam 100-year; intermediate SPF; large dam PMF.** Overtopping is the leading cause of **embankment** dam failure — an earth dam breaches within hours, while a concrete dam tolerates it. In Nepal, **GLOFs** are a separate hazard that flood frequency analysis cannot address at all.

questions.stem: In a flood hydrograph, the portion of flow sustained by groundwater between storms is the:
questions.solution:
**Base flow.**

**Components of streamflow:**

| Component | Source | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| **OVERLAND (surface) flow** | Rainfall exceeding infiltration capacity | **Fast** — hours |
| **INTERFLOW (subsurface storm flow)** | Lateral flow through the **upper soil**, above the water table | **Intermediate** |
| **BASE FLOW (groundwater flow)** | **Groundwater discharge** into the channel | **Slow** — weeks to months |
| Channel precipitation | Rain falling directly on the water surface | Immediate, usually small |

> **DIRECT RUNOFF = overland flow + interflow** — the storm response.
> **BASE FLOW** is what **sustains the river between storms**, and it is what keeps a perennial river flowing through the dry season.

**Parts of a flood hydrograph:**

| Part | Description |
|---|---|
| **Rising limb** | Steep; shaped by the storm and the catchment's response |
| **CREST (peak)** | The maximum discharge |
| **Recession (falling) limb** | **Shaped by the CATCHMENT alone, not the storm** — an important property |
| **Point of inflection** on the recession | Taken to mark the **end of direct runoff** |
| **Time to peak** | From the start of rise |
| **Lag time** | From the **centroid of effective rainfall** to the peak |
| **Time base** | The total duration of direct runoff |

**The recession limb depends only on the catchment**, because by then the rain has stopped and the shape reflects how the catchment drains its storage. That makes the recession reproducible from storm to storm, and it is the basis of the **base flow recession equation**:

> **Q_t = Q₀ K_r^t**

where **K_r** is the **recession constant** — typically **0.85 to 0.99** per day for base flow, and lower for the faster components.

**Base flow separation** is needed to derive a unit hydrograph, and all the methods are **conventional rather than physical**:

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| **Straight line** | Join the start of the rise to where the recession rejoins the pre-storm trend |
| **Fixed base length** | Direct runoff ends **N days after the peak**, with **N = 0.83 A^0.2** (A in km²) |
| **Variable slope** | Pre-storm recession extended forward, post-storm recession extended backward, joined at the inflection |

> There is **no uniquely correct separation** — the components are not physically distinguishable in the record. What matters is **consistency**: the same method must be used to derive a unit hydrograph and to apply it.

**Factors affecting the hydrograph shape:**

| Factor | Effect on the peak |
|---|---|
| **Catchment SHAPE** | A **fan-shaped** catchment gives a **higher, earlier** peak than an elongated one of the same area |
| **SLOPE** | Steeper → faster, higher peak |
| **Drainage density** | Higher → faster response |
| **URBANISATION** | **Higher and earlier** peak; **less base flow** |
| **FOREST cover** | **Lower peak**, more base flow |
| Antecedent moisture | Wetter → higher peak |
| Storm movement | A storm moving **downstream** gives a higher peak than one moving upstream |

**The urbanisation and forest entries together describe the most consequential land-use effect in hydrology:**

> **Paving a catchment** reduces infiltration, so **more water runs off faster**: the flood peak **rises and arrives sooner**, while the **base flow falls** because less water reaches the groundwater. The river becomes **flashier** — worse floods **and** worse dry-season low flows, from the same cause.

That double penalty is why **sustainable urban drainage** — soakaways, permeable paving, detention ponds, recharge pits — aims to restore infiltration rather than merely convey the water away faster.

**The same mechanism operates in the Nepali middle hills** with deforestation and terracing: the flood response sharpens and the springs that sustain dry-season flow diminish. Reafforestation and recharge works address both ends of the problem simultaneously, which is why they are so often the recommended catchment intervention.

**The storm-movement entry is worth noting** as a subtlety: a storm travelling **down** the catchment keeps pace with its own runoff, so the contributions from successive parts of the catchment arrive **together** — producing a sharply higher peak than the same storm moving upstream. It is one reason observed peaks sometimes exceed what a uniform-rainfall model predicts.

examTip.trick: Split by speed: **overland flow** (hours), **interflow** (intermediate), **base flow** (weeks to months). Direct runoff is the first two; base flow is what keeps a perennial river alive between storms.
examTip.mnemonic: **The recession limb is shaped by the CATCHMENT, not by the storm** — which is why it is reproducible and why the recession constant is a catchment property. Base flow separation has **no uniquely correct method**; what matters is using the same one to derive a unit hydrograph and to apply it.

questions.stem: A catchment of 25 km² has a runoff coefficient of 0.4. For a rainfall intensity of 36 mm/h, the peak discharge by the rational formula is:
questions.solution:
**100 m³/s.**

> **Q = 0.278 C I A** (Q in m³/s, I in mm/h, A in km²)
> **= 0.278 × 0.4 × 36 × 25 = 0.278 × 360 = 100.1 ≈ 100 m³/s** ✓

**Check the constant.** Converting from first principles:

> **Q = C I A** with I in **m/s** and A in **m²**
> **I = 36 mm/h = 0.036/3600 m/s = 1 × 10⁻⁵ m/s**
> **A = 25 km² = 25 × 10⁶ m²**
> **Q = 0.4 × 10⁻⁵ × 25 × 10⁶ = 0.4 × 250 = 100 m³/s** ✓

**Both routes agree**, which confirms the 0.278 constant: it is simply **1/3.6**, converting mm/h × km² to m³/s.

> **Remember 0.278 = 1/3.6** — that is easier to recall and easier to check.

**The runoff coefficient's meaning** is visible in the numbers: of the 36 mm/h falling, **0.4 × 36 = 14.4 mm/h** runs off and the rest infiltrates, is intercepted, or fills depressions.

**A caution about this catchment size.** At **25 km²** the rational method is **at the upper limit of its validity**:

| Limit | Note |
|---|---|
| Preferred | **< 25 km²** |
| Absolute maximum | **~50 km²** |
| Above that | Use a **unit hydrograph** or **flood frequency** analysis |

**Why the method fails on larger catchments:**

| Assumption | Why it fails at scale |
|---|---|
| Rainfall **uniform over the whole area** | A storm cell rarely covers more than a few tens of km² at full intensity |
| Rainfall **uniform in time** for the whole t_c | A long t_c means a long storm, which is never uniform |
| **C constant** | Varies across a large, mixed catchment, and rises during the storm |
| Return period of rainfall = that of runoff | Increasingly approximate |
| No **channel storage** or attenuation | A large catchment attenuates its own flood significantly |

**An AREAL REDUCTION FACTOR** is the standard partial remedy: point rainfall intensities from an IDF curve are multiplied by a factor **less than 1** (typically 0.8 – 0.95 for catchments of this size) to represent the average over the area rather than the intensity at a point.

**And the intensity must correspond to the TIME OF CONCENTRATION** — the single most-neglected requirement of the method:

> **I is read from the IDF curve at duration = t_c**, because only then is the whole catchment contributing simultaneously at the highest sustainable intensity.

Using a one-hour or 24-hour intensity instead, without reference to t_c, is the commonest misuse of the rational formula and can be wrong by a factor of several either way.

**Alternatives for larger catchments:**

| Method | Suits |
|---|---|
| **Unit hydrograph** | Medium catchments; gives the **full hydrograph**, not just the peak |
| **SCS Curve Number** | Runoff **volume** from soil and land use |
| **Flood frequency analysis** | Wherever a **long gauged record** exists — always preferable |
| **Regional formulae** — Dickens, Ryves, Inglis | Ungauged catchments, preliminary estimates |
| **HEC-HMS** and similar models | Complex or multi-subcatchment systems |
