**The empirical regional formulae** take the form **Q = C A^n**, with n between 0.5 and 0.75 — reflecting the important general observation that **peak discharge per unit area DECREASES as catchment area increases**, because of storm non-uniformity and channel attenuation. A 1 km² catchment may yield 5 m³/s per km²; a 1000 km² catchment perhaps 0.5.

**A final check on the answer's plausibility**: 100 m³/s from 25 km² is **4 m³/s per km²** — a high but entirely credible figure for an intense storm on a moderately impervious catchment, and consistent with the regional pattern above.

examTip.trick: **Q = 0.278 C I A = 0.278 × 0.4 × 36 × 25 = 100 m³/s.** Verify from first principles: I = 10⁻⁵ m/s, A = 25 × 10⁶ m², so Q = 0.4 × 250 = 100 ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **The constant 0.278 is simply 1/3.6** — easier to remember and easier to check. At 25 km² this is at the **upper limit** of the method's validity; beyond about 50 km² use a unit hydrograph or frequency analysis instead.

questions.stem: Evaporation from a free water surface is measured directly by:
options: A class A pan, with the reading multiplied by a pan coefficient
questions.solution:
**A class A evaporation pan, with the reading multiplied by a PAN COEFFICIENT.**

> **Lake evaporation = pan evaporation × pan coefficient**, with the coefficient typically **0.7 for a class A pan** (0.6 – 0.8 depending on siting and season)

**Why a coefficient is needed** — the pan does not behave like a lake:

| Difference | Effect on the pan |
|---|---|
| The pan is **SMALL and SHALLOW** | It **heats up faster** and reaches higher water temperatures |
| **Metal sides absorb radiation** | Adds heat the lake does not receive |
| **Heat exchange through the sides and base** | A lake exchanges only at its surface |
| **Negligible heat storage** | A lake stores heat through the season and releases it in autumn, **lagging** the pan |
| Different **aerodynamic** exposure | The pan sits above ground in the wind |

> The pan therefore **OVER-reads**, and the coefficient of about **0.7** brings it down to lake values.

**The seasonal lag is the subtlest of these**: a deep lake **stores heat** in spring and **releases** it in autumn, so its evaporation **peaks later in the year** than the pan's. Applying a single annual coefficient smooths over a real seasonal mismatch, which matters for monthly water balances.

**The class A pan** (IS 5973): **1.21 m diameter, 255 mm deep**, unpainted galvanised iron, mounted on a **wooden frame 150 mm above ground** so air circulates beneath. Water is kept between 50 and 75 mm below the rim, and the level is measured daily by hook gauge; rainfall is added and the loss computed by difference.

**Factors affecting evaporation:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Solar RADIATION** | The **dominant** driver — it supplies the latent heat |
| **Temperature** | Higher temperature raises the saturation vapour pressure |
| **WIND** | **Removes saturated air** from the surface, maintaining the gradient |
| **HUMIDITY** | **High humidity REDUCES** evaporation — a smaller vapour pressure deficit |
| Atmospheric pressure | Minor; lower pressure slightly increases it |
| **Dissolved salts** | **Reduce** it by about 1% per 1% of salt — sea water evaporates ~2–3% slower |
| Water depth | Affects the seasonal timing through heat storage |

**Dalton's law** expresses the driving mechanism:

> **E = C(e_s − e_a)** — proportional to the difference between the **saturation** vapour pressure at the water surface and the **actual** vapour pressure of the air

So evaporation is driven by a **vapour pressure DEFICIT**, not by temperature alone — which is why a hot humid day evaporates less than a warm dry windy one.

**Methods of estimating evaporation:**

| Method | Basis |
|---|---|
| **PAN measurement** | Direct, × coefficient — the practical standard |
| **Water budget** | Inflow − outflow − change in storage; simple in principle, but errors in the other terms swamp the evaporation |
| **Energy budget** | Rigorous; needs radiation, heat storage and advection data |
| **Mass transfer** | Dalton-type equations with wind |
| **PENMAN combination** | **Energy budget + aerodynamic** — the most widely accepted |

**Penman's combination method** is the standard because it resolves a practical difficulty: the **energy budget** needs the surface temperature, which is hard to measure, while the **mass transfer** approach needs it too. Penman **eliminated the surface temperature** by combining the two, leaving an equation in ordinary meteorological variables — air temperature, humidity, wind and radiation — all of which are routinely measured.

**Reducing reservoir evaporation** — a real concern in arid regions, where a large shallow reservoir can lose a substantial fraction of its storage:

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Windbreaks** | Reduce the wind speed over the surface |
| **Floating covers or rafts** | Effective but costly at scale |
| **Monomolecular films** (cetyl alcohol) | Cheap; **broken up by wind** and must be continually replenished |
| **DEEPER reservoirs** with **less surface area** per unit volume | The most effective design measure |
| Compartmentalisation | Concentrate the remaining water in a smaller area late in the season |

**The last is a design principle rather than a treatment**: for a given storage volume, a **deep narrow** reservoir loses far less than a **broad shallow** one, because evaporation scales with **surface area**. Site selection therefore governs evaporation loss more than any subsequent measure can.

examTip.trick: A pan **over-reads** because it is small, shallow, metal-sided and exchanges heat through its walls — so the reading is scaled down by about **0.7**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Pan × 0.7 = lake.** Evaporation is driven by the **vapour pressure DEFICIT** (Dalton), not by temperature alone — so a warm dry windy day evaporates more than a hot humid one. Design lesson: a **deep narrow** reservoir loses far less than a **broad shallow** one of the same volume, because loss scales with surface area.

questions.stem: The double mass curve technique is used in hydrology to:
options: Check the consistency of a rainfall record
Route a flood through a reservoir
questions.solution:
**To check the CONSISTENCY of a rainfall record.**

**The technique.** Plot the **cumulative annual rainfall at the suspect gauge** (y-axis) against the **cumulative annual mean of a group of surrounding gauges** (x-axis).

| Result | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| A **STRAIGHT line** | The record is **CONSISTENT** |
| A **CHANGE OF SLOPE** | An **INCONSISTENCY** began at that year — the gauge's conditions changed |

**Correcting the record:**

> **P_corrected = P_observed × (slope of the CURRENT period / slope of the earlier period)**

and it is the **earlier (pre-break) record** that is adjusted, so the whole series is brought onto the basis of the **present** conditions — because the present regime is the one that will continue.

**Causes of inconsistency:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| The gauge was **MOVED** | Even a short distance, or a change of height |
| **Change in the surroundings** | **Trees or buildings grew up** nearby, sheltering the gauge |
| Change of **instrument** | Different exposure or catch |
| Change in **observation procedure** or observer | — |
| Change of exposure through land clearance | — |

**The critical requirement of the method:**

> The **BASE gauges must themselves be consistent**, and should be in the **same meteorological region** — subject to the same climatic influences. If a common climatic shift affects all the gauges together, it appears in **both axes** and the plot stays straight, correctly showing no inconsistency at the suspect gauge.

That is the method's elegance: it separates **local, gauge-specific** changes from **regional, climatic** ones, which a simple time-series plot cannot do.

**Using several base gauges averaged** also cancels random error, which is why a group rather than a single neighbour is used.

**Related record-processing techniques:**

| Problem | Technique |
|---|---|
| **Inconsistent** record | **Double mass curve** |
| **MISSING** data | **Normal ratio** or **arithmetic mean** method |
| Testing for **trend** | Mann–Kendall test |
| Filling short gaps | Regression on a neighbouring gauge |

**Estimating MISSING rainfall data:**

| Condition | Method |
|---|---|
| Neighbouring **normal annual rainfalls within 10%** of the missing station's | **Simple ARITHMETIC MEAN** of the neighbours |
| Normals differ by **more than 10%** | **NORMAL RATIO method**: **P_x = (N_x/m) Σ(P_i/N_i)** |

where **N** are the **normal annual rainfalls** and **m** the number of base stations. The normal ratio method weights each neighbour by how its long-term average compares with the missing station's — which is exactly the correction needed where the gauges sit in different rainfall regimes.

**In Nepal, the normal ratio method is almost always the appropriate one**, because **orographic effects** make neighbouring stations differ by far more than 10% — Pokhara at ~4000 mm and Jomsom at ~250 mm are only about 60 km apart. Using the simple arithmetic mean across such a gradient would be badly wrong.

**Why record quality matters so much:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Design flood estimates** depend directly on the record | An inconsistent record biases the frequency analysis |
| **Water resource assessments** | Yield studies |
| **Trend detection** | An instrumental artefact can masquerade as climate change — which is precisely why consistency checking must precede any trend analysis |
| Reservoir sizing | — |

**The trend-detection point deserves emphasis:**

> A gauge that was sheltered by growing trees will show a **declining rainfall trend** that is entirely spurious. Before any climate-trend conclusion is drawn from a record, the record must be **tested for homogeneity** — and the double mass curve is the standard first test.

It is a simple graphical technique, requiring nothing but a pencil and the neighbouring records, and it remains the first thing a careful hydrologist does with an unfamiliar rainfall series.

examTip.trick: Plot the suspect gauge's cumulative rainfall against the cumulative mean of its neighbours. A **change of slope** marks the year the record became inconsistent — the gauge moved, or trees grew around it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Correct the EARLIER record to the CURRENT slope**, since the present regime is the one that continues. Crucially, a common **climatic** shift affects both axes and leaves the plot straight — which is exactly what lets the method separate an instrumental artefact from a real trend. Always test homogeneity before claiming a climate trend.

questions.stem: Compared with a forested catchment, an urbanised catchment of the same area generally has:
options: A lower and later flood peak
A higher and earlier flood peak, with reduced base flow
A higher peak but greater base flow
questions.solution:
**A higher and earlier flood peak, with REDUCED base flow.**

**The mechanism** is a single change with two opposite-seeming consequences:

> **Paving reduces INFILTRATION.** More water runs off the surface **quickly**, and less soaks in to recharge the groundwater.

| Effect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Runoff coefficient C rises** — from ~0.2 to ~0.8 | **More total runoff volume** |
| **Time of concentration falls** — smooth surfaces and pipes carry water faster than soil and vegetation | **Earlier, sharper peak** |
| **Less infiltration** | **Less groundwater recharge → LOWER base flow** |
| Less interception and depression storage | Faster response |
| Channelisation and drains | Removes natural storage and attenuation |

**So the river becomes FLASHIER — worse floods AND worse dry-season low flows**, from the same cause. That double penalty is the central fact of urban hydrology, and it is why simply enlarging drains makes the downstream situation worse rather than better.

**Typical magnitudes**: full urbanisation can **double to quintuple** the peak discharge and **halve the time to peak** for the same storm.

**Land-use effects on the hydrograph:**

| Land use | Peak | Time to peak | Base flow |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Forest** | **Lowest** | **Latest** | **Highest** |
| Grassland | Low | Late | Good |
| Cultivated | Medium | Medium | Medium |
| **Urban, paved** | **Highest** | **Earliest** | **Lowest** |

**Why forest is so effective:**

| Mechanism | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Canopy INTERCEPTION** | Some rain never reaches the ground |
| **Litter layer** | Protects the soil surface from **raindrop sealing** |
| **Root channels and biological activity** | **Greatly increase infiltration** |
| Higher evapotranspiration | Drier soil before the storm, so more storage available |
| Surface roughness | Slows overland flow |

**The litter and root effects are the important ones**, and they explain why **removing forest is worse than the loss of canopy alone would suggest**: the soil structure itself degrades, the surface seals under raindrop impact, and infiltration capacity can fall by an order of magnitude within a few seasons.

**The same mechanism operates in reverse for compaction**: construction traffic, footpaths and grazing compact the soil and reduce infiltration even where vegetation remains — which is why a construction site sheds water almost like pavement.

**Managing urban runoff — the modern approach:**

| Traditional | Sustainable (SUDS / LID) |
|---|---|
| **Convey water away as FAST as possible** | **Detain, infiltrate and slow it down** |
| Pipes and channels | Ponds, swales, permeable paving, green roofs, soakaways |
| Solves the local problem | **Transfers** it downstream |
| — | Addresses volume **and** peak **and** recharge |

**Why the traditional approach fails at catchment scale:**

> Draining each development quickly simply **delivers its runoff downstream sooner**, and the peaks from successive developments **coincide** rather than being spread out. The downstream flood gets worse even though every individual drainage system "works".

**SUDS measures** and what each addresses:

| Measure | Addresses |
|---|---|
| **Detention / retention ponds** | **Peak** attenuation |
| **Permeable paving, soakaways, infiltration trenches** | **Volume and RECHARGE** |
| **Green roofs** | Volume and peak, at source |
| **Swales** and filter strips | Conveyance with treatment and infiltration |
| **Rainwater harvesting** | Volume, and provides a water supply |

**In the Kathmandu Valley** both ends of the problem are visible simultaneously: rapid urbanisation has increased flash flooding in the Bagmati and its tributaries, while **groundwater recharge has fallen** and the valley's aquifer is being depleted. **Recharge pits and permeable surfaces** address both at once — which is why they feature in the valley's drainage guidance, and why they are more valuable there than a purely flood-focused analysis would suggest.

**A note on scale**: these effects are most pronounced for **small and medium storms**. In an extreme event the soil saturates anyway, so the difference between a forested and an urban catchment narrows — which is why forest cover is excellent flood mitigation for frequent events and cannot be relied on for the design flood.

examTip.trick: One cause, two opposite-looking effects: **paving reduces infiltration**, so more water runs off faster (higher, earlier peak) and less reaches the groundwater (lower base flow).
examTip.mnemonic: **Worse floods AND worse dry-season flows, from the same cause.** That double penalty is why simply enlarging drains makes things worse downstream — it **transfers** the peak rather than reducing it. SUDS (soakaways, permeable paving, detention ponds) restore infiltration instead, addressing both ends at once.

questions.stem: Using Gumbel's distribution, the flood magnitude for a given return period is computed as:
options: X_T = X̄ + K σ, where K is a frequency factor depending on the return period
The mean divided by the return period
questions.solution:
**X_T = X̄ + K σ**, where **K** is a **frequency factor** depending on the return period and the sample size.

**This general form — Chow's equation — applies to EVERY frequency distribution**; only the expression for K changes:

| Distribution | K depends on |
|---|---|
| **Gumbel (EV1)** | Return period **T** and sample size **N** |
| **Log-normal** | T and the **skew** of the logarithms |
| **Log-Pearson III** | T and the **skew coefficient** |
| Normal | T only |

**For GUMBEL:**

> **K = (y_T − ȳ_n)/S_n**
> **y_T = −ln[ln(T/(T − 1))]** — the **reduced variate**

where **ȳ_n** and **S_n** are the **reduced mean** and **reduced standard deviation**, tabulated against the sample size N (approaching 0.577 and 1.283 as N → ∞).

**Reduced variate values** worth recognising:

| T (years) | y_T |
|---|---|
| 2 | 0.367 |
| 5 | 1.500 |
| 10 | 2.250 |
| **50** | **3.902** |
| **100** | **4.600** |
| 1000 | 6.907 |

**Gumbel paper** is the practical tool: plotting the reduced variate on a linear scale makes a Gumbel distribution appear as a **straight line**, so the fit can be judged by eye and extrapolated graphically.

**Plotting positions** for the observed data, ranked m = 1 (largest) to N:

| Formula | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Weibull** | **P = m/(N + 1)**, so **T = (N + 1)/m** — the standard |
| Gringorten | P = (m − 0.44)/(N + 0.12) — preferred for Gumbel |
| Hazen | P = (2m − 1)/2N |

**The procedure:**

1. Extract the **annual maximum** series.
2. Compute the **mean X̄** and **standard deviation σ**.
3. Look up **ȳ_n** and **S_n** for the sample size N.
4. Compute **y_T**, then **K**, then **X_T**.
5. Plot the observed data at their plotting positions and compare with the fitted line.

**Step 5 is not optional**: plotting the data against the fit is what reveals whether the distribution is appropriate at all, and it is routinely skipped.

**The fundamental limitation, which must be stated plainly:**

> Estimating the **100-year flood from a 30-year record** is a substantial extrapolation. Estimating the **1000-year flood** from it is little better than speculation.

**Confidence intervals widen dramatically** beyond about **twice the record length** — and they are rarely quoted, which lends the results a false air of precision. A 100-year flood estimated from 30 years of data may have a 95% confidence interval spanning a factor of two.

**Other issues in flood frequency analysis:**

| Issue | Note |
|---|---|
| **OUTLIERS** | A single exceptional flood can dominate the fit; tests exist for high and low outliers |
| **Non-stationarity** | Land use change and climate change violate the assumption that the record represents the future |
| **Mixed populations** | Rainfall floods, snowmelt floods and **GLOFs** are **different populations** and should not be pooled |
| **Regional analysis** | Pooling records from **hydrologically similar** catchments effectively lengthens the record — the best remedy for short series |
| Historical floods | Documentary evidence of pre-record floods can be incorporated and is very valuable |

**Regional (index flood) analysis is the most useful of these remedies** for Nepal, where individual records are short: catchments in a homogeneous region are assumed to share a **dimensionless growth curve**, scaled by each catchment's **index flood** (usually the mean annual flood). Pooling perhaps twenty 25-year records gives a far better estimate of the tail than any one of them alone.

**The mixed-population point is particularly important in the Himalaya:**

> A **GLOF** is not a rainfall flood. It arises from **moraine dam failure**, has a different magnitude distribution and a different physical cause, and including one in an annual-maximum series **corrupts the fit**. GLOF hazard must be assessed **separately**, as a distinct failure mode, not as an outlier in a rainfall flood series.

**And the non-stationarity point** is now unavoidable: the assumption that the past record represents the future — the foundation of the whole method — is weakening as land use and climate shift. Current practice is to check for trend before fitting, and to treat the resulting estimates as **one input to a risk judgement** rather than as a number to be designed to without further thought.

examTip.trick: **X_T = X̄ + Kσ** is Chow's general form and works for **every** distribution — only the expression for K changes. For Gumbel, K comes from the reduced variate and the sample size.
examTip.mnemonic: **Extrapolating a 30-year record to the 100-year flood is already a stretch; to the 1000-year it is speculation.** Confidence intervals widen sharply beyond about twice the record length and are rarely quoted. Two further cautions: **GLOFs are a different population** and must not be pooled with rainfall floods, and **regional (index-flood) analysis** is the best remedy for short records.
